"NOTHING," once said an old gentleman to us, "so much indicates the nature of a man's taste, as gn style of the pictures which decorate the walls of hie dwelling."—" But," we inquired, "suppose he has no piatures ?"—" Then he has no taste I" quickly responded the sage. A Ir; Lr.ow stole a saw, and on trial told the judge he only took it in a juke. "How far did you carry it ?" asked the judge. "Two miles," answered the prisoner. "hint's carrying the juke too far," remarked the judge, and the prisoner was com- mitted for further examination. How TO GET AN ENEMY.—Lend a man a mmailt gam of money for a day. Call upon him in a week for it. Wait two months. In three months insist upon his paying you. He will get angry, denounce and speak of you in abusive terms. We have seen this experiment tried repeatedly, and never knew it to fail. W lIEN the brave Corporal Caithness was asked, after the battle of Waterloo, if he was not afraid, he replied, "Afraid l—why, I was in all the battles of the Peninsula l" and having explained that the question merely related to a fear of losing the day, he said, "Na, us; I did na fear that, I was only afraid we should be all killed before we had time to win it." A FOEWARD CITXT.D. The other day OHO of widow B. 's admirers was complaining before her of the toothache. Mrs. B.'s smart boy immediately spoke. " Well, sir, why don't you do as ma does? She takes her teeth out and puts 'ern back when- ever she wants to." A few minutes afterwards the boy was whipped on some pretence or other. Two Snanrs.—An old man picked up half-a- crown in the street. "Old man, that's mine," said a keen-looking rascal, "so hand it over."— "Din yours have a hole in it'!" asked the old man.—" Yes," replied the other, smartly.—" Then it is not thine," mildly replied the old man; "thee must learn to be a little sharper next time, my boy." _ _

One of the latest progressive "pan, gained by *Omen has been the willing surrender on the part of Cardiff ministers of their pulpits to the lady speakers, who gave addresses in 20 places of wor- ship during the late conference. Some of the brat women in heart and general capacity are coming info the ranks of the British Women's Temperance Asaticiation,and it is a sign of progress when tem per- ante women Meet to discuss how they can best help on through eYery allied reform, the urgent one of sobriety, health, and commercial prosperity for the peaple. Lady Henry Somerset sailed for America accompanied by 'Miss Alp Pearsall -Smith, on Satur_ day in the SS. Paris from Southampton, where sh is going to meet her son in Coicago on his return from a bunting expedition in British Columbia. She will also attend the World's Pair Educational Convention of the Woman's Temperance Union to be held in Chicago October 16 and successive days.

People who are interested in the famous Tich- borne trial will remember the name of Jean Lute one of the most important witnesses on the claim- ant's side. He has just turned up in one of the Sydney courts as plaintiff seeking damages for malicious prosecution. He is now a debt collector, and seventy-four years of age. The judge; Sir J. G. limes, sent to the library for an illustrated record of the Tichborne trial, and when the book was brought Luie was shown his portrait and asked wasit agobd one, whereupon he replied that it was a very fair representation of his appearance when in London a quarter of a century ago at the celebrated trial. Luie, en being interviewed, said he continued to strongly adhere to the statement he made on oath in London, that he was steward of the Osprey at the time she picked up the survivors of the Bella, one of whom was Sir Roger Tichborne, who in his opinion was identical with the Claimant. Luie declares that "the last has not yet been heard of the Tichborue case." We hone it has.

" How many rods make a furlong?" asked a father of his son, a " fast " urchin, as he came home one night from the town school. "Well, I don't know, boss," was the reply of the young hopeful, "but I guess you'd think one rod made an acher if you got such a tanning as I did from old vinegar-face this afternoon." The parents aghast. A POETICAL auctioneer, well known in the county of Durham for his literary powers, concluded an announcement of a furniture sale with the follow- ing sublime comparison :—" And a host of domestio appreciables, in some degree countless as the glittering jewels which bestrid the lacleal turn- pike of the blue ethereal." "Din you say, sir, that you considered Mr. . Smith insane ?" asked lawyer of a witness in a criminal case.—" Yes, sir, I did."—" Upon what grounds did you base that inference?"—" Why, I lent him a silk umbrella and five shillings in money, and he returned them both—and a man who acts so strangely as that, I think must be crazy."

Father Ignatius is rather out of his element,at a Church Zongress. He happened at Birmingham.lo Mention the name of Christ, and this allusion very much startled the audience. They are not accus- tomed to it. The Her. Joseph Lyne is more fitted for masquerading in the mummery of medieval monasticism down at Llanthciny than in attending niodern cmiventione. There he can have visions aild dream dreams which the. sceptic scoffs at and the believer derides. Some years ago he alleged that the Virgin Mary appeared to him on the moun- tain side. I understand now that he keeps a Kodak in readiness in order to take a snap shot at t:-e next heavenly visitor, and by means of the negative con- vince the world with evidence of these apparitions. Perhaps it is not strange that Father Ignatius's bro- ther was connected with the stage. He wrote .seve- ral plays. Plainly the family has a dramatic tem- perament.

A QUAKMA giving evidence on a trial, was asked by one of the magistrates, who had been a carpenter, why he would not take off his hat?—"lt is a privilege we as cinakers are allowed."—" If I had it in my power," said the angry justice, "I would have it nailed to your head.' , —" I thought," returned Obadiah, "thou hadst given over the trade of driving nails." ' "A DOZEN children may seem a large family with some folks, who are moderate," remarked Mrs. Fastington, "but my poor husband used to tell a etory of a woman in some part of the world, where he stopped one night, who had nineteen children in five years, or five children in nineteen years, I don't recollect which—but I remember it was one or t'other."

The death of Mr. Edward Hughes, J.P., of Belfast; removes from Ulster politics a most striking figure. He was one of the leading Nationalists of the city— indeed of the province; and being a man of great wealth and social position, he was a tower of strength to his fellow-Nationalists and fellow- Catholics. His munificence was unbounded, and his name appeared in every subscription list in connec- t ion with the national movement. He was on of the trustees of the Irish National Fund, and when the differences arose between Mr. Dillon and Mr. Healy in connection with the " Freeman's Journal" he was unanimously chosen as one of the board of arbitrators.

Mr. Hughes was a miller by trade, and his baker- ies and flour mills are probably the largest in Ireland if not in Great Britain. He was repeatedly pressed , to enter Parliament for Irish constituencies, but 'being a very retiring and unassuming man, he could never be induced to do so. His loss will be keenly flat by myriads of.admirers, for his devotion to his country and Kis religion, even though it entailed,as it (lid, no small business penalties in the citadel oi Orangeism, commanded the respect even of his opponents. •

By the way, Lord Allied Paget was one of the ioroprietora of the Cannock Chase collieries, where at the present time so much destitution prevails. Lord Alfred was a son of the Waterloo Marquis of ' Anglesea,and was one of the first of aristocratic , ematettros to drive the engines of express trains. As a direc•or of the L. & N.W.R. and other railways he had opportunities for indulging in his hobby which would have been denied to other men, He has been known to drive Her Majesty. The late Duke of Sutherland was another nobleman who had a pen- chant for turning engine driver. When the London And North-Western Railway laid down the troughs by which water is picked up at full speed,the Duke and Lord Alfred were on the experimental engine. Owing to some defect in the mechanism the water, in.tead of rushing into the tank, flooded the tender and the platform, and it was with difficulty that the two prevented themselves from being swept off. %.,'lkati:e K 7-31 •C'il --, E,...

UNSOPHISTICATED ELOQUENCE. A country- woman WAS carrying on a very simple process against a neighbour in one of the mail courts of Germany. The attorney of the opponent pestered her with so much of chicanery and legal subtleties that she lost ell patience, and interrupted him thus s— "My lord, the ems° is simply this: I bespoke to my opponent, the carpet-maker, a car- pet, with figures which were to be as handsome as my lord the judge, and he wants now to force me to take one with horrible caricatures, uglier even than his attorney. Was I not right in breaking off the bargain?" The court laughed at the com- parison, the attorney was stupefied, and the woman won her suit. PADDY'S EXPEDIENT FOR REDUCING A FINE.— An Irish weaver just. imported hem tile sister tdie, took to his employer in Kilmarnock, the other day, the first cloth he had woven since his arrival.

, His employer detected in the cloth two boles, within half an inch of each other, mid told him he must pay: a fine of a shilling for each hole. "And plaze ye, ' returned Pat, "j 5 it by the number of holes, or by the size of them that ye put the tine on us ?"—" By the number of holes, to be sure." —"And a big hole and a small one is the same price?"—" Yes, a shilling for every hole, big or little "—"Then give me a houtd of the piece," replied Paddy. Getting the cloth into his h.in ,s, he tore the two small holes into one, and exclaimed. "By the Hill of Howth I and that saves me ons shilling, any 1"

At Warrington Police Court on Mrinday,Wm.Wright,2, rdy-st.,Patrick Burke, 13, Rose Yard,Win.Bottomley, D'al-st.,were each charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in the Market Place on Sept. 30.—P.C. Hollings- Worth said that prisoners Burke and Wright were fish hawkers, and Bottomley was also with them. They were selling fish in the market on Saturday night and making a great noise by shouting. They were also very drunk. Witness warned them to stop their disorderly behaviour. Wright upon this became somewhat quieter, but the wier two became more noisy, and witness took their oames and addresses and summoned thecs.—Mr. M inks asked if it was against the market regulations to shout.— The Chief Constable said he never saw such shouting in a market in his life as in the Warrington market, although shouting was against a bye-law of the Corporation. He %Tendered that the market inspector did not enforce it. fie himself had given up trying to do so.—The magis- trates hoped that the market inspector would enforce the bye•law, , and fined Burke and Bottcmley -ss. and Wright 2s. 6d.

Rtitle.ge Chester acknowledged the introduction to the two ix:lollies by a low bow. Ho was a little vewildered. He ha.i never before seen two such young girls. lie ilimght the golden•haired fairy the swestest and fairest., yet the dark, glowing, tropical beauty of the girl who stood by her sine dazzled Lim. ".What do ' yon think •of the senator's son, Verlie?" cried Uldene, breathlessly, when the two girls found themselves alone. "Is he not grand? No other word would suit him. Do you like him i" Verlie turned aside quickly, but not before Uldeic had seen a vivid flush pass over her face; and that did not quite please her. "Ho is very agreeable," said Verlie. "I can better answer the Tiestion if I like 'him when I have known him longer and better." ":What a strange, cold nature yours is, Verlie," cried Uldene, impatiently. "I always make up my mind the first instant I meet persons, whether I am to like them or hate them." "Eirst impressions are not always correct ones," sei4 Verlie.

Tho two girls brought with them an atmosphere of youth and gaiety to Senator Chester's stately home. No day passed without some amusement. Grand dinner parties were given in their honour, to wnich the elite of the city were invited, balls were given, sleighing parties were formed, and pArties to concert and theatre.

4 And in all these festivities it so happened that Rutledge Chester was always the escort of both his mother's lovtly guests. This did not please Uldene. Secretly she was wishing, from the depths of her heart, that Verne had remained at home.

Two months rolled by on golden wings—months that were destined never to he forgotten by both Verlie and Uldeue—and at the end of that time strangers began to see what the stately senator and his wife never dreamed of—that both of their beautiful guests loved their handsome son. But it was quite impossible to decide which—if ,cither—would he Rutledge Chester's choice. He seemed to have a kindly liking for beautiful !Thiene. He laughed with her, talked to her, hung over the piano when she sung tender, vent love ballads, enjoyed her satire, admired her constant animation, for it was impossihle to led t dull where this beautiful, brilliant beauty was ; but it was uncertain whether he loved her.

Alany thought that he preferred the pure and ntle girl whose face was like a sunbeam, and whose voice wAs like music. He talked less to Vet lie ; but there was quite another expression on t,is face when he addressed her—one of the deepest :everence.
Verlie Sefton, often sitting in the solitude of her owu room, would allow her thoughts to drift dreamily back over the two months she had passed in the senator's home.

Whether Rutledge Chester liked her or not, she could not say; but she cared for him more than 'or any one she had ever Been, yet she would have died a thousand deaths lather than that he should ,ticos her secret. The very consciousness that she 'lid care for him made her shy, cold, and reserved with him - so much so, that at times he ,0 ft her to seek refuge and amusement with gay Ijaleue.

And how was it with beautiful, passionate, faulty [Thiene ? It had been "love at firet sight" with her. Her heart had gone out to Rutledge Chester when first they met. She had said once, in speaking of t.c-self, that, with her love would be a tire, not a utiment. Now she was to know how true her words were.

With such ill-regulated natures as hers— Maperious, wilful, yet capable of the highest degree intense affection—love knows no moderation, no I,ounds, no medium. Loving Rutledge Chester, she had no thought ;cr any one else. Her ideas, her hopes all began md ended with him. Such natures as hers would !low little mercy to a rival, if fate chanced to place that rival in their power. Woe betide the •,,,rsou who might come between Uldene and the jtmt of her love. It was the restless torrent of love that destroys all obstacles, that brooks no opposition, that will not be stayed, that dashes impetuously on its way, reaching its limit, let the cost be what it might. A lire that destroyed all that opposed its progress, a tire that would consume and burn. Uldene had rightly named it. The knowledge of her love for him came to her suddenly, and was brought about in a strange way.

The horses had been brought around to the curb- ntone one morning for an early canter in the park. Mr. Chester and the two girls had set out in the gayest spirits. An hour in the park, in the keen, frosty air, had brought roses to the cheeks of both Verlie and (Jolene, and brightness to their eyes. It was just as they were about turning their horses' heads homeward that a startling event occurred. A squirrel darting across the path caused Verlie's horse to rear wildly, and before Rutledge Chester could reach out his hand to avert the horrible cat- astrophe, the animal had wheeled suddenly about and plunged down the path with the velocity of the wind, threatening to throw the white-faced girl who clung to him in such terror, at every mad plunge. The kid bridle had snapped asunder, and the lovely rider, who had lost all control of the animal, swayed to and fro in the saddle like a slender leaf in.. gale. The piercing cry that floated back made Rut- ledge Chester's heart almost cease to beat. He could see that it was only a question of a few brief seconds ere the terrified girl would be dashed from the saddle, meeting certain death by striking one of the trees that lined either side of the road.

It was a circular path, and Rutledge Chester knew that in A moment of time the horse would be abreast again of the spot where he was standing. In an instaat he had made up his mind what course to pursue. He would save sweet Verlie Sthon's life, or he would die in the attempt. Springing from his own horse he turned that and trighteued Uldene's into a horse, path, that they might be out of the way; but it was not done an instant too soon.

Around the circular path, on with the speed of the wind came the coal-black horse, and again a wild, piteous cry floated to Rutledge Chester's ears; and that cry nerved him for the terrible order,l that followed.

He saw that the maddened steed must pass with- in a yard of where he atood fairly rooted to the apot, and if he should swerve a single hair's breadth in his direction, the plunging iron hoofs would ernsh him.

With a white, determined face, he wound his left arm firmly around the trunk of a tree, and stood breathlessly waiting to grasp the broken, swaying bridle of the infuriated animal with his strong right arm as it dashed past him. Thu few seoonds that passed, as he awaited the terrible moment, seemed the length of eternity. All in a moment a strange truth burst upon him— lie loved beautiful, golden-haired Verlie. Bread And Dyspepsia. The conclusion that wheat bread is unfit for dyspep- tics, sometimes jumped at becatue ill-effects are noticed to follow its use, is erroneous. On the coatrary it has een pointed out by Bouchard and others, that farina- ceous t ood is peculiarly adapted to some dyspeptic patients It is the microbes in the starch, which is capable of pro- ducing irritating acids, that cause the trouble. To avoid this, Bouchard recommends that only the crust or toasted crumbs ot the bread be used by dyspeptics, par- ticularly those whose stomachs are Oilated. The reason of this is explained by the fact that baking temporarkly, though not permanently, arrests the fermentation of dough. When it is again heated by the warmth of the stomach the fermentation is renewed. In cases were the bread is toasted brown through, the fermentation is stepped permanently.—" Food."

div.head: SHOOTING MATCH AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SHOOTING MATCH AT RUNCORN.

• A friendly match between the F and G Companies (Runcorn) of the 2nd Vol. Batt. Cheshire Regiment took place at Runcorn Heath, on Saturday. On account of the lateness of the season only eight men on either side took part. The weather was fine with no wind, and a bright light at the start, but speedily changed to a miserably wet afterßoon, with a gusty fishtail wind and a very poor light, which completely spoiled the prospect of good scoring. The conditions were as at Bislev—seven rounds each at 200, 500 and 600 yards. The result showed a victory for G Company by 37 points At the close the teams adjourned to the Drill H4ll, and partook of a welcome " hot-pot;" for which three or four hours on the Heath had given them a splendid appetite. They end reached theentrance to the conserva- tory, and there Rutledge Chester (for the plumed) knight was he) stopped with his fair partner at the. entrance. "Come with me and I will find you a flower- ier more suitable to the character you represent,. than the magnolia you are wearing. With a throbbing heart, Utdene permitted him: to lead her into the cool, green rose bower, dim with shadowy lights from the emerald swinging globes, and odorous with the breath of exotics. He found her a seat beneath a blossoming almond tree, close by the tinted, pet fumed fountain. Close by her an orange tree was in full bloom. Rutledge Chester detached a single blossom and banded it to her. Thie is the flower I would choose for you," he said, his. deep vice hu ky with emotion. "Happy would be the man in whose honour you would wear a crown of them.' " Verne," he cried, "forgive me. I know you ; I recogitized you in the corridor at home to-night. I know this is not the time or place to speak, but the words burn from my heart to my lips. I love you, little Verlie—love you with all my heart. I am not gifted like some men to utter elognent words at such a moment; my heart is too full for utterance. Could you ever love me, little Verlie—love me well enough to become my bride? "I realise that I have been abrupt; I have startled you. Ido not ask for your answer now; you shall have time to consider it. I ask but one favour, deer ,• be kind and grant it, You see I have gathered two flowers—a pure white- rose and a deep blood-red one. "If you mean to give me encourasement, wear this white rose on your breast at the time of unmasking. If you mean to discourage my inten- tions—to convey to ins in silence that we can never be snore to mica other than we are—let the red rose be the sorry signal of it. Wel you consent to this, Verne darlirg ?'' The trembling figure bowed her head in assent. " I an: bewildered ; leave me here to myself for a little while—to think," she murmured. Rutledge Caoster looked at her in wonder. The voice that spoke to him seemed like nothing human. He bowed low over the little hand in which he had placed the roses—turned and walked witty away. Slowly Uldene rose to her feet—she stood per- fectly ; the same shock would have killed some girls. She clenched her hands so tig,ntly that the thorns from the roses she held pierced her soft hands, but she never felt the pain. Heaven and earth seemed whirling around her. Death would have been a relief to the terrible agony of that moment; but the rest and silence of death were not for her. She stood so for what seemed to her an eternity'; it wee but is f.ew moments. Trent the reaction catne. With swift feet she hurried to to the further cud of the vast conservatory and flung herself, face downward, among time gorgeous blooms. It was a pitiful sight upon which the moon- light, slanting in from the windows, fell—a pine' trate figure in a white, gleaming dress and bridal veil, anti a white face, drenched with tears, upturned to the pale, silvery light. No human beings were near, or they might have been startled by the peesionate cries of a broken heart, crie.s that fell freely and clearly on the soft, sweet air—bitter, passionate sobs, that took with them the burden of at: unhappy soul. It had been her one prayer, her one ambition, to win Rutledge Chester's love. That lore Would have crowned her life, and now it was all over ; her wondrous beauty, her genius. her brilliancy, had all been powerless to win the noble heart that had been laid at timid, golden-haired Vcrlie's feet. Tears of mortification rained down her cheeks. . It was not only that the hope and treasure of her life were wrecked, but she was humiliated. S° had loved in vain, and her haughty, passionate nature writhed at the thought. Without an effort, Verlie had won the prize for which she would freely have given her life. "It shall not be l" she cried, wildly. "I c3nne6. bear it ! I could sooner die l" It was well that the swell of music and the patter of dancing feet drowned her bitter cries. Uldene lay sobbing on the ground whore she btu flung herself in the frenzy of her grief. / Slowly the moments dragged their slow lengths by. What strange thought had come to her in the green, leafy solitude? What strange, bewilderiite idea? For suddenly she raised her white hanhis: and sprang to her feet with a shudder Auden awl,"

Uldene turned toward the window again with an Impatient gesture. " You talk like a child, Verlie," she cried. "Of sourse I cared whether you lived or died. When you spoke to me so suddenly I W D.B thinking of quite another matter—whether or no you would be bl e to attend the mask ball at Mrs. ‘Varrington's to morrow night. For, of course, if you were too ill to go, I would st•Ay at home too."

"You shall make no such sacrifice for me, Uldene, exclaimed Verlie, throwing her arms around her sister's neck and affectionately and eagerly kisAing lildene's beautiful false face Of course we shall go to the grand mask ball. I wouldn't miss it for worlds. I am not 111, you know. I am not even hurt; only shook upend frightened. I shall be all right by to-morrow.' A tap at the door interrupted their conversation. It was Mrs. Chester.

" What! up arid around so soon, dear?" she exclaimed, pleasantly. " Rutledge will be delighted to hear such a pleasant account of you." "I was more frightened than hurt, Mn. Chester," replied Verlie, with a blush : adding, falteringly You must thank your son for me, for his timely assistance ; but for him I should have met a far worse fate."

"Yon must keep your room for a day or two," retutned the lady, kindly, "even though you forego the festivities of to-morrow night." "Indeed, I am not as weak as you imagine, Mrs. Chester," exclaimed Verlie, gayly. " Why, I wouldn't think of missing the mask ball, not for world a."
"As you please, my dear," responded Mrs. Chester, smiling. "Of course, young girls will be your g girls. I have often known them to plead to get out of a sick-bed to attend such gala affairs."

"But you know I am, not ill," persisted Verlie, lifting her blue eyes coyly. 'lnc grand raAsk ball which was to be given in a neighbouring mansion had been a much antici- pated event to both Verlie and Uldene, it being the lire, of its kind which either had been invited to attend.

The costumes had taken fully a month's planning; they were marve!s in their way. Uldeue was to take the character of the beautiful, fatal, irresistible Helen of Troy, whose smile was more dangerous than a draught of poisoned wine, and .whome wurdrous dark eyes led ine,n on to their doom.

Her dress was to be cloth of gold, draped with crimson tulle, caught up here and there with clusters of blood-red passion roses; crimson i.sdin slippers were to inclose her tiny feet; glowing criolbon rubies were to encircle her white throat and her bare, rounded arms. Her dark, curling hair was to be completely concealed behind a golden veil, and a golden mask to, cover her dark, lovely face—all sAve the red lips and dimpled chin.

Verne was to be a fairy bride. A fierce pang of envy shot through Uldene's heart as she saw her golden-haired sister standing, dressed and ready, before the long i'rencli mirror in their boudoir the next evening. It was in ieed a beautiful picture the gilded mirror reflected—a lovely slender, girlish figure, draped in shimmering white satin that fell in graceful folds to her slender ankles ; white kid gloves, extending to the elbow, set oil the pearly pinkness of the lovely rounded arm above it, and white kid slippers that Cinderella herself might have worn, they were so exquisitely tam and dainty, peeped coyly out from beneath the shim- mering silver skirts. " All I need is a magnolia blossom to make the costume complete," laughed Verne. " You can get one in the conservatory," remarked Uldene, indiderently. "Ring for one of the ser- vants to fetch you one." "I will go myself," declared Vcrlie, darting from the boudoir, tossing her white silk mask into Ul- dene's lap as she ps.s.?ed her. But in less than s moment she came fluttering back, her cheeks all aglow with xciteinent. "Oh, Uldeue ! I had such a narrow escape ! "she panted. "I had no sooner reached the corridor vrhen the library door was suddenly opened and Rutledge Chester came hurriedly out. I slipped behind a marble Yews., but I am not positive whether he saw me or not; but I think not, though. He passed on toward the conservatory; so I did not go there. Oh, dear! It would spoil half the fun to have any one recog- nise me before the time for unmasking came. Mr. Chester has not connnenced to arrange his toilet yet. Isn't it gettiog rather late ?"

cry. "Not that!" she murmured, hoarsely. "I am not wicked enough for that, though maddened by the. cruelest pangs of jealousy. Aye, Pan° more tatter than deu.tu to endure calmly." But after a time she grew silent. The passionate cries, the bitter sobs had died away. The idea Ilaa taken possession of her. Like a ghost she glided suddenly back to the ball-room, and sought out Verlie. "Let us change back into our own costumes again," she said. " You must be dressed in your own white dress qs the fairy bride when the bour for unmasking comes. It is better suited to yo". Do not demur, Verde. I—l—insist*" (To he continue(l.)
"I suppose so," returned Uldene. The senator is to accompany us there, and Rutledge is to bring us home. I believe that's the arrangement, isn't it?"

Verlie nodded. Ah ! there is the coach at the door now. Wrapped and hooded, they were SUOII whirling away toward the grand ball. " Weil, well," declared Seuator Chester leaning back in his seat, with a hearty laugh, " I shunt.: never be able to determine which was which. WONDERFUL OCCURRENCE AT TA.UNTON. (RESULT OF INQUIRY BY OUR REPORTER.) From the " Somerset County Gazette," Sept. 23, 1893. Rewbarton, a suburb of Taunton, has, during the last few years, grown at a tremendous pace. This portion of the town is, to a great extent, populated by people employed on the Great Western Railway, or at the New- ton Electrical Works. Among the streets at Ilowbar- ton is one named Willia.n-street, and in this street at No. 33, lived a Mrs. Lawley, wife of a fitter, employed at the NewennElectrical Works. Mrs. Lawley had been attacked with rhsumatism in May, and the malady stuck toter for three months to such an extent that it was painful even to see her walking or crawling about She tried several remedies, professed to be a sure and quick cure for rheumatism, but without avail. At length she was induced to try Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for (ale People, and was at once most miraculously cured. Having become aware of these facts, a "Somerset County Gazette" reporter interviewed Mrs. Lawley, and she most willingly told the story of t e wonderful cure which had been effected, inorder, as she put it, to benefit other people who might be suffering from the same dreadful and most painful disease. Mrs. Lawley, on the reporter knocking, was on the doorstep, awaiting admission, with a baby in her arms but our representative, although taking a good look at. her, never thought for a moment that the active won an whom he saw was she who a month ago was suffering' from rheumatism so acutely as to render her walking anout almost impossible_ Oa explaining who he was, our reporter was at once asked to go inside, where in. a cosy room, a chair was placed for him, and Mrs. Lawley told her story so well that very few questions were necessary. She is a comparatively young woman who looked as if it was a very long time since dho had a day's illness, but her story will show that for three months she must have endured most acute agony. She said she bad lived the greater part of her life atWel- verhampton but came to Taunton about eighteen month- ago. In May she became aware,of a swelling in one f her feet, accompanied by rheumatic pains, and gradually this became a great deal worse until she felt most awn:s- ing pains not only in her feet but in her legs and ,knees. She also felt some pain in her hands and arms, but this was not so acute. The pains continued for threemonths and gradually got worse. During the greater ,part ot that time she was unable to do anything in the house. She could not even find any rest in bed, and repeatedly got up during the night, lit the fire and sat 'before it. She could get no sleep, and her appetite was 'very bad. "The only thing that relieved me at all," she said, " was to put my feet in boiling hot water, and this gave me some relief, butthe pain soon came on again as bad as ever." After sitting dawn, she had some difficulty in walking whea she got up. Asked if she had been to a doctor or had tried any remedies to alleviate the pain, Mrs. Lawley said she had tried a number of remedies which were greatly advertised. It was the last time she went out that she went to a chemist's, and to use her own words she "could scarcely crawl home again." Her husband was reading in the paper one of the remarkable cures Dr. Williams' fink Pills had effected and he advised her to try them, but she said she had noSfaitls in them. However, she received a letter from a friend in Stafford- shire who had tried'Dr. Williams' Pink Fills, and who advised her to give them a trial, and her husband also again advised her to try a box. She did so, and tried them. She told the reporter : " I only took one box , before I was able to walk, and have been all right ever since. If felt anything of the kind coming on again I should soon fly to them. I have recommended the Pills to two or three friends already." TIM CORPORATION ACCOUNTS OF - WIDNES. At the Monthly meeting of Widnes Town Council on Tuesday. the professional auditor's report was presented by Messrs. Russell and Walmsley of Man- chester, auditors to the Corporation. The books and accountsexamined, exten led from Nov. 9th, 1892, to 25th March, 1893. The auditors state, " We have prepared a general balanee sheet of the actual assets and liabilities of the Corporation, which will be found attached to this report, and which shows a sur- plus of assets over liabilities of £36,782 6s. 11d. The range of our work has embraced every book of account. Every entry has been checked, and all the postings to and balances of the ledgers certified and extracted and compared with the abstract. We have also devoted carelul attention to the invoices, separately scrutinising every one to ascertain that the purchase has been ap- proved by the Committee, and the payment authorised audthat the amounts have been passed to their reTective accounts in the ledgers. The mortgage bonds have also had Our attention, and we have examined all the dis- charged bonds for loans repaid, all which have been can- celled, and all of which had the seals detached before coming into our hands ; we think, however, that it . would be better for the Committee or council to simply cancel the seal and allow it to remain attached, each to its own bond, for the auditors' satisfaction as to the " bona fides "of the bond. The amounts had and un- collecuel written off in the Gas and Water Funds are only part ally covered by the amounts authorised by the Committee, and we recommend that separate columns for empties, allowances, and extra discount should be provided in the rental books. In that the whole can be adjusted at balancing, and all the shrinkages sanctioned by each committee. The inventories of stocks and stores in hand, have also been examined and are duly certified by the responsible official of the department,but they lack evidence of having received the examination and approval of their respective Committees. The deeds of the Corporation have been produced to us, but in order to facilitate their inspection or reference by Coun- cil or auditors, we should recommend the keeping of a detailed register of deeds in duplicate, one kept by the Town Clerk, and one by the Accountapt, with every deed allocated or " earmarked" in its respective capital account in the ledger. The Sum of £19,863 ss. 6d. stands to the credit of the Gas Fund Profit and Loss and £7,744 13s. 6.1. to Water Fund Profit and Loss Accounts, representing, presum- ably, accumulation of profits earned since the purchase of the respective undertakings in 1867. After this lapse of time, the whole question of revaluation of these assets might be advisable, with a view to adjustment of these litige balances. We notice that the gas and water street mains arid services have not been depreciated in any way, the only depreciation charged against revenue being 5 pei:cent. off meters accounts. The question of

WARRINGTON

' 1761 to 1767, when he became minister of Mill Hill Chapel, Leeds. It is worthy of note that he came as classical tutor. It U'a,9 sub.equent to this period that he attained his scientific fame, though Warrington may justly have the credit of several of his scienti- fic experiments and of his history of electricity. Did time permit there are other names worthy of more roan passing reference. Dr. Reinhold Foster, the nat ,ral list, who acuompanied Captain Cook on his aecona voy- age: Gilbert Wakefield,the classical scholar ; Dr.Enfield, author of" The Speaker," who combined the offices of tutor of the Acadamy and minister of this congregation. Let me, however, close my biographical references with the names of two of the students, not that there are not others eminently worth mentioning, but these two have la special interest. The first is that of Dr. Bruce, who settled in Belfast, and, taking with him the free tradi- tions of Warrington across the channel, became the founder of the Liberal school among tho Ulster Presby- terians. To me it is not without inter at to remember that this old Warrington student preached at the ordina- tion of my grandfather by the Presbytery of Antrim in 1800. The other name is that of Dr. Barnes, of Cross-at. Chapel, Manchester. To him I shall have to allude again next week, for it was he who took the Warrington learn- ing to Manchester,and became first principal of the Man- chester Academy, which now exists with changed name and locality as Manchester College, Oxford. As War- rington had taken up the torch of the older Academies beginning with Frankland, so Manchester now received it from Warrington. The affairs of our local institution were finilly wound up in 1786, and what estate it stood possessed of, and best of all its ancient traditions of freedom, were handed on to Manchester Academy, that the old work might be continued under new conditions.

div.head: HEAVY WIDNES FAILURE. -- PUBLIC EXAMINATION OF THE DEBTOR.
div.p: THE HEAVY WIDNES FAILURE. -- PUBLIC EXAMINATION OF THE DEBTOR.

BORROWING AT 60 PER CENT. On Tuesday, at the Wrexham Bankruptcy Court, Major James Cross a civil engineer by profession, and at present residing at Llangollen again came up for his public examination. Mr. J. Hopley Pierce appeared for the Louden and Universal Bank, and Mr. Warren S. James. of London, for Captain Clency, manager receiver for the Lintchinson trus- tees. The statement of affairs showed gross liabili- ties amounting to £35,105 17s. 61., but of these only £10,591 10s. were expected to rank. The assets were put, down at .£77 56 7d, leaving a defi- ciency of £10,591 10s. The debtor was, from 1865, to aegust Bth, 1293,managi0g trustee to the Hutchinson estate, Whines, and from 1864 to 1868 he traded as a locomotive builder at St. Helens, under the style of Jas. Cross and Co. In the latter year he became insolvent, tne smaller creditors for the estate being paid in full,and the larger ones receiving 103. in the pound. The deb- tor's lire was insured for £9,000, but the policies were held as ,ecurity by Parr's Bank, Limited, and the Wid- nes and Diiton Land Co. The debtor was possessed of freehold and leasehold land at Widnes, but it had been taken possession of by the Liverpool Investment Society. The debtor alleged his failure to be due to his having be- come seceritc for a Mr. J. W. Weight, a London stock- broker, for £8,900. Major Cross said, in reference to his claim ae,ainst the Flutchinson estate, he believed the estates were worth £250,000 net. Be had only drawn one third of what he believed he was entitled to as a commission in connection with his management and development of the estates. Everything at Eirianfa. Llangollen, including the horses, carriages, furniture, plate, wine, &c., was sold to Mr. Richardson for ER/O.—By Mr. James : He claimed that there was £16,000 due to him from the Hutchinson estate. According to an account prepared by Mr. Price he had overdrawn his account in June last to the amount of £7,000; but taking the other certified accounts there was a balance in his favour of over £15,000. He had been drawing £l5 a week from the,estate since 1892, the sum agreed upon between Mr. Norwood and himself. He borrowed money from aMr. Nigel, of Great Marlborough-st , London, at 60 per cont. Re also borrowed money from others. In May, 1892, Mr. J. W. Weight, a London stockbroker, asked him to accept a bill far £5,040, and he did so. He knew that Weight was going to discount the bill, and that he was to receive £1,500 of the money. The money was ' obtained from the London and Universal Bank, and t Weight gave him £l,ooo—nt t £1,500. He afterwards gave Weight £5OO of the £l,OOO back again to lodge in the London and Universal Bank. The debtor wanted money at the time to pay to the Widnes and Ditton.Land Compativ, to whom he owed £3,700, in connection with an undertaking he had entered into to make certain ' reads. He was at one time a director of the Widnes and 'Ditton Land Company. In November 1892, he accepted another bill of £l,OOO, drawn by Weight. Be had none of that money. He also accepted another bill for £2OO. Weight promised him if he would accept these bills to purchase certain lands belonging to the debtor at Wid- nes, for £25,000, or get some of his friends to dos°. Weight got into difficulties and failed to fulfil his prom- ise. The land at Widnes was mortgaged to the Liverpool Investment and Building Society, and a Mr. Goriege. Ile had had na Stock Exchange transactions of any kind at any trine.—By the Registrar : Mr. Thompson, of Liverpool, valued bankrupt's land at Widnes at £21,000. The Official Receiver (Mr. Li. Hugh Jones) asked that the examination should be again adjourned, arid that the bankrupt should be ordered to furnish an account of his financial transantions with Jayvee W. Weight, the Widnes and Ditton Land Company, the London and Universal Bank, the Liverpool Investment and Building Society, the London Union Trust and Agency Company, , the Loan and Finance Corporation, the United Kingdom and Foreign Investment and Finance Company, Limited and several private persons. The examination was accordingly 'adjourned.

div.head: LIVERPOoL DIOCESAN SUNDAY SCHOOL INSTITUTE.
div.p: THE LIVERPOoL DIOCESAN SUNDAY SCHOOL INSTITUTE.

MEETING AT WARRINGTON. The quarterly meeting of the above institute was held at St. Paul's Schools on Monday night. There was a very good attendance of the local clergy and Sunday School teachers, and the following deputa- tion was also present representing the Liverpool Diocesan Institute, Bishop Royston D.D, Revs. Gil. Spooner, E. Snowden Smith, J. Denton Thompson (hon. secretary), G. B. Garrett, H. W. Baugh Verner, W. White &c., Messrs. W. Dott Goldstraw, Gardner,Suttbn, Brown Sec. The Hight Rev. Bishop Royston who occupied the chair expressed the pleasure of the Institute in visit- ing Warrington this quarter.—The Rev, J. Denton Thompson next spoke of the advantages to be derived by being in the Union after which the Rev. Morley Stevenson gave his paper on "The Sunday School of the future." He said that it was not more than a 100 years ago since the Sunday School system was instituted, The Sunday school of the past was very different from the Sunday school of the present. It was the object of the Sunday school 100 years ago to gather within its walls ragged and destitute children who played in the streets. The schools were after the lines of day schools. It was not only the object of the teachers to teach the truths of our holy religion, but also to teach them reading, writ- ing and arithmetic. The Sunday school of the past was partly secular,and partly religious. There has however a change come over the Sunday school. Twenty years ago Mr. Forster's Education Bill brought a great and wide change over the education of this country. Now every child was compelled to be taught such things as reading writing and arithmetic in the week day. It is therefore no longer necessary for the Sunday school to take up its time in doing what was better done during the other days of the week. The Sunday school of the present,he believed was divided into two clstses. He understood there were some people who regarded the Sunday school of to day as altogether a social matter, and that social questions should have the first place in it,but he thought that the Sunday schor I was the place in which the great truth of the gospel were systematically taught. (Ap- plause.) The teaching of religion was the first, second and whole thing. This was of great importance. There were numerous children in the day schools who received no religious instruction at all except the reading of a chapter each morning. In Birmingham there were 50,000 children who received no more religous instruc- tion than that. Re would now come te some of the deficiencies of the present Sunday schools. They wanted ,an alteration in the matter of room. At present the classes were close to each other and he maintained that discipline could not be kept under these conditions. The , teacher ought to stand while teaching as in day schools. They ought also to look after those who went nowhere as it was a mistake to believe that every child who went to the day school went to the Sunday school. The teachers also ought -to have a full knowledge of their subject, and devote much thought upon it,and sufficient use was not made of the blackboard which should be used as much as in day schools. As to the Sunday school of the future it was a mistake to believe that anybody and everybody would do for a teacher. Everybody would not make a clergyman, and the same applied to teachers. Rethought that the teacher ought to he on probation for a time, and then undergo some kind of examination, and be publicly initiated into his work. Also if possible a thoroughly experienced day school teacher should be engaged to have a free hand in superintending the school. He thought also that there should be more children's services, which might be held on the Sunday afternoon. There could also be inspectors appointed in day schools to examine the children in what they have learnt, and to encourage the teacher. Be believed that children were not afraid of examinations, but rather liked them, and for those who did well, prizes and certificates should be awarded.—After the rev, gentleman had finished his paper, Mr. Goldstraw opened the discussion, which a number of those present also joined in, and the meeting closed with the usual vote of thanks.

div.head: " RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE."
div.p: " RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE."
THE WARRINGTON PRACTISING SCHOOLS,

BOYS' DItPARTIIHNT.—The report of the Diocesan Inspector (he Rev. J. ralliblank) on the result of his examination of the above school in religious knowledge has been received. It is as follows :- -" What I have to say of this school may well be il summed up in a few words : it is emphatically a I strong school. All the members of the staff appear to have a clear understanding of the task before them and of the best means for its accomplishment. The results are mit irally of a very high degree of excellence. Know- ledge not of bare facts, but of the meaning ot the facts; intelligent interest in the facts and doctrines which are taught, and reverence which comes from feeling that these facts and doctrines have direct relation to life are 1 characteristics of the work d no by the boys under ex- amination. Of course certain of these characteristics are most to be noticed in the older boys, but the aim is very apparent even in the lowest classes. The written work throughout is unusually good; singing of hymns, and repetition of Collects,of Scriptures, and of Catechism are very god." Gums' DEPARTMENT.-4' The excellent discipline and the admirable tone which have distinguished this school are well maintained, and the year now at an end has :been one of good progress. What I should specially wish ! to recognise is the growth of firmness and definiteness. 1 When a question is put the girls, the elder ones more ! particularly, give a, definite answer as if they were sure

of their ground. I need hardly point out how such a manner of answering helps an exarniner to give a defi- nite verdict upon the week. Intelligence is cultivated, and the reasons for their answers which the children give show theught as well as good memories. Repetition is well learnt and said with good and reverent expresrion. The written work of Groups I. and 11. is good, that of Groups IlLand IV.is very good. The devout demeanour of the girls at prayers and the tuneful and reverent sing- ing of their hymns are especially worthy of notice." INFANTS' DEPARTMENT.—"The tone and discipline are all that can be drain d, and excellent work is done in all the groups. Hymns are very well sung,and bnth Scrio- tura and catechism are repeated clearly and accurately. In answering questions all the groups are above the average. The New Testament and Catechism (explana- tions) of Group I.are remarkably good. Group 11. does very good work Group 111. (babies) is unusually well t iught. The children show the results in the exceptional intelligence of their answers." PADGATE. The report of the Scripture examination in connection with Paclgate day schools held on the 13th September is as followt, :—" The order aud tone are excellent, and the results of the examination are full of promise. Written work shows a slight wfalcness which by, another year will doubtless be remedied. The infants' division has happily continued under the teacher formerly in charge. Her very steady work is rewarded by the intelligence and very praiseworthy knowledge shown by her children."

div.head: BLUSTIING.
div.p: BLUSTIING.
blushing

Of all expressions of emotion, Darwin says . seems to he the most strictly human. Breaches of CO ventional rules of conduct often cause more intense blushes than even a detected crime; and enact which is really criminal, if not blamed by our equals, hardly raises a tinge of colour on our cheeks. In "Romeo and Juliet," we read : Steal immortal blessings from her lips ; Who, In pure and vested modesty. Still blush, as thinking their own kisses sin. It is not the conscience that raises a blush • for a man, in solitude, sincerely regrets some slight fault, or suffers the deepest remorse for an undetected crime, but he will not blush. A man may feel thoroughly ashamed at having told a small falsehood, and not blush ; but if he even suspects that he is detected by one whom he re- veres, he will insantly blush. Blushing, instead of be- ing a criterion of guilt, is a certain sign of innocence. Thus, we are told in" Othello " : A maiden never bolt : 01 spirit so still and quiet that her motion Blushed at herself. Wick( d, unteeling, or impudent people never blush, yet nothing occasions deeper feelings of shame than being caught in the fact by the eyes of a whole company. How then is blushing caused,? The circulation of blood is greatly influenced by the nervous system. Almost all of us have experienced palpitation or jumping of the heart whenwe have been suddenly startled or frightened. The whole of the blood vessels and the hale are connected by nerves with the brain and spinal marrow. The small arteries throughout the whole body possess a muscular coat which bycontracting is able to diminish the capacity of the arterial tube. Now, connected with the muscular tube of each artery are numerous nerves whose duty it is to regulate the calibre of these vessels, the result being that the nervous system is able to control the circulation of the blood in various parts. An emotion, sometimes painful, sometimes pleasureable, takes possession of the mind. Thereupon a hot flush is felt, the skin of the face grows red. The face grows hot and red, because the blood vessels contain an increased quantity of the red and hot fluid. Its vessels contain this increased Quantity of blood because the small arteries suddenly dilate ; the contractile power of the arteries being lost for a time owing to the nerves, which control the con- traction, time, affected by a mental emotion. Shake- spear's remarks on the point in question may be appro- priately quoted from the" Taming ot the Shrew" : If she be made of white and red, Her faults will ne'er be known : For bin hing cheeks by faults are bred, And fears by pie wlsite shown; Then it she fen' or be to blame, By this you shall not know : For still her cheeks possess the wane, Which nature she doth owe. And, again, in " Much Ado About Nothing' : Comes not OA blood as modest evidence To witness simple virtue? ,

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELEC-PION AT WIDNES.
div.p: MUNICIPAL ELEC-PION AT WIDNES.

The second municipal election of Widnes bids fair to be of a highly interesting character, if lacking some of the excitement which prevailed on the oc- casion of the firNt contest twelve months ago. The retiring Councillors are : Farnworth Ward, Mr. T. Shuttleworth ; Halton Ward, Mr. Fred Neil ; Simms Cross Ward, Mr. Samuel Owens; Victoria Ward, Mr. B. Singleton; Waterloo Ward, Mr. Thomas Carney; West Bank Ward, Mr. William Hodgkinson. In three. of these wards contests are assured. Mr. Owen is to be opposed by Mr. A. G. Lowry, secre- tary to the local Trades Council, by whom he is nominated, and in Victoria Ward, the tetiring Councillor will be opposed by Mr. Michael Mannion the nominee of the Irish National League; and Mr. Richard Tebhutt, an independent candidate. A labour candidate in the person of Mr. Fred Hart- land, a well known working man antagonises Mr. Carney in Waterloo Ward, and it is said to be highly probable that Mr. E. Gossage will seek the suffrages of West Bank in opposition to tho sitting member.

IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. A largely attended meeting of the Widnes (T. P. O'Connor) Branch, Irish National League, was held in the Committee-rooms, St. Paul's Chambers, Victoria- read, on Sunday last the Bth inst., Councillor H. O'Donnell, president, in the chair. Amongst others pre- sent were Councillor J. Gough, Messrs. P. J. King (St. Helens), J. Finnegan (Ditton), J. Kenny, 'F. E. Delaney, M'Cann, J. Campbell, J. Rowe, J. 11113ricle,J.Iagan, J. Batterton, T. Lock, J. Farrall, D. Carroll, M. Mannion, T. Loftus, P.lloran (secretary), etc. After the minutes of the previous meeting being read and passed and two new members enrolled, a lengthened discussion on the Nov- ember Municipal election took place, in which several members took part, after which, on the motion of Mr. T. Loftus, seconded by Mr. P. M'Cann, Mr. Michael Mannion, Kent•street, was unanimously adopted as the Nationalist candidate to contest Victoria Ward. The following resolution, proposed by Mr. D. Carroll, and seconded by Mr. J. Campbell, was also unanimously passed :—That we the members of the Widnes Branch Irish National League here present, pledge ourselves to give our utmost support to the candidature of Mr. Mannion for Victoria Ward, and to use every legitimate means in our power td secure his return at the head of the poll." " Alter some discussion on the state and requirements of the town and as to who should see to them. tha following resolution was agreed to :—That on the Sunday preceding each monthly Town Council meeting a portion of the League meeting be set apart for hearing and discussing ideas and suggestions from any member of the Branch regarding the sanitary state of the town and improvements thereon and other matters relating to the town." After a working Committee had been formed for Mr. Mannion's candidature, a vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meeting to a close.

There is no incident in a mother's life more deeply moving than whek she is alone for the last time with her daughter, shortly to become a wife, the training of whom for a useful happy life has been her constant care. There stands the young bride, full of hope and confidence in the future, scarcely giving a thought to the happy home she is leaving, and scarcel- asking herself whether she will be equally happy in the,home she is seekit .for herself. In a few Minutes the carriage will bear her away, and she will have passed from her mother's care to that of the man to whom she is confiding her whole future happiness. In these few minutes of waitin; the mother lives again the years that have flown past since her daughtek was a wee toddling babe, and asks herself if she could possibly have done more than she has done .to secure her daughter's happiness. At such time the mother finds the deepest satisfaction in knowing that whilst• hek daughter is fully accomplished for the ball-room, and for all the social duties of life, she is equally accomplished, and equally well trained in all the details of household management. These things are not trifles, as some would suppose; the happiness of a household depends on_cleanliness and comfort; with these the cottage is a HOME; without them the palace is a wilderness. div.head: T 144 OLD
div.p: T 144 OLD

On Sunday evening the Rev. W. H. Drummond, preaching at Cairo-street Chapel, Wal rington, took for the subject of his discourse " The W arrington Academy : A cluipta from the religious history of the past." The words of the text were, "Look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit where ye are digged." In the bourse of his sermon he wondered how many people who signed their roll of membership realised into what a noble fellowship they were privileged to enter, noble in its lone fidelity to the cause of freedom and truth. How many people, when they saw their Chapel described by its historical name, the Presbyterian Chapel in Warrington, as was still done in the Register of Marriages, were moved by a more than momentary curiosity, and found in the now almost discarded title,the link which bound them in the Olosest way to the great religious traditions of the first days of Nonconformity ? " Robert Yates, rector of Warrington, 1672-78." There it stood at the top of the list of those who bad ministered to that congregation. 4 gave the keynote of their history. It told them that the love of truth and freedom was the chapter of their Common life. In a diary kept by Henry Newcombe, the I first minister of Cross-street Chapel, Manchester, was he following entry, under the date of January 10, 1663: re" Mr. Yates and several good people in Warrington carried to prison yesterday." That indicated the stuff I of which the founders of their religious fellowship were I made. In 1672, during a time of temporary indulgence, license was issued (the original was in the vestry). to !is allow a roome or roomes in the Court House of War- rington, in our County of Lancaster, to be a place for the the use of such as do not conform to the Church of England, who are of the persuasion commonly called Presbyterian to meet and assemble in, in order to their publick worship and devotion." That permission was soon withdrawn, and further persecution followed. The middle of the last century was a critical period for Nonconformist education. Several academies were given up on account of the death at their teachers. Dr. Doddridge, of Northamp- ton, died in 1750; Dr. Rotheram, of Sendai, whose academy stood in lineal succession to that of Frankland, in 1751; Dr. Latham, of Derby, in 1754. The outlook, especially for the old Dissenting congregations of Lan- cashire and Cheshire, became serious. It was clear something must be done to put the higher Nonconform- ist education on a more prominent basis. The man who ' came forward with a scheme was John Seddon, War- rington. He had been trained in Rotheram's Academy at Kendal, and he may accordingly be considered as linking the Warrington foundation with those that had gone before. Mr. Seddon was ordained here in 1747. He was, I should gather from thenotices that have come down to us, a somewhat self-important man' and per- haps of no great parts as a preacher. But he did a use- ful work, for which we must do all honour to his memory. He was the real founder of our Academy, and remained its energetic secretary till his death in 1770. Ele succeeded in interesting wealthy men in Liverpool, Manchester, Birming- ham, and other towns in his scheme for an institu- tion, with the twofold object of providing adequate education for students for the ministry, who should be " free to follow the dictates of their own judgments in their inquiries after truth, without any undue bias imposed on their understandings,"and likewise of giving '" some knowledge to those who were to be engaged in I commercial life, as well as in the learned professions, in ! the more useful branches of literature, and to lead them to an early acquaintance with, and just cone rn for the true principles of religion and liberty, of which principles they must in future life be the supporters," I There was a brief skirmish between Liverpool and Man- chester on the subject of locality. Liverpool evidently I thinking that the choice of Warrington was favouring the Manchester interests, and putting forth arguments why Ormskirk should be selected instead. But in the end Manchester—or shall we not rather say John Seddon? —had his own way, and in 1757 the Warrington Academy opened its career with two tutors and three students. It is difficult for the modern inhabitant of Warrington to go back to the time when one of the new tutors received the following instruction from Mr. Seddon for his journey : "You will do well to come prepared for riding, for you will not meet with any carriages at Stockport, nor are the roads to Warrington from thence proper for them:" It is perhaps not less hard to picture "a range of buildings at the north- , west end of the bridge, to which was attached a considerable extent of garden ground, and a handsome terrace-walk on the banks of then Mersey ; possessing altogether a respectable collegiate appearance," which was the home of the Academy for I ten years. In 1767 it was removed to the new and more I commodious buildings in Academy-court, the memory of which remains in the name of a street possessing ! otherwise few Claims to so high sounding a name. There the Academy remained till its final dissolution in 1786. It is, however, the men and not the buildings in which they laboured which are of chief interest to us,for in the twenty-five or thirty years of its brief life the Academy brought together a remarkable group of teachers, who among them managed to turn out 393 students, laymen and divines, more or less fitted for the duties of life. There was Dr. Taylor, usually known as Dr. faylor of Norwich, the celebrated Hebrew scholar, and first prin- cipal. He was one of the men whose wide learning fills the modern minister with diffidence and shame till he remembers that perhaps -the minister of a hui eked years ago had a quieter time of it, with only occasional meet- ings, few committees, and no tea parties, and consoles , himself with the thought that overy time has its own duty and opportunity. He died in 1761,and was buried in the chapelyard at Obowbcnt. Of Mr. Holt,the mathe- matical tutor who was Dr. Taylor's sole colleague at the opening of the Academy, for Dr. Aikin had not yet ar- rived, not many particulars have come down to us. He is described as a sort of " reasoning automaton," and is said to have cherished the sentiment "that he could live happy in perfect solitude, to all eternity, meditating on the perfections of the 'Deity." Of all the tutors Dr.Arkin strikes me as the most attractive and lovable, entering with perfect sympathy into the lives and stu- dies of his pupils. _born in 1713, and educated at Dr. Doddridge's Academy and the University of Aberdeen, he came to Warrington in 1758 as classical tutor, annexing also to his department the French language, grammar, oratory, criticism, logic and history. On Dr. Taylor's death he succeeded to the thee; logical chair. Never very robust in health, he still managed to throw himself with strong sympathy into the thoughts and pursuits of the students, one of the highest graces of the good teacher. In his own house, where he loved to gather the young men around him, he would eempletely unbend. seasoning the conversation with telling anecdotes and shrewd advice; in all thins a fine teacher and an inspiring man. He died in 1780, and is buried on the north side of the Parish Church, and a tablet to his memory, written in stilted Latin by Gil- bert Wakefield, is one ef the adornmeete of our chapel, which we should always regard with pious veneration. Before we pass away from him let us also pay a word of tribute to his gilted children, who often worshipped in this place, his son John, Dr. John Aikin, the. author of "Evenings at Home" and himself for a short time a teacher in the Academy, and his daughter Anna Ltetitia, Mrs. Barbauld, the poetess. Her poems are little read now, but the swest rha thm of her "Hymns in Prose" is ; for many, of us an :incising part of cur childhood's reli- gion. One other name at least claims our attention: it is that of Joseph Priestley, the most widely keown of all the Academy tutors. He was here for six years, from

div.head: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUF,
div.p: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUF,
THE PEERS v. THE PEOPLE.

The winter el.:, ion of Run Corn Li • ral Club, was opened on Tuesde y esenilig, when the Rev. D. s. Prosser, of Monet ester, delivered a lecture to a good audienee. entitled "The Peers v. The People." Mr. A. R. Norman presided, and he was supported by the lecturer and Mr.Thos.Lea. In opening the meet— ing, the Chairman said he was very pleased to be at that meeting as a member of the Club, more especially became to a certain extent taking a new departure that he was afraid they had been rather slow In taking, and that was doing something for the educational part of the members. (Hear, bear.) 'Joe Committee had long had a feeling that there had been something wanted in this respect and they hail been doing semi-thin to release this. He thought they would agree that they had made a good start in bringing Mr. Prosser there that night. (Applause.l This lecture was open to all Liberals, but if there were any Liberals present who were not members of the Club, he • urged them to become members. The subscription was very low, only a shilling a quarter, so that there was no money barrier to membership, and he hoped those who had not joined the ranks would do so at once. The Com- mittee intended to form a programme which would tend to the mental, polittcal,and social education of the mem- bers of the Club, and lie hoped they would be supported by the members. (Applause.) The Lecturer, who was well received, said the House of Lords was in direct antagonism with the House of Com- mons. The great measure which had been under dis- suasion on the eletform and in the press for some seven years, which had been the supreme question upon which I the last General Election was fought, and which had ; been passed by the House of Commons by undi- minished ministerial majorities after a discussion un- precedented in its character and in its duration. had been ruthlessly and contemptuously, alters few nights debate rejected ; and so the work of an entire eession ' ;lad been rendered void, and the issue placed before the electorate as a result was, "Shall this non representa- tive this irrespoasible body of men thwart the will of the people." That was the question the people and especially the Liberal party had to consider. (Applause.) The House of Lords as at present constituted was both an anachronism and an anomaly. It was intolerable that a house so constitutA should have it in its power to stand between the nation and the carrying out of its deliber- ately expressed will. The House of Lords consisted of 2 Archtaseepa. 21 Dukes, 19 Marquises, 118 Earls, 26 Vis- counts, 24 Bishops, 259 Barons, 16 Scotch representative Peers, and 28 Irish representative Peers, a total of 519 or 520 persons altegether.They represented one interest—the land, were Ignorant of the conditiens and needs of the most numerous class in the community.By their environ- ment they could nut but be largely influenced by the prejudices of their order. Their whole history showed that to be the case. Out of 70 million acres the members of the Rouse of Lords owned neatly 15 million acres, or more than twenty per cent., with a rental of twelve millions sterling. They had in their possession 4,800 Church Haines (no wonder so many parsons were Tories) and they received in pay and pensions some £640,000 a year. Their aim had ever been to preserve the privi- leees and advantages of their own order. They had viewed wh h suspicion every movement celculated to increase the influence or the people, and had seen in every reform, in every adv inee of civil and political and religious liberty a menace to their own monopoly of power. The lecturer narrated the many reforms-which tile House of Lords had rejected during the present cen- tury, but which they hail eventually been crimped& ba pass by reason of their fears ot an angry people. They had always yielded to fear what they had denied to jus- tice. If there had to he a conflict between the House of Commons and this irresponsible Chamber, it UM not the House of Commons that would go to the wa'l. The Lecturer ridiculed the arrogance of the Lords in demand- ing that Mr. Gladstone should go to the country and said that appeal would not be made until" one man one vote "and other reforms had become law. They (the Liberal party) did not doubt the issue of an appeal to the electorate. Mr, B. Kniveton moved" that this meeting congratu- late the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone and his supporters in the Peoples House, at the successful passing of the Bill for the 64 ter Govern merit of Ireland, urges upon them to press forward the remaining portion of the Liberal programme, aid decline to permit a non-elective House of Lords to constitute itself the arbiter of the rights of the democracy."—Mr. J. D. Jones seconded the motion which was carried unanimously, and a vote of thanks having been accorded to the lecturer, and chair- man the proceedings terminated.

SUGGLSTED NLTERATION BY A RUNCORN

IJt)UTOU. On Wednesday, at Runcorn Sessions-house, Mr.J. E. Worsley, district coroner, held an inquiry touch- ing the death of Albert Edward Rushton,inlant son of W. Rushton, chemical labourer, who died suddenly on Frii'ay last. Dr.Ormsby said the child was brought to hurl, and he found it stiff Ting from bronchitis. Be pre- sc.e hed for it, but did nit see it alive again. The post. mortem showed that death was due to congestion ol the lungs and bronchitis. A verdict of "Death from natural causes" was returmd.—At the conclusion of the in- quiry, Dr. Ormsby said he thought a slight alteration ought to be made in the form of death certificates. If they could be worded to the effect that the medical man attended the deceased for a certain time,mentioning the time, there would he, no difficulty in giving certificates. in an emergency. It could then be left to the police ot. the coroner to decide whether an inquiry was necessary, or not.—The Coroner said the suggestion was an excel- lent one, and if adopted would save him considerable. trouble, but the present state of the law did not allovt it. They had to comply with the law as it stood.—Dr. Ormsby said there was an agitation in the medical papers with reference to the point, and if some notice of it was taken by the coroner it might have some eff,,et in. pro_ ducing an alteration which would he beneficial to all parties—Ti's Coroner said the reform would come better from the Medical Association.
