div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 14, 1893.

THAT is the question which is now Di it a ed with regard to the action Stale? being ask of the coal-owners. There are many indications that the great lock-out, which has worked such disastrous results, will come to an end by the employers, one after another," throw- ing up the sponge" and allowing the miners to resume work at the old rate of wages. Every day that passes shows a more marked disposition on the part of the colliery owners to stampede from the policy which they deliberately entered upon tes or twelve weeks ago. Last week the owners who responded to the bait held out to them by the Miners Federation were not numerous, and .the pits that were re-opened were mostly of the smal- ler kind. But still there was a distinct beginning in the break-up of the masters' combination. It is now evident that there were many other owners only hanging back with a view to seeing what turn events might take at the Conference between the Mayors and the representatives of the two eon-

tending parties at S?:efileld on Monday. This Conference has not succeeded in formulating the terms of settlement. The Vlayors' suggestion was that the pits should be re-opened at once the old wages being paid for six week 4 and that at the end of the six weeks the miners should submit to a reduction of ten per eent, in their wages instead of the twenty-five that had been demanded of them. These terms, it would appear, are not acceptable to either side. The masters met in conclave the very next day, and instead of adopt- ing the proposal of the civic dignitaries, they passed a resolution insisting upon an immediate reduction of fifteen per cent. On the other hand, the position of the men has been clear and consis- tent from the beginning. They contend that, allowing for all deductions, the wages they have been recently paid afford them a bare subsistence, and that they could not and would not submit to any reduction. They have fought their battle heroically, and it is now well nigh certain that their fortitude will he crowned with an unqualified success. Within the last two or three weeks the public has rallied to their support in a fashion which has not been eq ualled since the memorable Dockers Strike in London. On the other hand the claims and pretensions of the coalowners have been riddled and dissected with a completeness that leaves very little in the way of apology for the original demand for a reduction, and nothing to excuse a continued stoppage of the collieries. The conduct of the colliery proprietors could not be placed in a more heinous light than it has been by one of their own members—Mr. BATLEY, a large coalowner in Derbyshire. A demand for twenty-five per cent. reduction made, as every one knew, a strike in- evitable. But then, in effect says Mr. BAYLEY, whether there was a strike or no strike the masters stood to win. If the men accepted the reduction there would be a great reduction in the wage bill; if they did not the great accumulations of coal would be got rid of at large prices. It was, in other words,a greatgambling speculation in which the conditions were, so far as the coalowners were concerned, "heads I win, tails you lose." And through that speculation hundreds of thousands of people—men,women and children—have had to suffer untold privation and misery, during the last few weeks. Then the details which have been made public as to the low contracts for the sup- ply of coal which have been entered into do not redound to the credit of the masters, We are told that Birmingham Gas Committee has secured contracts at a lower rate than has been known for twenty years back. Why? Is it because Bir- mingham, if it did not obtain its coal at this low figure would cease to make gas, or because, for the sake of an extra shilling or sixpence per ton, the order would have been sent to Belgiu m or Germany? Not at all. These low contracts are the result of the reckless competition of coalowners who have calculated upon being able to recoup themselves out of the pittance that is paid to the miners. It will be a great public gain if the present lock-out emphatically demonstrates that such calculations cannot be safely relied upon.
Tim farmers seem to be thoroughly The Land aroused at last in reference to the Laws.

urgent need of land law reform. In Wales they are laying evidence before the Gov- ernment Commissioners which will almost corn- pel the House of Commons ta give attention to their grievances. While not without its tolerant, broad-minded and generous landowners, the Prin- cipality seems to have been a Paradise for that class of landlords which neglects its own duties yet exacts all kinds of subsevience from its tenants, and appropriates with scarcely a pretence of corn- penSation all the improvements which are made by the occupier. What with negligent and ab- sentee landlords, arbritary and unsympathetic ' agents, and the still more obnoxious gamekeepers the lives of many Welsh tenants have been filled with anxieties and humiliations. In England,too, farmers are beginning to find the position into , which they are being forced y the operation of unjust land laws absolutely intolerable. In , Lancashire, in particular, they are displaying a wholesome independence and outspokenness. At Preston on Tuesday, there were laid before an Assistant Commissioner a number of the ridiculous restrictions which are imposed upon many tenants. With regard to some of these restrictions it is hard to think of any reason for them unless it be to harass the tenant and pre- vent the land from being fully utilised. On Wed- nesday a meeting of farmers was held at Warring- ton with a view to bringing local witnesses before the Agricultural Cornmission,and a Committee was appointed for that purpose. It was suggested that the evidence of Mr. KNOWLES who recently had to quit the Yew Tree Farm, Appleton, because he would not "ride with the Yeomany," would be valuable. Mr. KNOWLES' evidence would certainly go to show that there are still landlords who seem to forget that they live in the nineteenth century, and that what is now expected from a farmer is that he should make the best use of the land he occupies and not to cut a ridiculous figure RS a modern imitation of a feudal retainer.

MEMBERS of the House of Corn- • Long mons are not without experience of Sitting. 4 all night " sittings, but it seems that the American Senate is bent upon beating the record in this line. The bone of contention is the proposal for the repeal of the Sherman Silver Purchase Bill, a Bill which was recently con- demned in emphatic language by President CLEVELAND. The Sherman Act was passed ap- parently for no other purpose than to subsidise the great " Silver Kings " of America. It put the governm en t of the United States under the obliga- tion of periodically purchasing immense quantities of silver, and the quantity of that metal now lying uselessly at Washington is so great that new vaults have been built from time to time to acco- modate it. It might have been thought that a piece of legislation which has proved to be so en- tirely for the benefit of the few at the cost of the many, would have been quickly repealed. But vested interests are powerful in the -United States, and it is to the advantage of a particularly power- ful interest that this statute should not be repealed. Therefore, a very large number of the " Upper " House are determined to fight hard for privi- lege and profit. It seems that, so peculiar are the rules of the Senate, when a minority declines to yield and a majority will accept no compromise, there re mains no way of settling the point at issue except for one party to wear the other out by sheer physical endurance. This is the task that has now been undertakes by the majority of the senate, and the legislative buildings have been transformed into a sort of camp. The hero of the moment is a Mr. ALLEN of Nebraska. The feat which he has' accomplished is that of making a speech fift eon hours long, and, we are further told, that "when hefinished his speech his eyes were as clear,his voice was as strong,and his gestures were as vigor.
()vs as when he started." After this, it is to b hoped that America is proud of her Senators

CONCERT AT WESTON POINT. On Wednesday evening an 'mere ling concert was given in the Church Schoolroom, Weston Point, under the presidency of the Vicar, the Rev. Mr. Bowen. A glee party sang a selection ; Miss Simkin and Mr. Morris gave a duet; Mr. Branch, Miss Taylor, Mr. Morris, and Miss Simkin interpreted songs ; Master Arnold Povali played a couple of solos on tile violin ; and Misses Tay- lor, Crosby, and Simkin contributed a trio. The accompaniments were performed by Mr. W. E. Lan- caster. WIDNES CYCLE CLUB BALL. The annual ball in connection with the above club was held on Thursday evening in the Conservative Club Assembly Room. During an interval the prizes to the successful riders in the various races during the past season were distributed by Miss Deacon. The following were the recipients :—Five miles championship : D. Dagleish, silver cup and gold medal ; 2nd, W. Sher- ratt, gold medal ; 3rd, F.Sherratt, gold medal. Twenty- ' five mile handicap :Ist, F. Sherratt ; 2nd, W. Sherratt ; 3rd, W. Norris ; 4th, C. Bridgestock. Special prize, D. Dagleish. Mr.Dagleish was also presented by the mem- bers of the club with his photograph, neatly framed, as a recognition of his special merit as a rider. RUNCORN LICENSED VICTUALLERS ASSOCIATION. The annual meeting of the members of this Associa- tion was held at the office of Messrs. Linaker and Linaker, solicitors to the ASS9CiatiOD, on Thursday after- noon. Mr.T. Jones presided and there was a fair atten- dance. The financial statement and report having been adopted, Mr. John Jones moved and Mr Whitfield seconded that Mr. John Coxhill be,president for the en• suing year, and the motion was carried unanimously. Mr. John Jones was unanimously elected vice-president on the proposition of Mr. T. Smith, seconded by Mr. H. Grundy. Mr. J. J. Linton was re-elected secretary and Mr. T. C. Price treasurer. The committee was con- stituted as follows : Messrs. H. Grundy, Geo. Shone,T. Whitfield, Arthur Hough, and T. Jones. Mr. John Jones referred to Mr. T. Jones's assiduous and successful labours during the two years he had occupied the posi- tion of president, and he proposed a vote of thanks to him for his serviva, aLcl also for in conjunction with Mr. Hough, fighting the cause of the licensed victuallers at the recent Commissioners' election. The motion was carried by acclamation. MARRIAGE OF MISS SanTa, OF RUNCORN. At Runcorn Parish Church on Wednesday afternoon, Miss Clara H. Smith, of 2 Stanley Villas, Runcorn, youngest daughter of the late Mr. John Smith, was mar- ried to Dr. Julius Raschen, chemist, of Runcorn, son of Mr. H. Raschen, of Birkenhead. The bride who was attired in a dress of ivory bengaline, trimmed with lace, wore a veil and wreath of orange blossoms, and carried a lovely shower bouquet of flowers. The bridesmaids, Miss Smith and Miss Raschen, wore dresses of ivory cashmere, and beaver coloured velvet hats, with yellow trimmings, and also carried lovely bouquets. Their costumes were clasped at the throat with gold brooches, set with pearls and rubies, the gift of the bridegroom. The bride was also attended by Miss May Raschen, and Master George Hermann Raschen, niece and nephew of the bridegroom, who presented a charming appearance in costumes of cream and blue. Mr. J. B. Holland acted as best man, and Mr. E. M. Arthur (London) was a groomsman. The bride was given away by her brother, Mr. Frederick A. Smith. The Rev. Canon Maitland Wood performed the ceremony,and subsequently an " At home" was held at the residence of the bride's brother. Later Mr. and Mrs. Raschen departed for North Wales. Many handsome and costly presents have been received.

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD FINANCIAL STATEMENT. A special meeting .of the Runcorn School Board was held on Thursday evening in the Town Hall. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Pritchard, and there were also present the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, Mr. T. Handley. Mr. E. Irnison, and Mr. G. Moss, clerk. After the pass- ing of the minutes of the previous meeting, thd Clerk submitted the financial statement for the past year. It showed the year to have commenced with a balance of £430 12s. ld. „and the receipts had been :—Annual grant from Education Department, £578 12s. 6d. ; grant under Technical Instruction Act, £2l is. 61.; tree grant from the Education Departm en t.£316 183.4 d.; under the Tech- nical Instruction Act, £5112.; contributions from local authority, £170; other receii.t;, £46 16a. Bd.; school fees £l7 is. id.; sale of books, £23 81. 11d.; from the rating authorities, being equivalent to a rate of 414. in the pound, £1,050 ; hire of room, &c., £ll 145.; total receipts with balance, £2.717 17s. The expenditure was—tor administration, £4Ol 6s. 4d. ; maintenance of public ele- mentary schools. £1,163 64. 4d. ; industrial schools, £52 las. 9d.•, under Technical Instruction Act. £299 14s. in respect of loans, £l6B 13s. sd. ; interest. £165 13s. Bd. balance in hand, £466 12s. 6d. ; total, £2.717 17s. The loans outstanding from the Public Works Loan Com- missioners stood at £4,308 6s. Bd. The Clerk explained that the expenditure -vas about the same as that for the past three or four years. An additional £lOO was drawn from the rates for banking purposes.—On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. T. Handley, the accounts were approved.

DEATH OF AN OLD INHABITANT. Mr. Henry Hallwood. one of the oldest tradesmen of Warrington died at his residence, Fennell-st., on Monday morning, at the advanced age of 79 years. He for many years cart ied on the business of baker and confectioner in Buttermarket-st.,and retired 12 years ago. Deceased, who was well known and highly respected, leaves four sons and four daugh- ters. Two of his sons carry on business in Warring- ton as grocers end provision dealers. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT ALL SAINTS' MISSION. The harvest festival in connection with All Saints' Mission,which was commenced on Wednesday night week, when the Rev. Gibson Smith, rector of Hale- wood, preached, were continued on Sunday. The preacher at the morning service was the Rev.ll. V. Pigot (vicar). A children's service was held in the afternoon, conducted by the Rev. T. M. R. Young- Hughes. In the evening the Vicar of St. Peter's Church, Warrington (Rev. B. Percival) was the preacher. The church had been very nicely decorated by a committee of ladies. There were good congregations at all the services, and the col- lections taken were in aid of the mission fund. MEETING OF THE WARRINGTON DAY SCHOOL TEACHERS. A meeting of the Warrington branch of the National Union of Teachers was held on Saturday afternoon at the Heath Side (Girls') School. There was a good number present, and the chair was occupied by Mr. Stansfield, president of the War- rington branch. A letter of apology for non-atten- dance at the meeting was received by the hon. sec. Mr. Frank Blackwell, from Mr. Charles Twiss, head master of Peoples' College. The Chairman said that in the Warrington district there were 120 day school teachers, but the number in the local branch of the N.U.T. was only 37. If they wished to be of any use at all in the town or wished to make their voices heard, they must certainly have a larger membership. There was such a thing as sympathy of numbers and the Warrington Trades Council was an example. The president of that body had been chosen as a magistrate. The teachers did not aspire to the dignity of magistrates although he must say that they would make very good magis- trates, but if the Association were larger, its influence would be more felt and recognised. As a sphere in which the teachers' assistance would be useful, he mentioned the Technical Committee. He said that this was a Committee of the Town Council augmented by a few educational people, but how many teachers were on this Committee? Then again there should be a teacher on the Museum and Library Committee. Among other reasons for join- ing the association was the fact that the teacher's position would be more secure if he did so, and in such matters as corporeal punishment, etc., he would have the support of the association.—Dr. Beach, D.D., L.L.D.,of Macclesfield, next gave an address on the duty of the teacher to the Association and was followed by Mr.Johnstone, of Stockport, who spoke on the general working of the Association. After the meeting the company adjourned for tea after which a social evening was spent.

ferred back to the Committee. This was agreed to and the minutes were passed. THE HEALTH COMMITTEE. The Health Committee reported that they had investi- gated the charges against the management of Infectious Diseases Hospital, referred to by Mr. Alderman William- son at the last meeting of the Council, and after hearing the statements of the several persons interested, hac re- solved that the charges made were entirely baseless. The Medical Officer reported that during September there were 90 births and 52 deaths, being at the rate of 36 0 and 20-8 respectively. The deaths included 16 children under one year and 8 children between one and five. Zymotic diseases caused 11 deaths. The Medical Officer further added :—" It is satisfactory to note that the epidemic of typhoid fever is gradually abating. In the month of June 4 cases were notified, in July 27 eases, in August 49. and in this month (September) 42. In June there was 1 death, in July s,August 9, September 4. The beds in the hospital have been fully occupied during the last five or six weeks, and when any vacancies occurred they were immediately filled up. Several cases had to be treated in their own homes through want of accam- modation in the hospital, and in two of these cases it was necessary to provide an assistant nurse, one being at 21, Albert-road, and the ether at 141, Mersey-rcad. During the period above mentioned the hospital staff have been fully employed both day and night in admin- istering to the wants of the patients, but notwithstand- ing the constant attention and great kindness shown to every inmate, certain allegations were made against the management which were entirely without foundation. The committee had resolved unanimously,subject to the approval of the Local Government Board, that the salary of the Nuisance Inspector be increased to £125 per annum, from the date of the expiration of his pre- sent appointment,and that the Town Clerk make appli- cation to the Local Governmentßoard accordinglv.—Mr. G. I. Neil moved the adoption of the minutes, and refer- ring to the charges against the hospital, said since the inquiry he had received one or two communications from persons who were in the hospital at the same time as the persons who complained, approving of the hospi- tal management. Before allowing a thing like this to get into print from a baseless source, it would be better if it were mentioned to the committee, and if it were not taken up, then bring it forth into the eyes of the public. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Smith seconded the motion. THE INSPECTOR'S SALARY. Mr.Shuttleworth asked on what grounds the Nuisance Inspector's salary was to he increased. It was a most inopportune time to raise any officer's salary. It would be better for the interests ot the ratepayers if the Coun- cil would go in for reducing some of the higher paid offi- cers.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT
RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The Rev. John Simpson, of Runcorn Congrega- tional Church, has received an invitation to become co-pastor of Great George-street, Congregational Church, Liverpool, in consequence of the Rev. J. K. Nuttall having been ordered, by his medical a,;tendant,to take a rest from his ministerial duties. The offer was a very tempting one as the church is a very large and prosperous one, but Mr. Simp- , son has decided to remain in Runcorn where he has 1 laboured successfully for three years and a-half, and his decision has given great satisfaction to the members or his church. Since Mr. Simpson became pastor of Bethesda, the church membership has dosibled.

The Runcorn Tonic Sol-fa Choir, who can now add the word priza to their title give their first grand concert of the season in Runcorn Public Hall on Tuesday evening next. Miss Bessie Holt and Mr. Stanley Cookson are the vocalists, and the in- strumentalists are the sisters Nunn, who are old, and ever welcome favourites in Runcorn. Amongst the items to be sung.by the choir, are the pieces given at the choral competition at Manchester, in which they achieved so signal and ' well deserved success, and altogether the first concert promises to be of a higher enjoyable and interesting charac- ter.

The Runcorn Musical Society have this week is- sued their programme for the present season, and those who are preserving these programmes as a re- cord of the history and performances of the society will add the present one to their collection with great pleasure. It is a triumph of the typo- grapher's art. The cover is of imitation crocodile skin, of a delicate primrose tint, while the leaves are of a deeper colour, and the whole are fixed to- gether with crimson ribbon. The types are boll and clear and ornamental, and while those on the cover are printed in gold, the inside pages are printed in a rich tone or terracotta. The produc- tion is a credit to Mr. Bellamy of the." Examiner " Office, whence it has been issued.

The arrangements include a ballad and instru- mental concert on October 30th, when the vocalists will be Madame Fanny Moody, Miss Lily Alk)ody, and Mr. Charles Manners. The ihstrumentalists are solo violin, Mr. Frank H. CrosPley ; solo pianist, Mr. F'. W. Reynolds. On Wednesday, the 13th Decem- ber, will be produced Handers great work Samson, in conjunction with the Warrington Musical Society. The band and chorus will number 200 performers,and the artistes engaged are Miss Thudichum, Madame Alice Bertenshaw, Mr. James Gawthrop, and Mr. Bantook Pierpoint. For this work it has been deemed advisable to engage the Drill Hall. The third and last concert takes place on Wednesday, March 14th, and it will be invested with consider- able interest because of the performance of Mr. Crossley's cantata Adele, this work which has been highly spoken of, forming the first part of the pro- gramme The second part will consist of miscel- laneous items. The artistes on this occasion are Miss Maggie Davies, Mr. Braxton Smith and Mr. David Hughes. This is a bill of fare creditable to the enterprise alike of the conductor, officials and Cummittee, and one would think, which cannot help but "draw" large audierces.

One of the first duties I rr. F. C. Larkin, of Liver- pool, had to undertake on his return from his wedding trip, with his bride (formerly Miss Nellie Lightburn of Runcorn) was to occupy the chair at the meeting of the Liverpool Microscopical Society of which he has the honour to be president. lie was cordially welcomed by his fellow members,who on the motion of Mr. Wm. Oelricos, seconded by Mr. Alfred teicester, formally placed this resolution on the records of the society :—" That the heartiest congratulations of the society be offered to our president Dr. Larkin, on the occasion of his recent marriage, with best wishes for his happiness."

The unanimous requisition to Alderman Fred 11. Gossage to again become the Chief Magistrate of Widnes, on the completion of his present year of office chimes in with the feelings and anticipations of the general body of ratepayers. It was expected that he would occupy the responsible position not only for another year, but for many years to come. There is no member of the present council so well able to dispense the honouis and hospitalities of the position to which Alderman Gossage may justly be Laid to be entitled by reason of his prolonged and able labours in the public interest.

It is very regrettable that a pleasant and unruffled year should have been disturbed by a disagreement such as occurred at the meeting on Tuesday between Alderman Williamson and the Mayor. It was quite evident to the unimpassioned spectators that it was the result of a misunderstanding. Alderman Williamson had no intention to defy the Mayor's Authority, but feeling that he was in order in giv- ing reasons why his amendment should be accepted he displayed more feeling and heat at the Mayor's interruption than perhaps the occasion warranted, and the Mayor appealed for and secured a vote of confidence from the Council, Alderman Williamson forming one of the majority. It is always unfor- tunate to introduce personalities and Alderman Williamson was led into a grave mistake when he charged the Chairman of the Health Committee with collusion with other officers. The charges made against the Hospital management are very serious and ought to be dealt with in an impartial and judicial spirit in justice to all concerned. The Council Chamber scarcely appeared to be a satisfac- tory court of inquiry on Tuesday.

The resolution respecting the berough bench re- ceived very little recognition at the hands cf the Council. Silence followed the reading of the com- munications, It appears somewhat early in the municipal life to commence such an agitation. The Corporation must have time to walk ere it runs. Now that three new pictures have been added to the local bench, suitors will have less cause of complaint. The new J.P.'s are Major Blackburne, of Hale Hall, and Messrs. W. W. Gossage, and H. S. Timmis, of Widnes.

Mr. T. E. Delaney, Becret4u to the idnes branch of the Irish National League forwarded the following reso- lution which had been unanimously adopted at a public meeting of ratepayers held in the rooms of the National League :—" That this meeting of the burgesses of Wid- nes having considered the many disadvantages, delays, and unnecessary expenditure caused through the borough having to depend upon the County magistrates for the administration of justicP, and the exercise of magisterial powers, declare that a separate co.nmission of the peace ought to be granted to the borough, and call on the members of the Conneil to take immediate steps te peti- tion her Most Gracious Majesty, the Queen, to obtain such grant."—No comment was made on the resolu- tion.

HIGHWAY COMMITTEE. The Borough Surveyor submitted to this Committee plans, section, and estimates, for the sewering and mak- ing of the following private streets, viz. :—Rose-st., Rhyl-st., ; passages (1) between N 09.3 and 6, Rose-st., (2) rear of Nos. 8 to 14 inclusive, Moor-lane,and 3to 15 inclusive, Rose-st., (3) rear of Nos. 16 to 22 inclusive, Moor-lane, and Nos 2to 16 inclusive, Egypt- st., (4) rear of Nos 21 to 49 inclusive, Moor-lane, and (5) ' between 27 and 29 Moor-lane. Resolved—That notices be given under section 150 the Public Health Act, 1875, requiring the owners or occu- piers of the premises fronting, adjoining, and abutting on such streets, within one month from the service of such notices, to sewer, level, pave, metal, flag, channel, or make good, and to provide proper means of lighting the said streets, as shown upon the said plans sections, and estimates ; and that in case such notices be not com- plied with the Corporation, being the Urban Sanitary Authority under the said Act, do execute such works and recover the expenses incurred by them in doing so from the owners in default in the manner prescribed in that behalf.

div.head: OLD CLOTHES.
div.p: OLD CLOTHES.

Mr. Quinn wished tO—i.;,--ii-the committee would open the market for the sale of old clothes. Old clothes were freely sold about the town, and he did not see why they should not be sold at the market. The working- men could then buy clothes for a few cAppers that would serve their purpoSe equally well as more expen- sive clothing.
_ THE HOSPITAL SCANDAL.-SERIOUS ALLEGA- TIONS.-HEATED DISCUSSION.

Alderman Williamson said the inquiry had been taken up by the Cemmittee with a prejudiced mind. He wished to ask the Chairman of the Committee several questions. Was it fair or just to ask the Council to accept the resoluVon of the Committee without submit- ting to each member a copy of the evidence ? What was the object of refusing admission to the inquiry of one of the most important witnesses, while others who were only casual visitors to sick patients were brought to the inquiry ? What did casual visitors know about the general conduct of the Hospital. Why two doctors in attendance on typhoid patients were asked to the inquiry and not other than who were also in attendance ? How could the Committee come to the conclusion they had when the witnesses adhered to their statement and there was no contradiction by nurses, doctors nor visi- tors in the report. In July there was a row at the Hospital between the matron and a nurse ; one doctor found that after ordering mire milk, milk and water was given. One charge was that there was an insufficiency of milk given to the patients and it was a strange coin- cidence that while the number of patients had bsen decreasing since July the milk bill had bean increasing. In July the milk bill was LS 10a., in August £lB 153. 91 and in September £23 ss. Did these figures prove that they did not know they were not giving a sufficient quantity of milk. All through the inquiry had been a bogus inquiry ;it had been a farce of an inquiry. The inquiry was held with the object of askine a few per3one well known before, and those who were more implicated, knew more about the Hospital and whom the Chairman of the Committee knew, knew more about it, were not asked. The Medical Officer's report showed that that officer had suddenly become very friendly with a man whose throat he was trying to cut a menth or two back, figurativelr speaking.—(Mr. Neil : Bosh). Bosh or not bosh, it was true.—The Mayor: You must not impute motives. —Alderman Williamson : Very well, I will not do so. He asked how it was that the Medical Officer had not brought these facts of notification before the Com- mittee except in the ordinary way until new. 'flie whole matter had the appearance of a bogus inquiry, got up in order to screen certain per- sons. The Mayor : You must not imnute mntives.—Alderrnan Williamson : I am not.—The Mayor: You ere.—Alderman Williamson continuing said one patient was sent to the washhouse at half-past eight at night and kept there until ten o'clock against her will. Another patient said she went of her own aeeord. This was a distinct contravention of rule 39. And it was only the woman's Second day Out of bed. It was had enough for a strong healthy woman to have to perform the duties required by a typhoid patient, but it was far worse to put a sick woman only two days out of bed to do there duties, while the officials paid for the work stand by And Watch. How would the Caen:illors like their wives or daughters to do thee duties. He argued that the inquiry should have been a public on—Mr. Neil, in reply, said the nusience inspector's duties and position demanded the increase in his wages. Old clethes could now he sold in the market. As to the hospi- tal Ye was very sorry that Alderman Williamson had an idea that he was in collusion with any official or mem- ber of the Council. He read a letter placed in his hands a few moments ago from A. Mayers of 39 Jnhn-st., in which she said "I was an in-patient of the Fever Hospi- tal at the same time as Mrs. Cunningham and Mrs. Gillooley and found the nurses attentive and the food of good quality and sufficient quantity." The Committee courted every inquiry. If all the witnesses, who were outside were net called it was the fault of the witnesses themselves because they were asked if they had any more witnesses to call. As to calling all the doctinrs in the town, he thought it was necessary only to call the doctors who attended upon those who complained to, strange to say they had never made a single complaint to the doctors during the whole timet hey were is ha hospital (Alderman Williamsom They did to the nurses and to you). With reference to the milk and water business, the food given was in accordance with the doctor's orders. The question between Dr. O'Beeffe and himself was a public matter and such it should remain, and he did not know anything about the report until it was presented to the Health Commit- tee. With reference to the washhnuse, the woman mentioned by Alderman Williamson said she was sent there ten days after she was convalescent and not throe days; the other said she went on her own account. One who had made a complaint, found fault both with thel quality and quantity of the meat given on a certain Sun- day, but as she had not tasted the meat, how she could find fault with the quality ha did not know. The other woman admitted that had it not been for Mrs. Gil- looley she would not have made a complaint at all. —Alderman Williamson moved an amendment that the matter be referred back for further inquiry and that in the meantime conies of the report he elven to each member of the Council. Be refrained from mentioning one case. He wanted to know if the Committee inquired into the case of a patient who jumped over the wall at five o'clock in the morning be- cause of the treatment he received. The case of a small- pox patient was not inquired into at all. After he had been disinfected it was found that he had no clothes to put on and he was left in a cold fireless kitchen from five o'clock in the afternoon until seven o'clock in the even- ing without a stitch to cover his nakedness except an old mackintosh. Did they consider this proper treat- ment.—The Mayor: Move your amendment.—Alder- men Williamson : I don'tthink I should be interrupted in this way, when trying to do my duty.—The Mayor : Will you go on and move your amendment—Alderman Williamson : lam giving reasons for it. I have not come here to be gagged. I have come here to represent no clique nor officials either.—The Mayor : I shall have to appeal to you directly to support the chair. (Several members: Yes.)—Alderman Williamson: I am not, disputing the authority of the chair.—The Mayor : I think you had better withdraw what you have said at once —Alderman Williamson : I withdraw if I have said anything to put myself in the wrong or hurt you in any way.—The Mayor : In reply to me you said you are not to be gagged. I appeal to the Council. lam not going to be put down in this way, 1 put it. Have you confidence in the ruling of the chair.—With one or two exceptions the whole of the members of the Council rise s their feet in assent—Mr. Quinn I don't think that is the question at all. I think Alderman Williamson would be the last to do it at all. Alderman Williamson: I would be the last to dispute your ruling. A certain amount of argument and liberty of speech should be given in nine,. lug an amendment. He moved the amendment. Mr. Quinn seconded so that they could have the report.— Mr. Owen thought there had been a misapprehension with regard to Alderman Williamson. Ile was adduc- ing his argument first and then formally, moving the amendment afterwards. The Mayor said if Alderman Williamson had moved his amendment and then asked what question he wished there could have been no ques- tion at all hut from thebeginning to the end he was con- tinually imputing motives and if all round the table called one another well not exactly names, they would have such a council that they would never be able to get through the busineis.—Alderman Williamson: I think you misunderstood me! put the motion first—The Mayor : You have not got it now. Alderman William- son. I have not got it in writing but I will put it in writing. The amendment was unanimously carried and Mr. O'Donnell suggested that the inquiry should be public.

div.head: GAS AND WAFER COMMITTEE.
div.p: GAS AND WAFER COMMITTEE.

The Engineer reported with regard to the Winers' strike and the coal supply—that Thursday next will complete the tenth week since the supplies nder Cpn- tract of gas cowl and steam fuel were stopped. Daring the last few weeks great difficulty has been experienced in obtaining supplies from any source, even at the enor- mously enhanced prices just now quoted. Irr oreer to economize as much as possible in the output of gas, the district pressures have been reduced wherever possible, and lighting of a number of public kurips in the less im- portant positions throughout the borough has been tem- porarily discontinued- The quantity of fuel bought for Netherley will last four weeks trom to-day, while the most favourable estimate for that at the Gas Works is up to the 21st inst., i.e., provided the airwe rnentioaed checks on the consumption are continued. A list of the quantities bought and paicea paid is sutunitted.—The Committee had resolved—That the erection and supply of all public lamps in the borough, being in the hands of this Committee, no lamps be erected or supplied ' except through the officials of this department, and that whenever any additional lamps or alteratiims are recommended by the Highway Committee, the positions of such additions and alterations be pro- perly indicated upon a plan and forwarded to the Gas Engineer by the Highway Department. In moving the confirmation of the minutes, Alderman Wareing said the committee had that day felt it needful to obtain a further supply of fuel which would carry them on to the first week in November. They must keep on buying or close the works.—Mr. Davies secontled.— Alderman Sadler alluding to the resolution re lamps stated that nothing had occurred between the two. com- mittees to occasion such a resolution. The Highway Committee had no wish to encroach neon the privileges of the Gas Committee. The two officials were playing off the committees one against the other, and the resolu- tion was intended to bolster up the reputation of one official to the disadvantage of another.—Alderman Ware- ing said he was sorry Alderman Sadler had spoken in thei way he had. He had refrained from going into detail, but it was necessary now to explain why this resolution had been passed. The Highway Committee had supplied lamps to Halton View Ventilating Shaft. These lamps were ordinary corridor lamps not intended for outside purposes,and they consumed each 96 cubic feet per hour, whereas the ordinary street lamp burned only 4 cubic feet per hour. In addition to that it was almost im- possible to light them and the Gas Committee wouPd have to go to the expense of putting them in such a form that they could be used in as satisfactory a manner as outside lamps. Considerable expense would be entailed. The Gas engineer was an expert and these matters should be left to the Gas Committee.—Alderman Sadler said there was no difference between the two committees with regard to the resolution. It was all "tommy rot" what Alderman Wareing had said. (Laughter). The minutes were carried.

div.head: MR. JOHN TAYLOR. CONTRACTOR.
div.p: MR. JOHN TAYLOR. CONTRACTOR.

The Mayor said be had received a communication from Mr. John Taylor, contractor for the new gas tank at Ditton, in which that gentleman stated that he had not sublet any portion of the work of constructing the new tank. He had not only paid the proper rate of wages but something approaching 20 per cent above the rate at present paid in in the trade. The May,r said he was sure the council would consider that very satisfantory on on the part of their contractor.

PROPOSED BRANCH LIBRARY.
In reply to Mr. Shuttleworth, Mr. F. Neil said the Library Committee could not at present afford to esttblish a branch library at Fara worth out of a penny rate.

ALDERMAN GOSSAGE AND THE MAYORALTY. Alderman Wareing said it would be within the re- membrance of the Council that some months ago they passed a resolution of thanks tc his Worship for his veiy handsome and generous gift of a chain and pendant to the borough. It Was also decided that the resolution should be inscribed upon a scroll in an illuminated manner. He now held it in his hand, and it became his pleasur- able duty to ask his Wcrship's acceptance of the resolution in that form He truAel that his Worship would accept it as a memento not only of the first year of his mayor- alty, but also of the high esteem and regard in which he was held, not only for his great generosity to the top, but for his worthy self. ij. held further ig his hand a request signed by every member of the Council asking his Worship to again accept the position he had so ably and faithfully held during the past year, for another 12 months. •If he would accede to this request, he would gratify every member of the Council, and it would be a source of groat satisfaction to the whole commlnity. —Tbe Muor said he accepted this token Q their friend- ship with the greatest posi.sblt pieuare. Re felt that anything he could do to forward the business of the Cor- poration of Widnes it was his bounden duty to do. Fie thanked them all Individually for the courteous manner in which they had always treated him,aud the assistance he had always received from them whenever assistance had been required. the providing of the chain and badge had been a source of great pleasure to him; it bad brought him in contact with men he did not know before ; it had taught him a great deal of what was necessary un- der such circumstances; and he hoped the Corporation through this chain would have a memento of its time. in art work very hard to surpass in beautiful design and beautiful workmanship.. He had no doubt that in 50 or 100 years this piece of gold work would be pointed to as the highest class of work that could be produced in the year 12'13. If the Council sincerely and truly wished him to again accept the mayoralty, he should be very happy to occupy the pisition for one more year. (Applause.) This concludei the business.

div.head: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.

A meeting of this board was held in Daresbury Court House, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. T. S. Burgess occupied the chair. There were also pre- sent Major W. V. Fox, Messrs. VV . Long. P. Derby- shire, J. Parr, T. Had, J. Derbyshire, J. L. Jones, T. Darlington, W. Bradford, J. Cooper, T. Chal loner, J. Routledge, E. J. Weir, C. Baguley, and W. Beswick.

MR. PARR TENDERS HIS RESIGNATION. The Clerk (Mr. Linaker) read letters from Mr. J. Charlton Parr, J.P., C.C., the chairman of the boar 1, resigning his position as chairman of the board owing to his failing healtb, cawing his inability to be present at the meetings. A resolution was moved by Mr. W. Bradford, seconded by Mr. W. Long. that Mr. Parr be asked to keep the position of chairman until the end of the year, when the matter will be reconsidered.

div.head: Tlllt CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL AND ROADS.
div.p: Tlllt CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL AND ROADS.

The Surveyor of the Cheshire County Council wrote. stating that the County Council Roads Committee bad decided to accept the Warrington to Northwich and Run- corn roads from the board, on their payment of £3,012 to the Cheshire County Council. A small committee consisting of Messrs. Burgess, Long, Hall and Darby- shire was appointed to meet the Clerk and Surveyor of the Cheshire County Council, to see if the amount asked for could be reduced, as the Board had spent a ennsider- able sum of money on the roads since the agreement for the transferenze of the roads was first drawn up.

COMPLAINTS ABOUT THE CANAL COMPANY. Mr. W. Long complained about the bad lighting of the new swing bridge in Knutsford-road. The roads, too,of the Ship Canal Company were not as they should be. The Ship Canal Committee of the Board met Mr. Henry of the Canal Company, and he promised to carry out the work the Board requested, but he (Mr. Lone) was sorry to say that they were not carried out. Mr. Hall proposed and Mr. Parr seconded that the Clerk write to the Ship Canal Co., that the Board would prosecute them unless lights were placed at the new bridges at once. The Clerk was also instructed to take proceedings against them unless the recommendation was carried out. A discussion next took plane as to the action of the Ship Canal Co., taking some temporary bridges down across the canal, without first getting the Board's permission to do so, and also neglecting to place notice boards, that the bridges were now pulled down. It was considered a very high handed proceeding, and the Clerk was instructed to write to the Co. about the matter. THE NEW ROAD FROM STAG INN TO ARPLEY. ' The following letter was read from the Manchester Ship Canal Company, pending the construction of the above road an arrangement was made by this company with the Cheshire County Council under which traffic which passed over part of Chester-road was diverted over a length of the new road on the south side of the canal and thence over a temporary timber bridge which was constructed across the Ship Canal near Tom Paine's Bridge. In order that the Arpley end of New- road may he completed, it is neces;ary to form an em- bankment across the present course of the river Mersey. The construction of this embankment cannot be com- menced until the dredging of the diversions of the river Mersey across Arpley meadows has been so far com- pleted as to admit of the traffic being turned through it. Much difficulty has been found in carrying out this dredging with the result that it has occupied a much longer time than was anticipated. At the rate the . dredging is now progressing we expect to complete

and to turn the traffic down the river diversion by the end of November, after which the embankment must be formed, and the road across it constructed. This opera- tion will occupy two months at the least, so that it would be in the early part, or probably the middle of February of next year before we could be in a position ' to remove the temporary bridge across the canal near Tom Paine's Bridge. With the exception of this obstruc- tion it is expected that there will be DO difficulty in. opening the Ship Canal for traffic to Manchester on the Ist of January next. The Cheshire County Council have (as concession to- the company to enable the canal to beopenetD agreed that the tempormy bridge should be removed six weeks betore the completion of the New- road ovate following condition. (1) fhat the traffic in the meantime be diverted from Chester-read via the New-roads on the south side of the canal to Northwich- road and thence over the new awing bridge and the road diversion to Wilderspool Causeway. (2), That the company indemnify the County Council 'against any- elaims that mar be made upon them arising out of theirconsent to this agreement. (...3) That the companr pas' a penalty of Eleper day for each and every day beyond the above mentioned SiK weehe-(tifter tbe pulling down of the temporary bridge) duringwhich tho new road may remain unopened. for traffic. .0 have now on behalf of thvi Manchester SO), Canal Company, to request tnat the stinction of your beard may be given to the agreement between the County Council and the. company, and will be obliged if you will bring the seat- ter before your boardat its next meeting.—Yourstmly,. E. Leader Willianas." Mr. Parr thought the Boned • would not be doing their duty to the public,if they did not insist on the new road to Warrington being completed,. before they gave the canal company permission to pall, 'Tom Paine's bridge down. The company had'plenty et time now to finish the road before January if they woold only" pot their shoulders to the wheel." He moved that the bridge be not allowed to be pulled &cm untt the completion of the new road to Warrington. Mr. Hall seconded the-proposition. He said the Ship Canal Company had done nothing until recentilv for three ;yea,rs at the river diversion. He didn't thk the public should be put to thu inemavenience of going round Stock- ton Heath. Mr. P. Darbyshire proposed that the matter should be left in the hands of the Ship Car:a? Committee of the Board to deaf with it. Mr. Beswick seconded. Mr. W. Long said they must bear in mind that there were millions depending upon the opening of that canal. The County Council were quite as respon- sible as that Board, and they had given their consent under certain conditions. He thought they would not put themselves in the way of such a large undertaking as this. He thought the Ship Canal Committee would very well look alter the matter. On the motion being put to the meeting two members voted for Mr. Parra resolu- tion, and eleven for Mr. Darbyshire's.

div.head: DISTRESS IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: DISTRESS IN WARRINGTON.

The position of the works in Warrington does not show much change this week. Houghton's Sankey Wire Mills are still on short time, the steel furnace and forge being completely at a standstill. Monks, Hall and Co.'s forge is stopped altogether and will ' probably not be opened again until the end of the coal strike. At the Whitecross Wire Works, a por- tion of the men are working, but the forge is at a complete standstill. The same is the case with Dallam and Bewsey Forges. At Rylands'an attempt has been made to follow the example of the Cock- hedge Mills, via., each workman to pay so much in the shilling, or to consent to a temporary reduction in their wages, in order to defray the extra cost of coal. On ~itturday a meeting was held at which nothing definitely was settled and the meeting was adjourned to Tuesday. On Tuesday, however, although most of the tren consented to a reduct 'on in their wages, the wiredrawers refused, and as a consequence the works are closed. Householders in the meantime are compelled to pay exhorbitar prices for coal, and this adds to the general distress as great numbers of people cannot afford to pay these prices. Another body of people suffering greAly from the general distress are the property owners. It is a very difficult matterfor the tenants to find money for the rent and the result is that the landlord very frequently is obliged to go without what is due to him. div.head: FLIBLI(7ti'S TO THE RESCUE.
div.p: FLIBLI(7ti'S TO THE RESCUE.

During the week Mr. Datton or the Bowling Green Inn, and Mrs. Jenks of the Ship Inn have been bestirring themselves in relieving the distressed people in the San- keii Bridges district. The former hat distributed 80 lasives of bread and large quantities or potatoes and other vegetables and the latter 100 loaves. ACTION BY TUE CORPORATION.

- - For softie tiMe the Corporation have been employizi 200 unemployed men- In the makin-g of streets: The work has been done in the ptring and sewerage departrscnt of the Corpora`ion, and last wz•el: it was risen that owing to this extra expenditure, the estimated expenditure cf the committee in that class of work was already exhausted. It was then seen that it was neces- sary to either levy a supplementary rate, or obtain power to borrow money from Local Government Board. To keep the men further employed it was suggested that boulder stones should be taken upon in several of the important thoroughfares and repave them with sets. The Borough Surveyor submitted a list of wok to be (Irmo. the probable expenditure on which would be : £2,000 A deputation waited upon the L-ioal Govern- ment Board and we understand sanction was given that the loan which the Corporation are trying to get upon a 20 years repayment. PRIVATE BENEFACTIONS.

A correspondent has sent the following : —I notice with great satisfaction the subscriptions given by many of our leading townsmen towards alleviating the distress at present existing in Warrington. It is also a great blessing that other ladies and gentlemen open soup kitchens of their own accord, one whcm I can mention especially, namely, Mr. Samuel Wakefield, of Lovely- lane, As one who has lived in Bewsey for a number of years. I can testify to the great distress existing in this neighbourhood at present,especiallyam on gst ironworkers. Mr. and Mrs. Wakefield haVO bees distributing soup and bread for some weeks past on Sundays and Wed- nesdays to hundreds of people, not only ironworkers, but anyone that stood in need of it. Over 700 persons I received soup and bread on Sunday. In fact since the present coal strike commenced some thousands have I been the recipients of Mr. Wakefield's generosity. My object in writisg this letter is because I know of plenty people who although sadly in need of it, are ashamed to fetch soup through the streets from the Drill Shed. If we had more independent soup kitchens opened in I different parts of the town by people of the stamp of Mr. and Mrs. Wakefield, a great deal of the painful pauperised feeling might he avoided." A MUNIAL ARRANGEMENT. Tha employees of Messrs. Crosfield's Soap Works have consented to a reduction of a penny in the shilling in order to defray the extra expense of the coal, consequent upon the coal strike. The reduction takes effect this week end. WEEKLY MEETING OF THE COMMITTEE. ENCOURAGING REPORT. The weekly meeting of the general relief committee was held yesterday afternoon, Mr. F. Monks occupying I the chair, and later on the Mayor. Mr. F. Monks in giv- ing the weekly statement said that it was the most satis- factory statement they had yet presented to the commit- tee. The distribution during this week had been 20,348 pints of BMW, compared with 20,972 pints last week,and 28,9101bs of bread compared with 24.2201bs last week. There had been a slight decrease in soup and a consider- able increase in bread. The decrease in the soup was due to a considerable number of hotpots being made during the week as a change in the diet. The increase of bread was due to a considerable number of people thrown out of work during the last week or two. They had also dis- tributed I-250 packets of tea against 905 last week, and 1,250 half lbs o sugar against 946 last week. The cost this week had been £l3B 19s. 4d. against £l4l 12s. 4d. last week. The total subscriptions up to date was £947 ITs. 10d., the amount expended was £.665 Ms. 51. This showed that the appeal in the statement last week had not been in vain, because the amount received since the last meeting had been £197 15s. 10d., and the weekly contributions £29 Bs., bringing a total for the week of £227 35.10 l.which was very satisfactory. Re must how- ever say that the committee still missed several names from the listond he hoped that they would have further subscriptions from those friends of theirs, which would enable them to tide over the distress, because he thought In another fortnight or three weeks, po4sibly some of the works would te at work again. He could not say very much of the iron works,because unless the contracts were renewed, they would he idle for sometime vet. He had ' nothing particular to report as to the districts, they were working satisfactorily. One of the statements he had made to him by the relieving officer that a reduction cf £3O to £4O per week would be made by bringing the re- lieving officer into the work he thought should not he taken too literally. He did not think that the imposi- tion had been so great as they had thought. Mr. Button (manager of Monks. Hall, and Co.) said that many of the men of that firm had been very pleased at the work provided by the borough, but some 30 or 40
S -
I men had no work at all. If the executive committee IC.ould prevail upoi the various officials of the Corpora- tion to give work where possible, they would be mos:. grateful. _

Mr, Monks explained that the §urn for street paving had been used up, hilt the Corporation. was applying for power to borrow some more. I.llr.Monklalso announced that if the 3tlb.s cri ptione came in as satiifactorily as they had done during the last week, the queen of giving coal as well as food would be considered.

div.head: SANKEY BRIDGES.
div.p: SANKEY BRIDGES.

IThe usual tea to the unemployed --at Sankey Bridges' washeld in the Wesleyan schoolroom on Saturday night when 150 men were present. After the tea, instead of the usuaA miscellaneous entertainment, Mr. said Mrs. Evens of Liverpool, who during the whole of Om past week had been engaged at a very successful series of evangelistic services in the chapel adjoining, took charge of the meeting. Mr. Evens gave a very interesting and racy account of his trip to America, and Mrs. Evens, who is of gipsy extraction, and sister to the well-known evangelist, eripsy Smith also sang a capital American. song. Mr. and Mrs. Evens had made themselves very popular daring the short tine in which they were in, Sankey Bridges,, the former, by his stirring addresses and the fatter by her tine contralto voice and also byher addresses. A,fter the lecture on Saturday night ara evangelistic meeting was held. Mr. T. Brough pre— sided at the harmonium. On Sunday collectims in aitP of the distress fund for the Sankey Biidges and Penketh Wesleyan Chapels and satisfactory sums were realized' at each place. On Tuesday 430 children were provided with a tea, on Wednesday there were 230 women,and on Thursday 480 children. During the week Evangelistic services have been held with very encouraging results.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS,
littOßT FOOTBALL.

As I predicted in these notes last week, the Rangers diik meet with more than their equals on Saturday, when they met Standish (South End), the holders of the Wigan Charity Cup. The match was originally fixed to be played at Wigan, but owing to the coal dispute, they are unable to get a" ga " there at present. 1t was therefore decided to play at Warrington, and a good number of spectat-irs witnessed the match, although a goad number hadn't got tbe wherewithal, to pay the admission money. A good game was witnessed, and the teams seemed t be very evenly balanced. At half- time each team had scored a try, but in the second half the "black diamond getters managed to score a second try which proved to be the Winning point. The Stan- dish men were by far the heavier team-and also brought twe excellent players from another Wigan club.

"Victory, thy name is Uncertainty." At least so far as its relation to the Warrington first team is concerned it is "Uncertainty "and considerably uncertain at that. as it were. Last week everyone was quite certain that the tide of misfortune had been stemmed. But " alas and Mack," one cannot get any comfort now from that. When people saw every reason for defeat in the match with Tyldesley, shouts" victory" rent the classic high- way to the brewery at the conclusion of the conflict, and the Warrington players had wreath d around their variously shaped brows, imaginary laurels; whilst some, who had been' bumped contented themselves with modest handkerchiefs around their craniums. Then. last Saturday when there was every reason to expect a win against Wigan, 10! there came the dark ominou& clouds of defeat, and some scoring which Warrington did not participate in. Beaten by seven points to never a minor!

Stay, there were miners in plenty—Not minors ! Of course not. Still I repeat there were miners in plenty, several hundred of them, and they forced their way through the gates on to the field twice without paying. So anxious were they to see the match that they begged for admittance, and being refused asked to be allowed in on" tick." But as Giveum has been desd since the strike,and Lendum has gone for a holiday,these requests were not acceded to.

Perhaps Warrington had some reason to lose heart of grace—(good phrase that !)—because their opponents are. holding the premier position in the competition. In. previous years it has generally been a keen fight bet- ween the two teams, but there has always been the shade of superiority in Warrington's play. In this match, however, they did not seem to be able to get a fair chance to introduce aggressive tactics, and were all the time sufficiently well occupied in feats of defence. Al— though they played nine forwards against Wigan eight, there was a palpable lack of power to repel the charges and inroads into their ranks made by the Strong Eight of Wigan. But they did their best ; they fought hard and incessantly, and there was never a shirker awing them. Indeed,though I'm not of a superstitious nature, I do confess to being inclined to believe somewhat irk luck in this match. Accident more than once came be, careen Warrington and their chance of scoring. Potts made a couple of really brilliant attempts to get over the line, but couldn't manage it, and Massey, who had a good chance at a drop at goal, couldn't make the ball rise worth more than a bad cent. He soon distinguished himFelf considerably at centre, and although be I played w? 11, he was ra' her uncertain, and as a contem- porary said, "was like the price of lard—fair to middl- ing." This was not a generous comparison, but was pro- bably made in jest, for 'side splitters " are generally in- terspersed about reports in the journal in question, with qnite an orderly regularity. Boscow played well in every respect, except for his fielding, which was certainly a little faulty. Otherwise he was the same admirable. . . . . . Sure cot,

It seems Warrington do not play the four three- quarter business with any amount of regularity which might lead people of a suspicious nature to suspect an at- tachment to the system. The "Athletic News" com- menting on this,remarbe with native "smartness' " War- rington are not yet converted to the four threequarter system or perhaps they think three of their men are equal if not better than four of any other club. Possibly this may be so, but they didn't get too many chances to show their agility." No they didn't get any chances and that is just the reason they couldn't show people that three of their men were as good as four men of another team. If they had only been given chances they could have done it easily, maybe.

div.head: Broughton..
div.p: Broughton..

I notice that in the first trial match of Lancashire county, Feveral Warrington players are included in the teams. In the whites there is Nevins amongst the for- wards, and in the stripes John T. Bate, the Warrington captain, is given a place at half hack, and Dakin among the forwards. Evans, the Warrington sub-captain, is also on the reserve for three-quarter back.

The Warrington A are having a bad time of it this season. To be beaten pointless on their own heath is anything kut their usual form. They have won very nairow victories during the past few weeks, and per- haps this defeat, when they met a strong combination like Wigan A, was the natural corollary to them. It is a usual, though not praiseworthy practice to attempt to explaia away defeat by the beaten side,but nevertheless there is one circumstance which will go a long way in explaining at any rate the severity of Warrington's-de- feat. To lose such a player as Westall who broke his collar bone early in the match is enough to throw a dam- per upon any team. This is the first serious accident that has befallen a member of the Warrington club this season, and let us hope it will be the last.

Still another defeat of a junior club tn chronicle v. Pemberton Recreation journeyed to Warrington to-play the St. Mary's team. Ths defest they inflicted on the " Saints" was not anything to make the St. Mary's men ashamed of, for after all, the visitors victory rested with one well-judged kick? The final score was St. Mary's, two tries, rembert(ri Recrea'ion, one goal, one try. The play of the St. Mary's team at the bitter end of the game was far better than their opponents, Lie% they were unlucky in not again crossing their lines. ter luck next time, perhaps.
TALLY Ho!

The Cross country se has now commenced, an i d' Warrington s not behind in having packs to follow the trail. The Y.M.C.A. Barriers Club has now been formed. I notice also that J. Hinch!Hie and J. Price, of the Orford Harriers were amongst the 200 runners at the invitation race given by the Sefton Harriers. The run was about seven miles, through Ailerton. WAvertrer Hunt's Cross to Aigburth-road. Here a one mile break was commenced, and the first " novices "to arrive 111 were Hinchliffe and Price of the Orford Club.

DICATH OF CANON Hoewoon. The death, occurred at Colwyn Bay on Tuesday, of the Rev. Frank Edward Hopwood, M.A , rector and rural dean of Bury, and honorary canon of Man- chester. The late canon was connected with two distinguished Lancasliire families—on his father's side with the tfopwoods of Hopwood ; and on his mother's with the Stanley' ot Knowsley. He was the eldest son of the late Canon Hopwood, for many years rector of Winwick, near Warrington, his mother being the youngest sister of the 14th Earl- of Derby. The late Canon was educated at Eton awl Christ Mira.
