div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A FR.AITDOLENT NEWSBOY.

John Edward--JeMTin:-..:5--(12) was brought before the Warrington Borough mag,is,rstes, on Toursday morning charged with having stolen from his employers Messrs. W. H. Smith and Son, oh the 25th September 64. their moneys ; and also charged with stealing 3. 9 I. on the - 29th of September, and 6s. sd. on the 2nd October. Prisoner pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) stated that the lad was a servant of Messrs. Smith and Sons, at the Central S,ation. It was found that between the 25th September sal theZrd inst , the lad hail appro- priated 16s 25. to his own use,which he had taken from five different persons. Information of the theft was given to the police and D. S. Monaghan when in search of the lad and found him. On being charged with the theft the lad replied "Yes, I did, I spent it in shops." Mr. W. H. Pritchard, manager of the baokstall, taid it was the lad's duty to collect 2s.from Inspector James, at the Police Station, every Monday morning. For two Monday mornings the lad's excuse for not bringing the money was that" Inspector James was on his holidays" On the following Monday, the lad absconded, and his (witness's) suspicions were aroused. It was discovered that the lad did collect the amounts in the usual way for three weeks. Evidence was also given of the thefts of the other sums. The bey was ordered to receive twelve strokes with the birch rod on the first charge,and a conviction was recorded against him on the other two charges.

- - PROSECUTIONS BY THE INLAND' PEVENITH AUTHORITIES. At the Warrington Borough Court yesterday morning, John Cosgrove, Pinners brow, was summoned by the Inland Revenue adthoritics for having on the 31st July kept a refreshment house,without taking out a license as required by law. From the evidence given by the pro- secutor or the Inland Revenue authortties it appeared that the defendant took over the refreshment house in April last, and had kept it without taking out a license. He was called upon by an Inland Thvenue officer, but the defendant kept postponing the matter, and never took out a license The authorities 'decided to com- promise the case with the defendant, if he would pay them a fine of ss. and take out a license, but he would not, and the case had ta be brought before the magis- trates. Thr oefendant had now taken out a l'aelise and the authorities did not press the case. The defendant was fined Is.and costs 7s.John Boughton Nettles,was charged- - with carrying a gun without havithz a license on the 3rd September. P.C. Barnet said on the date named h 7 VIES in Dial-street when from information received from a woman who said a man bad pointed a revolver at her, be went in search of the man and found him in Church- street. He took the man to the woman, and she said the defendant was the man who had pointed a revolver at her. The defendant denied having a revolver at all, and was searched at the Police Station by P.C. WI lag- too, who f.und a revolver, produced in court,upon him. No cartridges were found upon the. defendant, but the revolver had one empty case in it. !le was fined ss. and costs. '
THEFT OF WIATART ROOTS.

At the Warrington Borough Court. on Tuesday rn"rn- ing, John Conroy was charged with stealing from Orford Barracks four pairs of military boots, value El, on the 13th October, the property of the military authorities, and also with absenting limself from the training of the South Lancashire Militia in October,last year. The Chief onstable stated that the prkonet was a blacksmith, and belonged to St. Helens. On Octnher 13th four pairs of beets wtre missed from +Nord Barracks. The prisoner had been seen to enter the ripens where the boots were kept at midnight ots the date named,and was missed the next Morning, together with the boo*S. It Was found that prisoner had pawned two pairs ef military boots in Warrington, and these were identified as the stplen pro- perty. It was ascertained some time afterwards that the prisoner was serving nine months in Preston Gaol for another offence. On being liberated from gad he was met by O.S.Nfoaighan,ami admitted taking two pairs of boot.—Prisoner was fined 40s. nr one month's imprison- ment on the second charge, and a conviction teeorciPd against him on the first charge.—P.S.Motaghati received the usual reward. . . •

. . THE ALLEGED AssAtm' Wirt a KNIFE.' John Mc Cone, 4, Friars-lane, was brought up on re- mand, at thy 13,,rough Court, on Tuesday , charged with c.ommitting an aggravated assault en his wife; by kick- ing her on Tuesday the 3rd inst. Pri.ioner made his 30th adpearance. Mrs. M. 0.. Cone gave eYidomce, and now said that her husband kicked heron. the leg'. Th ,s. Welsh spoke as to being in corovany with „Mrs. McCone and drinking together, in her house, hut did not see the assauit. D Monaghan and Inspector Spinks repeated their evidence, as to the complainant stating that her husband had used a knife, Dr. Starkey Smith said he' was called upon to see the complainant by D.S. Monag- han on WednesOav laq. The woman had a contussil wound over the right eye and , discolouration on tho breast and other parts 01 the body, On. her leg he found a wound two and-a-half inches long, cut straight down the leg, and about half-an-inch deep. There sass no contusion about, the wound and he was certain that it was not done with a kick The woman tor the first few days told him that it had been done with a knife but the previous day she said it was done with a kick. The prisoner was sent to gaol for three months hard labour.
MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

SATUHDAT.—Before Mr. John Burgess (in the chair) and Mr L. Voisey. ASSAULT ON A MOTHER-IN•LAW.—Martin Quinn, an army pensioner, was charged with having unla.wfully beaten and assaulted his mother-in-law, Mary Hughes, on the 25th September. From the evidence of Mrs. Hughes it appeared that on the, date named, the pri- soner knocked her on the floor, knelt on her, and was about to strike her with a hammer when the prisoner's Wife prevented him from qpiag :so. The magistrates liberated the prisoner on payment of five shillings. lidosney.—Before the Mayor (chairman), Messrs. F. Monks, J. W,IL,y ward. and S. Wright. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Thorpas Browne, no ad- dress ;Martin Lyon, Wigan ; Martin Towev, Scotland- road ; Margaret LAWIPSS, Acton Grange ; -.l.hn Collins, Chesterfield ; Margaret Gibbons. 7, Walsh's Yard ; Patrick Connolly, 1, Speakman's Yard, Old-road ;Frank Burke, 4, Fses Yard ; were dealt with for this offence. REFUSING TO QUlT.—Anni Quinn of no address was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Saturday night in Mersey-street, and with rousing to quit the sv Victoria Vaults arto also breaking a glass indow of the public house. Prisoner Was very abuslve in court and herto toep her quiet. prisoner 103. and crabs, also or- deredby her to pay the cost,of the windovlOs.; or its de- fault a months' imprisonment. . PITCH AND TOSS.—Johrs Griffin, 13, Pinners Brow was fined ss. and costs,.or seven )ri the chargeoSplay- lug pitch and toss in Pieshop Yard on Sunday after- noon .—Joseph Taylor. 63, Factorilane, and Ernest Graceson, 43, Nicholson-srreet; Veri. fined 'a' simP, r aintiunt for committing the &MO' offence in Factory.. yard on Sunday. DESERTION OF FAMlLY.—Michael Macnamara, last from Manchester. was c`.arged with running awas from Warrington on July 27th, 1892. and leaving two chil- dren chargeable on the Warrington Union.--Mr. fi. Shearer, inquiry officer said that prisoner's children had cost the Union -£l6 4r., and there had been a anecirl re- 'ward offered for his apprehension. gepad not been sea

since. the above date until Sunday.—Prisoner was sent to gam! for two months.- DESEETHE.—Georgo Watson was remanded to Strange- ways Gaol on the charge of deserting the South York- shire Regiment, stationed at Belfast Mace the 7th inst. r.c. Evans applied for and received the usual reward. Asset:Li. ON THE POLICE.—JEIDES Mannion, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Regent-st., on Saturday night and with assaulting P.C. Burrows at the same time and place. Prisoner was fined 53. and costs for being drunk, and 103. and costs for the assault on the constable, cr in default 14 days' imprisonment. DRIVING BRE n3LIC.ANS OUT.—John Murphy, Union- et., was charged with being drunk while in charge of brake and horse on Sunday..—P.G. Jones who proved the case said that prisoner had been driving a party of publ,cans out in the country, and had got too much drink. He (the constable) was obliged to get on the brake at Bridge Foot and drive it himselLand when they got to Market Gate, prisoner became so abusive that he was put in the brake and driven to the police station. Prisoner was fined ss. OBSCENE LANGTJAOIS.--WITI. Dumbell, 25, Greenall-st., was charged with using obscene language in Howley- lane, OD Oct. 4, to the annoyance of passengers.—Mr. Arthur Browne who appeared to prosecute, said the de- fendant had married the daughter of Mr. Fairhurst, a shopkeeper in Howley-lane,but they had been separated, and since then, defendant had continually caused un- pleasantness. On Saturday night he came before the shop and commenced to call his father-in-law all kiiils ot foul names. His father-in-law had taken out the sum- mons but he was prepared if defendant would promise not to coine to annoy him for six months, and pay the costs of the summons, he would consent to adjouin the case for six months.—This was consented to and the magistrates fell in with Mr. Browne's suggestion. PLAYING Jitors.--George and Thomas Ashton, 18, New-road, and Alfred Wilcock, Brown-st., were charge with playing a game of chance called jinks for money on Sunday.—P.C. Berry proved the case. The magistrates appeared to be somewhat in doubt as to whether pats Was a game of chance, but reprimanded defendants for playing on Sunday when they ought to be at church. They dismissed the cage. ALLEGED FILTHY SWEET MANUFACTOEY.—John Lee, 50, Academy-st., was charged that on Sept. 24th, he failed to keep his workshop used for manufactory 01 sweets in a clean state.—lnspector Norman said that de- fendant kept his workshop behind some property it 95, Mersey-st. He visited the shop on the above date and found that the slabs used to put the sweets upon were covered with excreta of hens, and hens were also in the place. The place had since been given up.—Defendant's wile who appeared in court said thet she always cleaned the slabs before they were used for sweets.—The magis- trates inflicted a fine'of ss. and costs. TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. E. J. Guest (chairman) Dr. S.

Smith and. Councillor J. H. Fleming. TEMPORARY Aurnomry.—Mr. L. Flood, applied for, and received temporary authority to sell at the Nag's Head Hotel. Sainsr AND DISORDERLY.—For this offence, the follow- ing persons were dealt with—Patrick Mahon, ss. and coats; John Cummings, 10s. and costs; Susanah Lee, dismissed on promising to leave the town. Taxer OF A SHAWL.—EIIen Walker, was charged with having stol, n from the dwelling-house of Bridget Ward, 5, Bay Horse Yard, on Sunday, the 23rd July, a shawl, value five shillings. Prisoner pleaded guilty. From the statement of the Chief. Constable it appeared that the woman had been living with the complainant, and on the date named, the prisoner suddenly disappeared, and the shawl was missed. Information was given to the police and the prisoner was apprehended by DS. Monaghan on Friday night. On being charged with the offence she replied that she had pawned it tor 2s. She was sent to goal for 14 days' hard labour. A ROW AT TEE CENTRAL STATlON.•—Caroline Bray, of Liverpool was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street, and also with assaulting John John- son at the same time and place. The evidence showed that the prisoner and another man load to be ejected from the station for being drunk, and also refusing to show the railway ticket. The prisoner seen lying on the parapet outside the station drunk, and using obscene language, by P. C. Turner. She refused to move away and commenced to kick and bite the officer. Johnson came the officer's assistance, and he Was kicked abiont the legs and bit on the thumb by the prisoner. She was fined ss. and costa or seven slays. IVEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough (chairman), ' Councillor J. H. Fleming, and Mr. John Geddes. LICENSE TRANSFERS.—Mr. Longland, solicitor, applied on behalf of Peter Lythgoe Hill,for temporary authority to sell at the Crow Inn, until the neat transfer day, the 6th November. The application was granted. The fol- lowing persons were alsc granted transfers r—E rtbeth Ann Coop to the Hop Pole, Wm. Waiter to the Unicorn, John Conroy to the Royal Arms, Bank-st. ; Tilos. Burke to the Bird in Band.

A DRUNKEN HUSBAND AND HIS WlFE.—George Pove,v, employed at Messra.Forshaw's boiler works,was charged with besting his wife, Martha, on Monday. From the evidence of the complainant it appeared that the prZsonet went to his work in the morning, but returned borne drunk at dinner time. He took some of his .lothing from upstairs and pawned them,and spent the money in more drink. On his going out again, his wife followed him and told the publican not to fill him any More, whereupon he run alter her and struck her. It was all caused through drink. The Chief , Con- stable said the prisoner had brutally treated the com- plainant for bver two years. The prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for six mouths in sureties of £2O, or two months' imprisonment. THEFT OF Boors.—John Sweeney, described as a la- bourer on tramp, was charged with stealing from the shop of Messrs Scales and Sons, the previous evening, a pair of men's laced up boots,value es 6d.Prisener pleaded guilty. The evidence showed that the prisoner was net by Sergeant Smith, who noticed something under the prisoner's coat, which was found to be a pair of boots, with the mice ticket still attached to it. Messrs.Snales and Sons identified the boots as theirs, and the booti had not been sold to the prisoner. He was sent to gaol for one Fnonth with hard labour. THEFT By Bois.—James Fiddler (12), and Samuel Fid- dler (8), living at Back Cros.4ley-st., were charged with stealing from the shop of James For•ter, 54, Mersev-t•t., a quantity of tobacco value 4s. James pleaded not guilty and Samuel guilty. The youngest brcther was seen in the shop by Mrs.Forster,and when asked what be wanted answered that his mother wanted a halfpenny- worth of snuff until Saturday. Be was refused, and on leaving the shop he was noticed to drop'a piece of to- bacco. The woman gave chase, but the youngtt.r, who WAS joined by his brother, were too quick for her, arid they got clear away. Mrs. Forster went to the boys' parents, and the tobacco was found near the fireplace. D.S. Monaghan went to the house and the youngest lad 'admitted taking the tobacco. They were each ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod, and to be de-. tamed until six o'clock.
Trwasnay.—Before Councillor James Fairclough (hi the chair.) . . .

A DESERTEIL—Thomas Oakes, was charged with being a deserter from the Ist Border Regiment, stationed at Woolwich, since the sth August last. The prisoner sur- rendered himself at Orford Barracks, the previous thy. He was remanded to Strangeways Gaol to await an eecort. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—Mr. G. Riley prosecuted in the following cases of irregular school attenda'oce William Lythgoe, glasscutter, Pcrtland-street • John Burton, forgeman, Haydock-street ; John Naylor, 42, Nayhr-street ; William Lomas, labourer, 16, Glazebrook- street ; thomas Kilcourre, 8, Town Hill; Mary Rounds, 2. Prince's-street; Patrick Sheening, tanner, 3, School Brow; Thomas Pemberton, 14, Charles-street ; and Sarah Ann Cho:goy, laundress, 29, Orford-lane.
TEMPORARY AIITHORITY.—James Payton was grantei temporary authority to sell at the beerhouse, 16 and 18 Greenall-street.
FRIDAY. —Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Alder-
man Wright, Mr. W. Pierpoint, arid Dr. Onrnall

listimmTs.—Elizalleth Massey, 4, ,Pmes'-hui di n g,s, was charged with assaulting and beating Sarah Harrison, 10, Jones'-buildings. on the sth inst. Mr. P. Davies appearod to prosecute. The assault was committed near Hi.ham's cutting shop, and was the upshot of some illfeeling be- tween the two parties. The magistrates bound the de- fendant over to keep the peace for six months, in the sum of £5, ani the costs.--Thomas Hogan, Cambria Place, was summoned for assauliing his wife, Jane, on the Ist inst. He was bound over to keep the peace for six Montt* and pay the costs.
WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. WEDNESDAT.—Before Mr. John James Bleckly.

DESERTER.--billa• Johnson Newton, was charged with deserting from the South I:ancashire Regiment, on or about the 15th September. P.C. Forbes (Newton) overheard a conversation the prisoner was having with some other men, which led him to go towards Johnson, who then ran away. P.C. Forbes gave chase, and caught him. Johnson then admitted being a deserter, and was wearing an army shirt at the time. The pri- soner had only joined the regiment in August. He was remanded to Strangeways to await an escort.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. J. Reynolds and Mr. P. Speakman. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—James McTurk, Catherine McConn, John Moore, Patrick Murley, Frank O'Brien, Jno. Ryan, and Robert Hackett were each fined for drunkenness; James Lawson and Alice Crank were each fined for using obscene and profane language. FIREWORKS IN THE STILEET.—Isaac Foster (14), was summoned for firing fireworks in Halton-road, and was ordered to pay 4s. 6d. costs. WIFE ASSAULT—John Edward Jones. of Weston, was summoned for assaulting his wife Ann Jones. The woman said she had been married twelve years and had four children. He had illused her more or less since she was married, and for the last six months he had thrashed her unmercifully many times. On Friday he " slat" her out of the house, and beat and kicked her until she was black and blue. She had since been afraid to return home and had had to sleep where she could.—The de- fendant was lined ss. and costs 14s. 6d., and the Bench also made a separation order the defendant to contri- bute les. per week to the support of his children. PIDING WITHOUT RElNS.—Williarn Moore, a carter, was fined 6d. and costs Us. 6d. for riding on his lurry with- out reins, at Aston.

WAP charged with being drunk and disorderly.—Super- ndent Atherton said there were three pages ot con- victions against the woman.—The Defendant: Yes I've been here over forty times.—Mr. Reynolds; The Bench have decided that you shall be kept sober.—The Defend- ant: Well lean% help it. The woman, who Was under the influence of drink created a great disturbance and was forcibly removed to the cells.

, lion of the game proved to be worse than the first, very little football being played. The homesters were pressed nearly the whole time, and off-side play on the part of Carey, who was playing hill-back, completely spoiled the game, the referee taking no notice whatever of appeals. On the whistle sounding after 25 minutes play a miserable display of football thus ended in a draw. RUNCORN " A" V. OLD EDWARDIANS "A."—The first meeting between these organisations took place on Saturday afternoon on the Irwell-lane enclosure before a fairly large gate. The match proved to be a thoroughly interesting one, it being of a fast and open character. , The display of footwork on the part of the visitors es- pecially was fine. They, however, lacked finish, and the result was that they only succeeded in crossing the Run- corn lines on one occasien, when Biekley secured a splendid try. The home team played an excellently combined game, and as a result of their aggressive work they obtained one goal and three tries, the brothers Robinson being responsible for three tries and Gayter one.

RUNCORN RECREATION V. RAINSOOMR (B BOUGHTON). —The Recreation team journeyed to Manchester on Saturday to play the Rainscough Football Club. No point was scored up to the interval. On re-starting, play was mostly in favour of the visitors, the home for- wards being completely overplayed, and it was only the good defence of their backs that prevented the Recs.mak- ing a big score. A fine piece of play on the part of Sut- ton and Harrison enabled the latter to score a try,Light- foot adding the premier point. Final score r—Runcorn Recreation, one coal; Rainscough, one minor. Ef ALTON V. SP RINCII-TA RD, Ru NCO RN. —The return match between these teams took place at Halton. The borne forwards by a combined rush enabled Brereton to score, and Smith kicked a goal. Splendid passing bv Brereton. Wilkins, and Foster enabled the latter to score but Smith failed at au easy place. In the second half Wilkinson scored and Potter improved. Halton won by two goals, 4 tries to nil.

DONATION BY MR. ACLAND, M.P. Mr. Acland, Minister of Education, visited his con- stituents at Rotherham on Wednesday, in an un-official capacity, to inquire into the extent oi the distress, and gave another £5O to the relief fund, making £llO in all.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

.• Secretaries of Poetlonli Clubs are requested to note that roporta of matches played on Saturday , must be gent to the head office. Bewsev-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. WIGAN.

It was with feelings of uncertainty that Warrington met on Sazurday, the team which holds the premier position in the statistical table of the competition, and also the team which has detracted, somewhat from the laurels which crowned metaphorically the winners of the cup last year. Wigan have so far won all their games in the League, defeating Salford and Rochdale Hornets on their own heaths, whilst particular credit is laid on the fact that the colliers' lines had not yet been crossed. The doings of our local team are too well known to need repeating here, suffice it to say that the latest performance against Tyldeslev bad given their admirers hope that the tide of ill-luck which had ap- parently set in had been stemmed, and the club would perform qnite up to its old reputation. There was a tremendous crowd when the teams entered the arena, and twice were the gates broken open by the colliers on strike. Warrington were without Nevins and Daktn, I whilst John Bate was still an absentee, leav;ng the captaincy in th.? hands of Evans. Wigan played their full strength. and at 3-40 Winstanley kicked off, and Boscow and Whitehead in turn exchanging the Warring- ton man eventually found touch at the Wigan quarter flag. Nothing of moment occurred during the first few minutes, until Evans and Bate passed well, and Thorn- Hey, fligham and Turner led the way to the line, only to be checked by Irow. ' Bate and Evans again passed, and Beesom was forward in accepting one, and ultim- ately Massey punting over the opposing backs, and the ball went dead Boscow was in One form, and kicked splendidly, his judicious punting end- ing in Warrington attacking once more. Some grand passing, in which Mitchinson, Seddon, Rigby, Winstanley, and Whitehead took part, ended in the last named going over the visitors' line, but, the ball was brought back for an infringement. Mitchinson, at Or this, punted to &scow, who unfortunately " mulled," and let Bollough and Whitehead get a "bulge" on him. Atter Winstanley had tried to drop a goal, Grundy made his mark off a kick by Bates, and Winstanley again es-ayed to send the leather over the bar. Wigan con- tinued to press, and at last Roberts got possession, ran along, and then passed to Unsworth, who got over near the corner. The place kick failed, and at half-time Wigan led by a try to nothing. During the interval an exhibition was given of the manner in which pigeons get goals. It was a very intellectual entertainment, and no d übt was intended to inspire the home placers The second half opened in the usual manner, and after each team had been penalised for off-side play, Winstanley gt.t possession of the ball in the visitors' quarters, and , dropped a goal. Then Warrington had a spell of press- ing, hut they could not break through the home defence. A mark was made by Potts in a good position, and the halt placed for Fair Turner, who failed to utilise the cnance. From this point to the end of the game, play was of an even character, each side in turn assuming the offensive, and though several individual attempts were made to score, the defence in every case was too good, and when the final whistle sounded the score was as fol- lows :—Wigan, I.dremped goal, 1 try (7 points) ; War- rington, nothing.—Teams :—Warringtoa : J. Boscow, hack :0, Potts, F. Heesom, and J. T. Massey, quarterbacks;three- James Bate and J.- W. Evans captain), half-backs; Fair Turner, J. Jol:ey, W. Bandies, J, Berry, E Bailey, r. Donohue; J. 'F. Thorniley, J. Taylor and J. Eligham forwards. Wigan :A. Trow, back; Whitehead, Seddon:Winstanley, and Roberts, three-quarter backs; Mitchinson and Halliwell, half-backs; Bosworth, Rigby, Lowe, M`Namara, Fairclough, Grundy, Arkwright, and Horrocks, forwards.

div.head: RUNCORN v. OLD EDWARDI&NS.
div.p: RUNCORN v. OLD EDWARDI&NS.

There was a very poor crowd indeed to give the Run- corn boys a welcome to Birmingham, the dull weather perhaps accounting for the lack of interest. The visi- tors, who won by two goals and& try to a try, have still got a lot of ability and pluck in the team:notwithstand- ing the absence of their crack three-quaiter, and in Abrams they have a leader as" up to date "as any go- ing, and who plays for his side right up to the finish. The game was not a particularly bright one, being some- what scrambling, and without polish for the most part, but one or two bouts of passing were extremely pretty— albeit the scoring was done from none of this if the first try of Runcorn be accepted. this was the result of some extremely pretty play between 'I aylor, Morris, and War- der. The forwards were not quite so smart as former packs we have seen, and Boughton is preferable to But- terworth at back. The three-quarters were better in defence than attack, strange as this may appear from the score. Abrams was quite himself, and played ad- mirably throughout. Of the Old Buys' play it is impos- sible to sky much in the way of prai-e. The pack appear to be a very sturdy let, the halves are all right, but on Saturday the three-quarters had certainly not got into theirstride properly, and combined but poorly.

WARRINGTON A V. WIGAN A.—These old rivals met at Warrington on Saturday to play their first match of the season. Warrington tiadan old score to repay, but they were unable tb do it, as history repeated itself, and now for two seasons in succession they have had to succumb to the superior prowess of Wigan. From the very com- mencement of the game the visitors started to press,and on one occasion lost a fine chance of knocking on, but they quickly returned to the attack in the mot deter. minded manner. Ed!eaten then showed up prominently, but in a very short space of time Taylor dodged in. Although the visitors' displayed very little football with regard to passing movements, it was soon evident they had the upper hand of their opponents. The dexterous manner in which the Wigan team used their feet was of immense service to their side. To make matters worse for Warrington, Westall had to retire with with a broken shoulder blade, leaving his companions to finish with 14 men. Edelsten twice in succession cleared splendidly, hut just on half time, Wigan made a fair mark from a foolish kick, Rawlinson placing a grand goal. With this advantage the ends were changed, Lawless, by some smart play, transferring the contest into Wigan quarters. The powerful rushes and kicking by Wigan soon removed any semblance of danger hut Erielsten cleared beautifully at the Warrington end. Ultimately Duckett secured the leather, arid running along touch easily eluded the weak tackling and get in behind the posts, the place failing. Several times Lawless showed up, on one occasion tackl- ing Duckett finely when this player was getting through. %Farrington then dribbled splendidly, but a flying kick by Rawlinson recovered all the lost ground, Wigan retir- ing winners by 1-2-3 to 0-0-0.

WIDNES v. MOSSLEY.—MossIey paid a visit to Widnes, and, although they made a gallant fight they were de- feated by nine points to five. There was a good gate, considering the distress which prevails in the town. The first half of the game was all in favour of Widnes, but a considerable time elapsed before the home team could , find an opening. At length, Wright scored behind the posts,a.nd great was the disappointment when Drummond failed at the easy place. Shortly afterwards, Widnes were awarded a free kick, and Brennan landed a goal. Towards the close of the first half Moseley made their i first attack on the home citadel, and Alford, n clearing, kicked the ball against Wrigley, who retained possession and scored an easy try. Lorrimer kicked a goal from the place. The second half was well contested throughout, but half way through Clarke made a brilliant run and scored for the home team. Brennan failed at goal. The game from this. point became rather rough, and the visitors were several times penalised. Nothing further was scored, and Widnes gained another vitory in the Competition by one goal (penalty) and two tries to one goal. The form of the home team was an improvement on the previous week, but their combination is still far from perfect. Brennan played a good game at back, and Bather was the best of the three•quarters. The forwards all played well. Mosley possess a fine hack in Eigland, and but for him the score against them would have been much heavier. Wrigley and Dawson also did good ser- vice for their side.

WARRINGTON ST. MARY'S V. PEMBERTON RECREATION. —Played at Warrington on Saturday in rather unsottled weather. The visitors kicked off, and play settled at midfield, where, from some neat passing by the Saints hacks, Burton rounded his opponents,and scored. Thomas failing a goal. The visitors' took the ball into the Saints 25, and spored from a rush by forward play, the place kick resulting in a goal. After the drip-out the game was of a very even nature, the home forwards holding their own, and nothing more being scored in the first half, the score stood—Pemberton, a goal; St. Mary's, a try. On re-starting the Rees had slightly the best of the game, and being heavier in the forwards gave the Saints backs a very poor chance, and the Recs. crossed the line again, the kick at goal failing. The ball being put in motion, the Saints' played up with determination, San- , tiers and Bill making several dashing runs, and after some rough sFrimmages the home forwards broke away, and ended in Thomas scoring. Berry failing at goal. The homesters played hard to win, W. Roughley making affairs look rather dangerous for the visitors, but thi home team had to retire' defeated by 1 goal 1 try to 2 tries.

STOCKToN TUTU v. WA"( lan's Ihniwetiv.—This match took place on Walker's ground, Arpley. Cares' obtained a try for the flame men but failed at place. The visitors again pressed the homestera back, and Crime obtaining, eluded several opponents. and threw nicely to Barber, who completed grand try, Glover just failing. After the drop out Cross had exceedingly hard lines, failing to 2a tiler the ball when a try was at his mercy. At half time nothir g further had been scored. The second por.

div.p: ASSOCIATION.

PENHETII VILLAGE V. HILLSBOROUGH SCHOOLS, FROD- snAH.—This ma:ch was played before a large number of spectators, on the recreation ground, Penketh, on Satur- day. The local team won the toss, and elected to play up hill during the first half. The ball was kicked off fr an the centre, and from the appearance of the play a stiff game was anticipated. At half-time the score stood Penketh, three goals; the School, nil. During the second half, the village team, owing to good combination, seemed to have it aU their own way and succeeded in closioe the game with the result of 13 goals in their favour, Hillsborough Schools nil.

WARRINGTON V. BROOKLANDS.--Mis match was played on Saturday, on the Cricket Ground, at Arpley, in fair weather and before a good number of spectators. Last season the visitors beat the then Cricket to the tune of seven goals to two, so a hard game was generally anti- cipated on Saturday. The game was of & vigorous and fast nature throughout, but the Warringtonians clearly showed themselves better in almost all departments than their opponents. Final score : Warrington four goals ; Brooklands, two.

FRIENDS' SCHOOL, PENRETH. V. FARbTWORTH GRAMMAR Scrtoot. (F.G S. OLD Boys).—This match was played at Penketh on Saturday. The visitors made things rather lively, and Barlow scored a goal for them. At length Sargent scored for the Friends with a high shot. Still p'aying strongly, and by good passing, Smith registered number two for the school, and at balf time the score was two to one in favour of Penketh. Final score— Penketh School, four; Farnworth Grammar School, one.
WARRINGTON RESERVE V. BROOKLAIMS RESERVE.-
This fixture was brought off at Brooklands on Satur- day, when the Warringtonians gained a victory by four go.tis to one. Pierpoint, Ogden, Plague; and Dandy scored for the visitors.

div.head: SCHOOLBOY'S EPISTLE.
div.p: A SCHOOLBOY'S EPISTLE.

A prcpos of children's letters, a correspondent of" The Spectator" has presented to that Journal a copy of a l'onuine letter" from a lad at school to his mother. After complaining generally of the school, and narrating some trifling mishaps that have befallen him,the young gentleman says :—" I hope Matilda's cold is better. I am glad she is not at schule. i think i have got con• sumption. the boys at this place are int gentlemanly, but of course you did not know this when you sent me here. i will try not to get bad habits. The trowsers have worn out at the knees. I think the tailor must have Cheated you, LID, buttons have come off, and they are loose behind. i don't Oink the food is good,but I should not mind if I was stronger. The piece of meat Isend you Is off the beef we bad on Sunday,but on other days it is more stringy. There are black beetles in the kitchen, and sometimes they cook them in the dinner, which cant be holesome when you are not strong. . . . do not mind my being so uncomfortable because i do not think I Shall last long. Please send me some more money as o Bd. if you cannot spare it I think I can borrow it of a boy who is going to leave at the half quarter, butper- haps you wd. not hke to be under an obligation to his 'parents as they are tradespeople. I think you deal at their shop.--yr. loving but retched son."

div.head: DUKE OF CONNAUGHT AND THE "QUEEN'S REGULATIONS." •
div.p: THE DUKE OF CONNAUGHT AND THE "QUEEN'S REGULATIONS." •

4 A. few days ago we, writes the "Daily Chronicle," discredited a statement that the Duke of Connaught ac- , cepted a costly silver casket as a parting gift from his 'Portsmouth staff officers. We are now informed that he not only did so but was entertained by them at a tarewell dinner in a Portsmouth hotel. Under these circumstances we have but to call attention •to paragraph . 8 section 7 of the cur- rent "Queen's Regulations," which has been worded 'substantially in the same way for years : • Deliberations or discussions amony any class of mili- tary men,having the object of convoying praise,censure, or any mark of approbation towards their superiors or any others in her Majesty's service, are strictlo pro- hibited as being subversive to discipline. Commanding 'officers are to prohibit the practice of raising suhicrip- tions for the purpose of presenting testimonials in any shape to superiors On quitting the service, or on being , removed from their corps. Every officer will be held responsible should he allow himself to be complimented 'by officers, non-ae,mmissioned officerS, or soldiers, who are serving, or who have served, under his command,bv means of presents of plate, swords, Sm., or by any col- lective expression of their opinion. Is there to be one rule for the Duke of Connaught and another for other officers?

Ira St. Petersburg every bicyclist is bound to have affixed to the back of his machine a metal plate on which the registered number ia displayed in figures large enough to be legible from a considerable distance. It something of this kind could be done in England it would be a little protection to the public against the " sccachers" who infest our highways.

Like Cleopatra of E2ypt, Queen Victoria has a sandal hearer. The office is hereditai y in the Earls o f Rothes, and the recently deceased Cnuntess claimed this privilege on the occasion of her Majesty's visit to the Tay Bridge, and presented Her Majesty with a pair of slippers in token of it.

div.head: GENEROUS GRANT FROM THE NORTH.
div.p: A GENEROUS GRANT FROM THE NORTH.

_ A ballot of Northumberland miners on Wednesday night, with the result that they have adopted a recom- mendation by tne committee, and voted £l,OOO to the I Miners' Federation, and £2OO a week while the members continue locked out. PECULIAR CONDITION TO A GENEROUS GIFT. A lady has sent a cheque for £lOO to Mr. Booth A. Coope, Farnworth, for distribution in Radcliffe*-cum- Farnwort h Division, for the relief of the distress amongst miners' families. A condition of the gift is that a copy of /Esop's fable "The Belly and the members "shall be given to each recipient of the relief ; £64 has been apportioned to the Farnworth district and £3B to Radcliffe. TEIE VICAR OF BURTONWOOD AND TFIE MINERS. . .

- The Rev. A. M. Mitchell, vicar of Burton Wood, Newtom-le-Willows, Lancashire, writes, describing the great distress among the miners in his district and the need for help. He adds :—" My attention has been drawn to a letter in Tuesday's" Standard," signed More No Nonsense. As one who knows something, if not a good deal, of colliers and their lives, I feel bound to pro- test against such cruel language. The man who can write in such a fashion must have a callous heart indeed and be little better, if anything, than a brute. Our colliers are not the monsters the brutal selfishness of 'More No Nonsense, would like to make them appear.

div.head: IMPORTANT NOTICES AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: IMPORTANT NOTICES AT ST. HELENS.

Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., .coalowner—s. of St. Helens and district, on Wednesday posted the following notices in their district, which comprises St. Helens, Haydock, and Golborne :-1. In accordance with the decision o: the Cealowners Federation, all the pits belonging to this company, will be opened for work on Monday, October 14th, 1893, at a reduction of 15 per cent, out of the 40 per cent, being equal to about 10 per cent, off present wages. 2. In order to relieve the pre- vailing distress, every man working will receive a sum of two shillings and sixpence per day during the first week, which will be paid in the afternoon of each day at the various pits. Boys and females will receive a sum of one shilling per day.

div.head: "UNIQUE INCIDENT."
div.p: A "UNIQUE INCIDENT."

At a meeting of the Executive of the Labour Electoral Association held in Bradford on Saturday, amongst thocie present being Messrs. Hobson (president), Milling- ton (vice president), J. Haslam (treasurer), W. Bailey (Notts Miners' Association), J. H. Wilson, M.P., W. Harvey (Derbyshiee Miners' Association), and Jamieson (Durham Miners' Political Association), Messrs. Haslam and Harvey, agents of the Derbyshire Miners' Associa- tion, reported that the funds of that Association having been exhausted, a considerable number of men had withdrawn their savings from the banks, ranging from sums of L 1 to as much as £lOO, and had unreservedly placed the money in the hands of their agents to be ii,ed to alleviate the distress. The amount so placed at the disposal of the officials was about £3,000. Several inembers of the Committee expressed the opinion that this was a unique incident in the history of trade unionism, and a resolution was adopted expressing high appreciation of the noble action of the Derbyshire miners. _ 10LONEL SEELY AND HIS COLLIERS. .

Instructions were received on WeTr-ead:Y. from Colonel Seely, M.P., at his pits in Derbyshire and Not- tinghamshire, which employ 4,000 men, that work be resumed at the old rate of wages. It is expected that the other large owners will follow suit. Colonel Seely, in tha course of his letter, says :—" It should be poihted out that we still think a reduction of wages desirable, and this in the interests cf the men quite as much as our own on account of the general depression in trade, the alteration in railway rates to the disadvantage of the Midland district, and the reductions which have been made in other districts. We are, however, unwilling to be in any way responsible for the great and increasing misery which the stoppage entails, and we think it is imperative that the pits should be started without de- lay." Colonel Seely suggests that the men should meet the owners during the winter and endeavour to arrange iome plan which will prevent the stoppages for the future.

div.head: FEELING IN NOTTINGHAMSHIRE. _
div.p: THE FEELING IN NOTTINGHAMSHIRE. _

The lockout in the Nottinghamshire colliery districts may now be said to be ended. Following the announce- ment as to the Babbington, Wollaton, and Clifton pits, intimation has also been given by Barber, Walker; and Co. to re-open at the former rates. Their colleries at Eastwood are amongst the largest in the Midlands, em- ploying some thousands of hands. Work was regumed on Wednesday at Stanton's pits, employing 2,000 men, and also at Broad Oak and Hurst Nc,ok pits. Five coalmasters on Wednesday refused the men's application for an advance of 121 per cent, but expressed willingness to meet the employees in confer- erica.

A Mansfield telegram states that there is great rejnitt- ing in the Leen Valley. The withdrawal of the notices affects something like 10,000 men in the district, and preparations for the resumption of work are being has- lily carried forward. Some of the masters have seen this defeat awaiting them, and have had men at work cleaning and repairing the pits ready for the resumption of work. A deputation of men waited upon the masters on Wednesday morning, and when it became known that the men were to resume work at the old rates the news spread like wildfire. Between Nottingham and Mansfield the principal pits will be fully employed by the beginning of next week. The Midland Railway will recommence the running of many trains which have been cancelled owing to the coal dispute.

div.head: MASTERS GIVING WAY.
div.p: MASTERS GIVING WAY.

At about eight pits in the Bolton district work has now been resumed at the old rate of wages, but in the case of Mr. H. Fletcher, at Little Levert Messrs. Scowcroft, of Rosehill ; and Messrs. Hardcastle, at Breightnet, an advance of 30 percent. has been conceded, to enable the men to meet the levy of is. per day which they are called upon by their union to contribute towards the relief of the miners still out. Mr. Herbert Fletcher has offered to give his men another advance of 30 per cent making GO per cent, in all, but the union say they do not want this. In the case of Darcy Lever Collieries, where about 1,000 men are employed, work has been resumed far about a week at the old rates, but dissatis- faction is now expressed because Mr. Settle, the proprie- tor,refuses to concede the thirty per cent advance which has been given at the pits above referred to. A deputa- tion waited upon Mr. Settle on Tuesday demanding the advanee.and an intimation was given that unless it was granted the men would again be brought out of the pits. Mr. Settle absolutely declined to accede to the demands, but promised to consider what course to adopt by neat week.and in the meantime the men will be kept at work. Work has been resumed at Messrs. Roscoe's Little Elul- ton Pits, the men having undertaken to submit to t reduction if the association generally has to submit to one.

The proprietors of reel Hall Collieries, Little Hutton, near Bolton, have intimated that their men may return to work on Wednesday at the old rate of wages, making the eighth firm which will have resumed work in the Bolton district.

div.head: AT lENIPTS AT CONCILIATION.
div.p: AT lENIPTS AT CONCILIATION.

Tho'Conference erranged by the Mayors of Sheffield, Leeds, Bradford, Nottingham, Derby, and Barnsley with a view to arriving as a basis on which the dispute in the coal trade might be settled took place at Sheffield on Monday. RepresentAtives of the Coalowners' and Miners' Federation were present, and for the first time since the struggle Wean, discussed together the position of affairs. The Mayors, at their own sug,gestion,left the room while the prineipals Of , both sides talked over the questions in dispute. At the end of two hours the Mayors were invited back again and informed that no agreement had been come to. Their worships then made a number of suggestions. The first was that, in view of the fact that the price of coal would not at once recede to the prices prevailing before the strike, the miners should be Allowed to commence work at the old rate of wages, and should submit to a reduction of 10 per cent, out of the 40 per cent, advanced since 1888 six weeks after the pits were opened and tree for work, say ma the 4th December. It was also suggested that repre- sentatives of teeth miners and coalowners should meet at an early date to formulate a scheme for the establish- ment of a tribunal of concilatiOn with a view to dealing with the question of wages. The members of the Coalowners' Association met at Derby on Tuesday, and had before them the suggestions drawn up by the, Mayors at the Sheffield Conference, with the proposals which the representatives of the men made at the same gathering. , The miners' representa- tivea, the Chairman (Mr. A. M. Chambers) stated, had proposed that the men should be allowed to resume work at the old rare of waets, and that immediately after the resumption the coalowners and the workmen should meet , and try and devise means of dealing with the wages 'question which would prevent such a dislocation of trade as now exists. The coalowners t Tuesday's meeting unanimously resolved that the proposal to resume work at the old rate of wages could not he entertained. After cordially thanking the Mayors for their interveotion, the meeting pivsed the following resolution:" That whilst reaffirming their conviction that the state of trade en- titled them to the reduction asked for, and regarding the present inflated prices as entirely artificial, yet, with the object and desire to end the widespread distress and general dislocation of trade, and in deference to appeals made to them as contained in the suggestions of the mayore, they make the following offer :—That the miners be allowed to commence work at a present re- duction of 15 per cent. mit of the 40 per cent, advanced since ISM and that pithead notices be given on Thurs- day that work can be resumed on Monday next, the 16th , inst., at that reduction." Another resolution provided ' for all the men being allowed to return, where possible snd as far as practicable, to their former places. The coalowners also agreed to meet the representatives of the miners at an early date with the object of agreeing upon a scheme for the establishment of a tribunal of concilia- tion, with the view of dealing with the question of future . advances or reductions of wages. The Lancashire and Cheshire Miners Federation held

a meeting at Wigan on Wednesday and discussed both the proposals of the Mayors and the resolutions pa,sed the coalowners at their meeting at Derby. The dele- gates unanimously rejected the proposal of the employers to resume work at a reduction of 15 per cent. They also refused to accept the suggestion made at the Sheffield Conference that they should accept a reduction ol 10 per cent in six weeks from now. Ihe other sugges- tions made by the Mayors were agreed to. A specially called meeting of the Miners' Federation of Gnat Britain was held on Thursday in Birmingham to discuss the proposal of the Federated Coalowners that the men should restart work at a reduction of 15 per cent, off the 40 percent. granted since 1888; at.d ,ilso to receive reports from the Sub-committee who attended the Mayoral Conference at Sheffield. The action of the Sub-cerhmittee was endorsed, and a vote of thanks to the mayors for convening the meeting was unanimously carried. On the motion of the representatives of the Derbyshire miners, seconded by the delegates from Lan- cashire, the following resolution was unanunou,ly adopted :—" That this Conference, while recognising and ap,areciating the good intentions of the mayors, at the same time is still of opinion that no reduction of wages is necessary, and none can be accepted ; and,fur- ther,we call upon all men to stay away from any colliery unless and until it is opened at the old rate of wages." The Conference then adjourned for the day.

div.head: TFIE DISTRESS AT WIDNES.
div.p: TFIE DISTRESS AT WIDNES.

On Wednesday afternoon the weekly meeting of the Catering Committee of the Widnes Distress Relief Com- mittee was held in the Council-chamber of the Town Hall Councillor Christie presiding. Accounts amounting to £228 4s. 9d. were passed for payment. It was decided to increase the number of hot-pots for distribution on Sunday next to I,llo.—Mr. T. Laws said the quantity of soup distributed by the committee from Gossage's Works was 17,225 gallons from the Bth September to the 10th October. Sundays were not included, and this made an average for twenty-nine days of nearly 600 gallons. On the Bth September 468 gallons were distributed, awl on the 10th inst. 674 gallons.—The general committee afterwards held a meeting, the chair being occupied by Mt. H. Wade Deacon.—The Chairman said that seeing the decrease in the income ana the increase in the expenditure, it would perhaps be better for the commit Pe to consider the advisability of continuing the distribu- tion of hotpots, and before passing the minutes of the Catering Committee perhaps they would hear Mr. Nil's financial statement.—Councillor F. Neil said the subscrip- tions last week amounted to only £ll4, against £l4O t he previous week, while the expenditure had increased to £228. The committee had spent from the commence- ment £Bl3 16s. 9d., and they now had in hand a balance lof £240. At the present rate of increase, however, rht would only be a week's supply. Something like 200 additional men had this week been discharged from the Widnes Alkali works, and the committee would thus see that they had a serious difficulty to face.—The question of continuing the distribution of hotpots was discussed at some length, but it was eventually decided to ;dee them next Sunday, and the minutes of the Catering Committee were confirmed. It was decided to make a further appeal for subscriptions. The Widnes Subscrip- tion Prize Band offered to give a sacred concert on the 22nd inst. in aid of the fund if the committee would provide a hall. The offer was accepted with thanks. MR. S. WOODS, M.P., AND THE SHEFFIELD CONFERENCE. On Tuesdaysa large meeting of colliers was held in the Assemnly Ball, Prescot. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. I'. Stott, and there were also present Mr. 8. Woi .ds M.P., Mr. T. Greenall, and others. The following reso- lution was proposed by Mr. Atherton, and seconded by Mr. T. Greenall :—"That this meeting of Preacot and Whiston miners, while fully recognizing the importance of an early settlement of the present unfortunate lock-out in the coal trade, are yet convinced that the present rate of wages is the lowest that can be accepted by the men." Mr. S. Woods, M.P., in supporting the resolution, said bethought it was a very wise interference on the part of the mayors. When the men met the masters after the mayors had retired, the miners' representa- tives made a proposal to the masters, but they did reit I see their way to accept it. He was not at liberi y to I 'mention that proposal, but it would be discussed tie the masters at Derby, and he hoped their better judg- ment would guide them, and that they would see their way to accept it. When the mayors were calted in ti make their suggestions the amount of reduction was left blank on the forms. The miners' representatives were naturally anxious to know what that amount was to be. The mayors said that they thimete 10 per cent would be a fair amount. (Laughter.) Mr. Woods then read the suggestions of the mayors to the meeting, and said he agreed with every one of them except that part relating to the reduction. He told the mayors frankly at the time that from his know- ledge of the determination of the men they would not accept the reduction. He told them frankly that he thought that part of the suggestion which related to the 10 per cent.would defeat the scheme. He suggested that the clause should be withdrawn,and that the men should go to work at the old rate of wages : and that after they had gene to work a conciliation board should be forineti to deal with the price of coal in future, and that neither party should be pledged to anything ; but that af' er a_ certain time, if the masters found themselves in difficel- ' ties,any proposition they made would receive the fullest consideration at the hands of the working men. He could only say this, if there was the slightest possible chance of keeping the present prices of coal up, the men would be entitled to 100 per cent. on their present rate of wages. (Hear. hear.) The price of coal was now 30e. per ton ;in London it was nearly 3. The price of conl when the men came out was only from 9s. to 104. per ton. They were now facing the winter ; was it not pro- bable that the price of coal, which was 10a. in July, cud be maintained at 14s. or 15s. per ton to the end id March next? On the face of it, therefore, would it not be much better for the mayors to have left out the pre- position for a reduction, and let the wage question be dealt with according to the state of trade and the price of coal in the market ? (Applause.) He believed that when the men got a 40 per cent, advance the employers got 50 per cent. OD the price of coal. It wee a gis at tactical error on the part of the masters to try and force a reduction upon them, and he thought almost every coalowner now believed that it was a fatal error. If the employers would only accept a fair proposal tor the men to resume work at the old rate of wages, without any mention of a reduction, the matter could be considered together at a conciliation b where the miners' representatives would perhaps put some backbone into owners who were underselling their brethren. (Laughter and applause.) When the miners' representatives at the Conference objected to the 10 per cent, reduction the Mayor of Sheffield did not like it, and told the men's representatives that if they refused this offer the public sympathy and generosity would be taken away from them,and probably the members would be leaving their Federation. (Laughter.) He told the Mayor that that was rather a one-sided suggestion. There were two Federations, and it was quite possible the country might think the terms very hard in the face of the present state of affairs. He pointed out that it was just within the range of probability that the masters might be leaving their union.—(Laughter and applause.) It was ten thousand times more probable that that would be the result. The masters were leaving the Federation in shoals, and if it had not been for the meeting on Mon- day no doubt other collieries would have been opened for work. During theten weeks of the struggle he had not come across a miner willing to accept a reduction, and so long as the men were in that state of mind lie would be the last to suggest that a reduction should be excepted. If the masters at Derby did not accept the proposal the men made to them on Monday—and which he was not at liberty to divulge—the leaders of the Federation would be bound to ask the men to ballot on the scheme sug- gested by the mayors. He did not want one word he had said to influence their votes,and if they accepted the suggestions they would be loyally carried out.—(Ap- plause.) The resolution was carried unanimously.

div.p: OUR LOCAL CIFUR,CHES-WARRINGTON.
THE P.S.A. AT WYCLIFFE CHURCH.

The usual P.S.A. meeting in Wycliffe Church, on Sun- day afternoon, was well attended. The chair was occupied by Mr. A. Birch, who considered the churches in the past had neglected their duty to the working- classes, and had lacked sympathy with them which accounted in a largemeasuro for their non-attendance at places of worship. The address was delivered by the Rev. E. T. Reed, of the Emmanuel Reformed Church, who spoke on" Reconciliation" in three aspects; namely between canital and labour, in families, and between God and man. The musical portion of the service was considerably enhanced by a solo by Mrs. R. U. Pearson, and a violin solo by Mr. Pearson. The accompanist was Mr W. H. Payton. The devotional part of the service was conducted by the Rev. J. Yonge. The membership of the brotherhood has now reached 935.

ST. OFIN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH. The Sunday school anniversary sermons in connection with the above-named church were preached on Sunda' by the Rev. John Huey, M.A., 8.D., of Manchester. There were large congregations at both morning and evening services. At the morning service the preacher chose for his text "And Samuel grew in favour with (iod, and also with man." The choir under the conduc- torship of Mr. B. Wadsworth, the organist, rendered the anthem "Incline thine ear to me," (Hammel). The solo part was taken by Mr. P. Berry. The harvest anthem "Lord, how manifold are thy works" (Barnby), was given at the evening service. ELLESMERE-ST. MISSION. At this Mission on Sunday night, Mr. and Mrs. Evens, of the Liverpool Mission, conducted a revival service. The place Was crowded, and Most encouraging results were obtained. Mr. Evens conducted the former part of the service and Mrs. Evens, who also sang "Ashamed of Jesus," conducted the latter part. This service was the conclnding service of Mr.and Mrs. Evens in the War- rington district, after bolding a most successful week's services at the Sanicey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel.

div.head: OCTOBER.
div.p: OCTOBER.
TILE GOLD FEVER. A CHAPTER OF AUSTRALIAN HISTORY,

That most valuable series of historical works known as .!* The Story of the nations," tas just been brought to a close by the issue by Mr. Fisher Unwin of the 35th volume---' Australian Commonweath," by Mr. Greville Tregarthen. A compact, well written and realiable trea- tise on the discovery, colonising and growth of Austra- lia was much needed, and this book adequately fills the blank space in the library. It is a succinct and enter- taining sketch of the rise and development of the great English ofhhoot. Its policy, customs, commerce, and natural features are lucidly described, and the follo,wing summary of one of the most entertaining chapters—that on the gold-mining industry—will give some notion of the contents and the other 32 sections into which the book is divided.

TIIIC FIRST ERSH. In view of recent events, it is, perhaps, satisfactory to learn that the feverish excitement which accompanied ihe birth of the mining industry in Australia was pro- bably all the more acute owing to the extreme depressir n which immediately preceded it, for it is a somewhat re- markable fact that, although only a small portion of the auriferous area of the continent of Australia has been explored, and a still smaller portion properly developed, so that the chances of marvellous finds are as great as ever, there has never since the rush between 1851 and 1859 been anything resembling the overmastering fas- cination which the search for the precious metal at first exercised Of course every now and then there is what is commonly called a " boom "in mining circles, but no considerable number of persons have been attracted from other pursuits. SAULT PROPRETS. It was well known by many in Australia that the precious metal had been found in the Bathurst district; and from time to time, since the very early days of occupation, reports had been 'made to the authorities l concerning the discovery of gold in various places. As far back as 1823 there is an entry in the field-book of a surireycr named James Mcßrain, under the date of February 18, which runs :—" At eight chains, 50 links to the river, and marked gum-tree—at this place I found numerous particles of gold in the sand and in the hills adjacent to the river.' The river referred to is the Fish River, about 15 miles from Bathurst. Again in 1839 Count Strzlif cke found gold,and informed the Goverw,r, ' Sir George Gipps, and although he was requested by the authorities to suppress as far as he was able the knowledge of his discovery, for fear of the gold fever rendering the convicts unmanageable, and • disturbing the settled industries of the country, there can be tittle doubt that the fact was disclosed to a large number Of people. In 1841 the Bev. W. B. Clarke found gold in the M.,cquarie Valley in the Vale of Clwydd, and stated that he was convinced that the metal would be met with in large quaetities in various localities throuhout New South Wales, and for some time previous to 1851, a shepherd named McGregor had, while tending his flocks, collected particles of gold, while other tersons had not unfrequently come across small deposits.

AN ENTHUSIAST. A man named Hargreaves, who was one of the numer ous adventurers who left the colony in 1848 for Cali- fornia, was much struck on his arrival there, with the great resemblance between the gold country and some of the places which are well known to him in Australia. The more he pondered upon the likeness, the stronger grew the conviction that there must be gold, too near his old home. Each day he felt more forcible inipelled to return to Australia and test the accuracy of his sur- mises.. At last he could resist the inclinations no longer, and on February 12, 1851, his enterprise was rewarded, and he succeeded in finding gold in the Lewis Ponds and Sumnderhill Creeks, and the very spots which had been in his mind during his sojourn in California. After this find the rush to the goldfields before long seriously affected other industries, and the apprehensions of col- lapse from stagnation was converted into fears of ruin from too great speculation. Indeed it was urged upon the Government by some of those engaged in pas- toral and agriculturnl pnrsuits, that martial law should be proclaimed, and all gold digging peremptorily pro- hibited in order that the inducement which seemed so irresistible for persons to quit their ordinary occupation might be removed. It is needless to say that such an absurd request was not entertained for a moment. GOLD IN CHUNKS. It is not surprising that ordinary methods of gaining a living became unattractive in the face of sane of the early finds of gold. He would, indeed, be a cold-blooded philosoph, r whose mind would not he inflamed by such a discovery as that made' by Dr. Kerr on the Turon. This gentleman, or rather a native employed on his tation, discovered accidentally a lump of gold weighing about 1061 b., and worth about £4,500; another mass of gold was unearthed in November, 1858, at Burrandong, near Orange, which after melting at the Mint, yielding £4,389 worth of the metal; and the Brennan nugget which was sold in Sydney in 1851 realised £1,156, while numerous other finds Of a similar character were quite sufficient to tempt even the most cautious to try their fortunes at the diggings. This condition of things, how- ever, did not last very long, and the alluring dazzle of the gold-seeker's life gradually became dimmed by the privation, discomfort, and disappointment which, as the nor bens of miners increased, and the alluvial beds became eXhaul od, In the majority of instances, were all that was experienced on the goldfields. In consequence, people rOurned to their former occupation in less fascinating but MOM safe and permanent paths of industry.

div.head: MR. TOM MANN'S SERMON. "IRRELIGIOUS CHURCHGOERS."
div.p: MR. TOM MANN'S SERMON. "IRRELIGIOUS CHURCHGOERS."

REMARKABLE DEMONSTRATIONS. The following is a report of the sermcn delivered at St. Thomas's-square Chapel, on Sunday evening by Mr. Tom Mann :—Mr. Mann commenced the service by reading some extracts from Matthew Arnold's poems. Mr. Mann said the under]) jug principle upon which his remarks would be based were in the words of Jesus, taken from St. John X.. 16, "And other sheep I have which are not of this told. Them also I must bring, and they shall hear My voice. There shall be one fold and one Shep- herd." Ile said persons might question his right and authority to condemn in a wholesale sort of way institu- tions which had existed for centuries, but in thechurches there was something seriously and shamefully lacking. There were tens of. thousands of young men and young women who regularly attended places of worship with the best intentions. They were influenced for good or for ill—he feared in many cases for ill (cheers and loud hisses). Ile did not find that the people who were closely identified with churches exhibited the requisitti capacity to understand wherein evil existed, nor did they show an earnest desire to uproot the evil in ordt r that good might take its place. Goodness existed. The human heart was a good heart. There was much that was good in every human being. There was very little that was evil in the average man and woman, herwise they would not struggle as they did year in and year out against the most adverse conditions which it is impossible 'to imagine. These people went on strug- gling, wosking, and never enjoying anything saving the reflection that they had done their best. Lie honestly believed in religion. Some people seemed to think that he ought to apologise for daring to claim to be a religious man. Be had no apology to make to any man or to any society. (Cheers.) His opinion aas that many of those who attended churches were distinctly irreligious. (Loud hisses.) By heavens ! they might hiss, but let them look at the destitution of the East-end, at their insanitary houses, the prostitution in the streets, the misery that everywhere existed. (Cheers and hisses.) Order was the first law of nature: but where was the order of the present industrial system? Did they see the orthodox churches and the orthodox church officials coming forward because of their religion —not in spite of it—and delving to the root of the evils in order to destroy them and to prevent their existence in the future. (Cries " Yes" and 6' No.") Why did the average orthbdox man and woman attend church ? Not for the purpose of gathering the increasing amount of knowledge to enable them to overcome the evils which existed, but they did attend in order to fall into a little respectable niche. (Loud hisses and cries of " False.") Some of his friends were apparently getting stung. (11.4 newed hisses.) Be reasserted that those pr.,- pie aid not attend church for the purpose of endeavour- ing to understand the difficulties he had mentioned. When it was suggeste3 that the church should endeavour to grapple with industrial difficulties they professed the most complete astonishment. Those people were bound down with an amount of class prejudice the like of which I had never been seen before--(cheers and renewed hisses) —they had much hypocriay in London churches and chapels asthe whole world beside could show. (Lend hisses.) Captains of industry went to church and mum- bled the Lord's Prayer, and then for the remaining six days of the week violated every principle contained in that prayer, and sweated their fellows without remorse. (Cheers.) The essence of religion was to be found in working for the common good, and he appealed to all to place themseves in the grand army which was endeavour- ing to make the world brighter and better, and to found a brotherhood of man. (Cheers.)

div.head: WARRINGToN MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. TORY DISORGANISATION. REVOLT AGAINST THE PUBLICANS.
div.p: WARRINGToN MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. TORY DISORGANISATION. REVOLT AGAINST THE PUBLICANS.

The most notable development ot the week in connection with the !municipal elections is the revolt of a large portion of the most intelligent Conservatives against the domination of the publi- cans. For some time past the local Conservative machinery appears to have been" run " entirely hi the interests of the brewers and publicans. Conser- vative magistrates have been expected to safeguard on the bench the interests of tnis dominant section of the party, and at the present election there is manifested an undisguised and insolent determina- tion to" pack" the Town Council with nominees at the liquor trade. No fewer than four out of the nine Conservative candidates are directly engaged in the liquor traffic. The tradesmen of the town many of whom are supporters of the Conservative party, and all of whom are large ratepayers and deeply interested in the good government of the town, are being completely ignored. This, as we have said, is too much for the more intelligent section of the Tory party, and dis- Censious have broken out in several directions.

In the Town Hall Ward, which is essentially a tradesmen's ward, Mr. Shillcock, landlord of the " Bay horse " Winwick-,greet, was selected at the Conservative ward mentiug as the candidate to oppose the retain of Councillor Fleming. This selection was received with oisfavour by an influen- tial section of the Conservative residents in the ward, but it was confirmed, in spite of an amend- anent, at the meeting of the Conservative Council on Monday evening—a meeting which, we ars told, was" packed "by licensed Victuallers from all part of the town. In spite of this, Mr. W. P. Skelton, of riorsemarkiVostreet, In response to an invitation, has determined to iVght the ward 68 an independent Conservative. Mr. Shiticock has issued which we we may fairly call comic election address in which he declares that "he is moderate in his views of thing in general."

As we have before announced, the retiring coun- cillor, Mr. J. H Fleming, is the Liberal candidate for the Town Hall Ward. Mr. neming's services to the town as a councillor are incontestable, and it may be confidently expectAd that he will be re- turned with a substantial majority.

--- As yet the fight;is being carried on most briskly in hitecross Ward. Councillor H. Roberts, who an., been again selected to champion the Liberal cause, is promoting 'his 'candidature with characteristic vigour. On Tharsday night he addressed one of the largest ward 'meetings ever held in Warring- ton, and his candidature was enthasiastically en- dorsed. 'Tbe cieech delivered by Mr. Roberts was aaable mid lucid review of practically the whole circle of Corporation business. It is reported in fall in atietter column,it is well worth the peru- sal of evetytatepayer, and especially of the rate- payers of iroitecross Ward. Mr. R. T. Smith who, after muck persuasion was induced by the Conser- vatives to come torwiLd in this ward, has no past services to appeal to, and no one anticipates that the butresses will have the sligh test difficulty in coming. to the conclusion that he is not likely to watctrand to promote their interests as Councillor Rabeta is able to do.

la. St. John's ward the Liberals have secured an etteklent candidate 'in Mr- W. Furniss to oppose th'eteturn of Councillor Shaw. Mr. Furniss's ad- dms will be found in our advertising columns- As M.r.Furniss has tived amongst the electors of the ward from boyhood upwards, and as his business is in the district., he is much better qualified to look after their interests than Mr. Shaw who has no 'personal connection with the ward. There are, besides, pretty much the same objections to be made to Mr. Shaw that so many Conservatives are making to Mr:Shillcock.

It is srid that dissensions are about as rife amongst the Conservatives in the Orford Ward as in the Town'Hall Ward. Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, solicitor, t inwick-street. was asked to contest the ward against Mr. Wtn. Pierpoint, who will repre- sent the Liberals. Mr. Jenkins consented, subject to the sanction ot the Conservative Association,but it is sai4 that there is a great divergence of opinion as to Who should be selected.

In the other wards of the town there is little change-/rom last week to be reported. At a meet- ing of the Liberal committee for Fairfield ward held on Thursday evening it was decided to invite 31r.5. Mounfield, jun., to stand, but Mr. Mounfteld has not yet given his decision. div.head: DREADFUL MURDER OF AN OLD COUPLE
div.p: DREADFUL MURDER OF AN OLD COUPLE

On Thursday morning af, caretaker named Thompson, residing in Kirkstall-toad, Leeds, was found in his house murdered. His wife, greviously wounded, was lying at his side. During the night some person, armed with a heavy hammer, entered the dwelling and attacked the old couple. Their son is suspected, and it is alleged that he was prompted to commit the crime in the hope of 'securing his mother's fortune.
ALLEGFD CHILD MURDER BY A LANCASHIRE MANUFACTURER;

Ashwr.rth Read, a Burnley manufacturer, was charged on remand on Thud* r at the Manchester City Police Court, along with Ehzabeth Ann Remington, a domestic -servant formerly in his employment, with murdering the illegitimate child of the latter. A further charge against Read was that he was an accessory both before and after the murder. The prisoners were again remanded.
