SPEECHES BY MR. F. MONKS, J.r., c.c., COUNCILLOR ROBERTS, & OTHERS.
REVIEW OF MUNICIPAL WORK.

A very largely attended meeting of the electors of Whitecross ward was held on Thursday evening, in St. Barnabas schoolroom, forth° purpose of bear- ing an address from Councillor H. Roberts, the Liberal candidate. The schoolroom was filled trom one end to the other, and the meeting throughout was of an enthusiastic character. The chair was taken by Mr. F. Monks, J.P., C.C., and amongst , others present, besides Mr. and Mrs. Roberts, were , Councillors Flood, and Beaman, Messrs. T. Morris, W. Pierpoint,J.P., S. Wright, J.P., J. W. Hayward, J.P.,James Evans,(chairman of the ward), J. Haley. T. Hawthorne, S. Blythe, A.. B. Bailey, A. Birch, and aeaeral other gentlemen closely associated rith Councillor Roberts' candidature. ,- Mr. T. MORRIS, who was unable to stay through the Meeting and was called upon to speak by the Chairman, said that Mr. Roberts was one of the best tried men in the Council Chamber. (Applause.) He was a man who had got his opinions end who knew how to express them. There were a good many who had no opinions and no method of expressing them. (Hear, hear and laughter.) He could not understand how it was that the other side should try to push the best man out of the Council unless it was that they were afraid of tho Liberals getting the best hand of them. (Hear, hear.) He advised the voters of Whitecross ward to give Mr. Roberts such a majority that the Conservatives would think thrice before bringing any man to oppose him again. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, said the first thing he had to say in reference to this election was that in view of the prevailing distress which existed In the town, he thought it was nothing short of absolute t folly if not criminality, to waste money in contested elections. (Heir, hear.) He didn't know who was rep , ponsible, but he judged from what be saw in newspapers, that the Conservative party were re. Avenen., ale for what they called fighting every ward ' town. He hoped that wiser counsels would . al 'tkas4 and that after all there would not be Nei t be tput , and that their fellow townsmen would et. to the expense of having to pro ,e.eee''' e__ ee e machinery that was absolutely necessa• „,„"MtbeLeigs% 67: contest in all the wards of the borour.n7 4" if it was to be done, and they were in for a fieet, be *les :.egngujug enough to believe that Whitecroes War d 'Would be able to give a very good account of itself . ilrerettrence to , i iv l Mr. Roberts' candidature—(alePlaleass)— speaking i fog I himself, he had known Mr. Rai:ler:a -ntvr-ferveYY'laggi time. He had known him Irma a beyosae elle siegea watched his career with vet', vet at interekt: Be thoughei, ..his career was one of which hia fellow townsmen might- well be proud of. (Hear, he' ,sr) Mr. Morris said ?dr. Roberts was able to give expression to , his 'ides and he could give e* xpression -to his thoughts sometimes in a ocaey . caustic way. 'He ethe speaker) bad no de' übt some Conservatives had felt the sting of Us remarks, and ' that might to some extent have created a feeling against him in refer- ence to his election +.O the Council. But every man who was worth his, salt said things sometimes that were not pleasant for somebody to hear, and the man who had not got an enemy, was in his. 'opinion a rather milk and water sort of a chap. That was not altogether a political meeting. But one could not altogether divest oneself of the fact. that whatever you might say of it,it must patteke more or less of the nature of a .political contest. Unfortun- ately he (the speaker) was one connected!, and very actively connected with the election in 1868, because he was very actively engaged in the Liberal party. They macie a very serious tactical blunder, and he must say they did not serve the Conservative party either fairly or considerately. If he had known what he knew shortly afterwards, he should have acted upon the impulse of the moment and walked out of the room and attended , a meeting which had been convened in the ordinary , way. Mr. Roberts knew that he had regretted the stepl , that was taken on that night, and he always considered it a blunder from even a party point of view. But he said this that although the Liberal party at that time were responsible for that blunder, they had been made to bite the dust a good many times since then and made to bite the dust insuch a way that he declared if he was of the Liberal party, he would fight until he had won' 1 the borough back again to Liberal principles, and teach them a lesson as to how they should conduct themselves (loud applausea He thought that the Conservative party had treated the Liberal •party most shamefully. They had not only put in young unexperienced men over the heads of older experienced ME n. but in the case of that old friend of theirs—Mr. John Greening—to whom the election of Aldermanship would have been a compliment which he would have appreciated—and they knew it—and although they knew it, and that his state of health was such that in the nature of things he could not enjoy it for a long time, yet they 'lfully and de- liberately and of set purpose put a young man who had never done one-tenth part of what he had done i for the borough of Warrington, in a position to which Mr. Greening was fairly entitled. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) Theysaid that a man who prophesies should , know beforehand,but there were some times when a taan might fairly venture to hint at, based upon a long expe- rience, and he did not hesitate to say this, that in his opinion the Conservative party by their present tactics, were sowing the seeds of their own discrganisation, and their own disruption. (Hear, hear.) Of course it rested with the Liberal party to fight its own battles consis- tently and fairly, because no one ever permanently gained anything by what was unfair or sh idv. (Hear hear.) With reference to politics, Warrington had ever since he was a lad always hung more or less on the balance and it depended entirely upon the candidates os to whether the 'return was Liberal or Conservative. For many years their old friend Sir ;Gilbert Greenall was a very popular man and he had a very strong following, and the Liberals were never able to brings man to com- pare with him in popularity except their good old friend Mr. McMinnies. (Applause.) Wnenever the Liberal party could bring such a man equal to Mr. McMinnies to take tbe field again the return for Warrington, he would venture to say would be Libeial (Hear, hear.) From a party point of view, he did not think the i Conservatives were acting wisely by forcing contests at a time like this, and by ignoring altogether the services of their opponents. Their . tactics at this time he felt sure would mot meet with the approval of the more thoughtful and more sensible of their fellow townsmen. With regard to the work done in the Council by Mr. Roberts, when he was in the Council himself, he was observant of the men who did work,and he could always say this that for the amount of time, Mr. Roberts had at his disposal, and for the duties he undertook, he always found him to be a most valuable member. He had shown by his speeches, and by the way in which he had taken up any question, not only sound judgment, but pluck and discretion besides. (Applause.) Speaking with regard to Mr. Roberts and his ability he could say from his own experience, and from what he knew of the work that had to be done in the Council Chamber, Mr. Roberts was by far away, the best man. (Applause.) He (the speaker),was not a member of the Council, but he was Chairman el the Museum and Library Committee, and i the Technical Instruction Committee, and he knew that 1 Mr. Roberts gave them very valuable help, and his ser- viees they would be exceeding sorry to lose,through any action of the voters of Whitecross Ward. There was a big work to be done in connection with Technical educe acion. His only regret was that the young men of Warringten did not seem to take alvantage et the oppor- tunity which they had. When he looked back upon the opportunities that many of the older men had 40 years , ago, as compared with the enormous advantages they possessed to-day, he could only say that in his opinion the young men of Warrington were mak- ing a mistake in not joining these classes. All the real upward progress of the working people must be obtained by the development of their own intelligence, by the development of their own integrityeand by the develop- ment of their own frugality, thriftiness and common , Renee. lie remembered that very nearly 40 years atp, he was anxious for the develeptuent of the industrial co-operative movement in Warrington, and along with several others he attempted to organise labour in such a form that it would receive its fair share, not only of what it earned, but also of the capital it employed. He ventured to say that had it not been for the ignorance, for the jealousy, and for what he called the pigheaded- ness ot the wiredrawers ef Warrington, if that day they would have had such an industrial concern in Warrington as would have astonished every man in it, and practically made every wiredrawer of that generation independent to-day. (Applause.) Some day he hoped to be able to give the history of that time, and of that co-operative movement, which he thought would be interesting as indicating what might have been done by a reasonable amount of capital at that time,and what could have been done then is possible now. He ventured to say that was the only true and legitimate way in which the workingpeople of this country could be lifted to that platform of comfort, intelligence, and independence which they all desired to obtain. (Loud sheers.) , Councillor H. ROSSITS upon rising, WAS greeted with loud and continued applause.- fie said : Ladies and gentlemen. I shall have to ask your indulgence a little to- night, as I have come from home feeling very much in. disposed . and in fact, an hour ago I did not think I should have been able to get here at all. But knowing what a keen disappointment it would have been to many of my friends, to say nothing )f the disappointment to myself, I have made an effort, and here I am. Well, gentlemen, I think the attendance at this meeting to- night is a broad and fair proof of what the remit is go- ing to he on the Ist November next. Three 3'ears ago we had a fight in this ward, and the electors did me the honour to return me at the head of the poll by a majority ,of 193. (Hear, hear.) Ido not think it likely, consider- ing the way in which I have been treated by the electors of this ward during the past three years, that the majority will be any less on the first of November then it was three years ago. It is perhaps only fair to myself that I should explain briefly my action during this period in regard to them. We fend out a long time ago that on the old Sanitary Committee,there was onlyroorn for one man's opirrion,and unless the other members'a the committee were prepared to fellow in a tame lap-deg kind of fashion, the views of the then chairman of the committee, there was no fur- ther comfort for us, and we must either retire from the arramit tee, or live in a state of perpetual fend with the &airman. The same condition of things took place When your preseritchairman was a member of the Sani- tary Committee. I thought the opposition to Alderman urges then wasonerely personal, but ,I have changed ray opinion. I have had the same bitter personal experience of the disposition of that gentleman as your chairman has. The work *which was included within the scope of the Sanitary Committee was itself so enormous, that it was utterly impossible for it to be done with anything like efficiency. It was absolutely necessary, if proper attention was to be paid to important municipal govern- ment, the committee would have to be divided into two separate ceortmittees. That was the beginning of the controversy. As soon as that was proposed, our difficul- ties with the chairman began. After so many years holding theposition of chairman and dictator on these matters, when the Council decided on a sub-division of labour, he perceived that it meant his removal, or his being only chairman of one Committee. The trouble began to assume an acute phrase when the then Alderman Burgess presented to the meeting of the Sani- tary Committee a tender from Messrs. Manlove, Elliot and ern., which, upon inquiry, we found had never been advertised for, and had not even received the sanction of the committee of Longford works. This was going too far. We protested against it, and the result was that it was referred back. After a time, we obtained another tender, and we accepted that tender after it had been duly advertised for,ln the face of the whole world. The tender we accepted was,'l believe I am right, nearly .£301) less than the tender which we had refused to ac- cepts few weeks before. When we accepted this new tender, we were immediately told that we were infring— . . .

complaint alleged against him. VLoud laughter and ap- plause.) Somebody is obliged to talk and if the talk is miideAlp of eonnd common sense I think it is the popper thing to talk. (Hear, hear.) I hope that Ido not waste the time ()Woe Council and trouble the attention e the

ratepayers too much, who frequently tell me that they have. read any speeches. (Hear, hear.) One thing is certain, if I had not talked so much there would not be the present'oonditinn .bf things in the town. (Hear, hear.) Anothv objection was that I know too muzb. (Laughter.) Well/ I believe that is partially correct. I will "t adnilt the sbft Impeachment" to this extent: I know too much for some yeople, and they find it out sometimes. (Hear, hear and applause.) I have a fault and I will admit it. I frequently say things which perhaps are stronger than some people like. Still, I cannot help it. 'Nobody gets harder kicks than I do, and my dispositions is such that if a man kicks me he is going to get kicked back again—(hear, hear, and laughter,) —on the first opportunity I have of ad- minstering a little personal castigation. (Hear, hear.) So much by way of preliminary. Now let me say this, further: this is not a political fight; if it had been your Chairman would not have been here to-night. (Hear, hear.) This is a question effecting the good govern- ment of the electors of this ward, and the electors of this town. (Hear, hear.) I do not know in what sense Home Rule has got to do with municipal Government ; I cannot see the connection. (Hear, hear.) So far as the last three years are concerned, there has been no politi- cal question, except the appointment of Lfdermen and Mayors, that has occupied the time of the Council for five minutes at a time. It is, therefore, nonsense for any- body to say that they are bound to v.to Liberal or Tory. (Applause.) they have got to do the best you can for youpelves and for the town, and if you think that that purpose will be served better by sending Mr.,, Smith, then send Mr. Smith and let me have a rest. I,

inga patent,and further than that, there was a contract infexistence which gave the whole of the work in tonnec- tita with the Longford for a period of 10 years to one firm. This was said with a view to preventing us carrying out On tender which wasnearlyg3oo less than the one we had refused to accept. We directed the Town Clerk to employ counsel, and we found that we were not infringing the patent which woUld expire the March following, and secondly; the agreement with regard to the erection of these works had ceased to exist. We were not allowf-d to carry on this work until the then Chairman of the Committee had been. removed out of the way. There was no member of Council that had more difficulty in bring- ing his mind to the painful necessity of renloving that gentleman than I had."l had been associated with Mr. Bu- rgess practically all my life in many meters. I had great 'respect for him.personally, and a very high opinion of him, but I found that it wasa question of duty on the -one hand against my personal feelings towards Mr. 'Burgess, and I had no difficulty as to what was the right thing to do, and I assisted with the best of my ability at his removal. (Applause.) What was the result of that? We have got a committee managing Longford Works consisting of a number of gentlemen who have a thoroughly practical knowledge of machinery. (Cheers.) The present committee manage to be successful because' everything works together. While we had this year to carry out tin extra work in connection with theextended portion of the borough which involves an additional 1,000 houses alone, yet the financial results at Longford are over £1,400 better than they were during the pre- ceding year. (Applause.) It is made up in two ways. In the fist place, although the ares to be covered is so much ,larger, the-cost of collection has been considerably less, and in addition the sale of dry manure has been considerably greater, and the net result of the under- takinr in favour of this year over last is a little over £1,400. Well, sir, as I said "just now in regard to the baths, I say in regard to this, if I had done nothing else than takes humble part in helping to free the Council of this borough from the intolerable tyranny of one man, I RM entitled to appeal .to you on that ground. (Loud applause.) Another feature of

I have to give to you an ACCOUNT OF MY STEWARDSHIP during the past three years. I had better begin by tel- ling von how much attention I have paid to my duties. In 1891 I attended 12 Council meetings, 18 meetings of, the Street Improvement Committee. 33 Sanit try Com- mittees, 14 Museum Committees, 14 River Committeett;2 Water Committees, 11 General Purposes Committee, or an actual total of 104 attendances in the year. (Ap- plause) In the following year I attended 15 Council meetings, 13 Street Improvement Committees, 35 Sani- tary Works Committees, 11 Museum Committees, 7 Rivers Committees, 5 Water Committees, 13 General Purposes Committees, and 12 School Attendance Com- mittees. This makes a total of 121 in the second year. (Applause.) In the year which is just concluding I attended 14 Council meetings, 13 Street Improvement Committees, 28 Sanitary Works Committees, 12 Museum Committees,"7 Rivers Committees,ll Water Committees, 11 General PurposesCornmittees,or a total of 129. (Hear, hear.) If I were not practically the, master of my own time, it would be absolutely imoossible, for me to give such attention to your w3rk, and I think you will find there is nothing to be gained in returning Mr. Smith in respect to the attendances alone. (Hear, hear.) When you remember this fact : that Mr. Smith is not his own

master,and necessarily engaged by his employers certain hours in the day, and the further fact that many com- mittees of the Council are of necessit; held during the day time, you will see the absurdity of suggesting that Mr. Smith should take my place in this particular. (flear, hear.) Well, in the next place, I wish to refer brief. y to the success that has followed eight years' agitation in regard to the construction of the

NEW BAUM. (Hear, hear.) It is eight years ago since that question came up first in the Council Chamber. I was absolutely alone,but as good old Abraham Lincoln advised I" kept pegging away "until this question absorbed the public interest to such an extent that what we weie agitating for so many years, this year became an accomplished fact. (Applause.) I was one of those who advocated the new baths on three grounds : First of all on the ground of health and comfort; secondly, on the ground Of teaching youngsters how to swim, and, thirdly, on the ground that I believed it would be a financial success. (Hear. hear.) What are the results ? In the last year of the old baths, from May 25th to October Bth, there were 143 bathers in the first class swimming bath, 996 in the . . . .

second class, and so on making a total of bathers for 11 that period, 10.960, and a receipt of £137 fis. 6d. Now for the same period in the first year of the new bath; this year—there are the following extraordinary results; first class bathers, 11,384—(Ap- plause)—second class, 8,146, ladies, 242, ladies special days 503,and 1332,in the private bath,of a total of 21,6681 bathers—(Loud applause)—making a grand total of bathers of all classes for that period this year of 40,677. With the grand receipt of £530 93. 10d. (Loud applause) It is just four times in number and in am -mint, as in the same period the year before. (Applause.) Now, Mr. Chairman, if I had never done anything or was never likely to do another thing in the interests of the people of Warrington than the connection I have had with the splendid improvement of these baths. I think that I should have earned the gratitude ot the bulk of the people of Warrington on that ground alone. (Ap- plause.) Rut then you know" talk too much. (Laugh- ter). There was another subject which I took up during my three years of office whill should alone be argument in favour of my services to the ward and the town. As you know the STREETS OF WARRINGTON WEAR UNPAVED and unmade, the result being that in times and seasons of bad Wf ather many of those streets which were quits new were almost impassible and people living in them were surrounded constantly with an atmosphere abso- lutely dangerous to health, to say nothing of the incon- venience to people who lived there. (Hear, hear.) There was a great obstacle to cartying on street making. ' Hitherto it was the system of the Corporation to enforce payment for street-making within a short period after the work was done. Therefore I agitated for the system of deferred payments, as that the payments for road-making would be spread over a number of years. This was what removed the obstacle in the way of small property owners who found it difficult to meet the costs of street-making and which removed at one blow the difficulty under which the Paving and Sewerage Ceromit- tee had laboured. After trying twice, with the assist- ance of Councillor Flood, I got the system adopted. (Hear, hear.) And what has been the result? It has been that 1,747 lineal yards of street paving has been done last year while this year 3,579 lineal yards of street- making has been done and the amount received has been double that of the year before. ,(Hear,hear.) Well, be- sides these advantages the added comfort and conveni- ence to those living in these streets is almost incalcul- able. (Hear, hear.) You know that in regard to infectious diseases, particularly in cases of enteric fever, there is nothing more conducive to it than to have badly naved streets and badly sewered streets. (Hear, hear.) I have no hesitation in saying that the grand results of this will follow not only in years to come, but may pos- sibly have saved numbers of valuable lives and it has certainly added materially to the comfort of men and women who live in those streets. (Applause.) Well now, I wish to refer to one other matter and that Is Tint WATERWORKS 'UNDERTAKING. That great undertaking has been acquired since T ad- dressed you three years ago. I was one of tbe commit- tee appointed to .consult with the proprietors of that

undeaking, with regard to it purcliatie-. MU one of thosepeople who believe that gas and water and all matters that are necessary for the czmfort and weil- beiug of the town should be Isupphed by the Cor.

poration et ;be town. (Bear, her underfakiOg • was purch tie you will, and which I think I Irive a right L 276,713 with the „gen, in July MI. for ito expec ,(amause)__l will promise you this, ther , At that it was to be I shall kr.) Well, the great 1 which lir 'OO a determination and I kuo.4 I Duaii be -upporte I repaid in 55 years, but the sin for five years. The result Angfund . was suspended 1 tr., get to know what these prices are. (Applause.) We the I are not going to the back them. (Laughter.) profits altogether obtainer r 16,1 ,heTa sti?jai_ that ___ ... . . . door for .. . ..

We will get Co know through the medium of the Cou.lo'd Chamber itself, so that every, ody may kn)w. right have the coal ownersi to be protected in this way by the corporatior ? My firm occasionally tender 'co the corporation. You will hear about that. (Larighter.) They do not seek to protect us. If they buy I vim going to say a pennyworth of pins, if they make t),m smallest purchase from us under contract, you will see that the price is published broadcast over the whol'o world, and it is not at all an unfrequent thing for a customer to say " Look here, you are not offering to us at the lowest prices. Is not my money as good as 'he C•uporation's ?" We have been supplying to the fJorporation at a less figure and we have to do the sarne with the customer. If I am subject to that,which I e:ontend is perfectly right and perfectly proper, because 'there cannot be too much publication of prices by the. Corporation, the pelple whose money they spend have a right to know why the coalowner is to be protec'.ed. (Applause.) In connec- tion with this, Councillo,.. Flood in February 1892, moved a resolution applying to the gas works business indirectly requiring our Corporation to insert in its contract forms in future, a clause requiring persons who make these contracts to state that they pay tire fair trade wages and employ their men a fair and proper number ot hours during the day. (Applause.) well, gentlemen, teat resolution was carried, but as far asl know, it has not been put into operation yet. That is another thing which we shall have something to say upon when we go ' baek again to the Council chamber, and if you as rate- payers and as workingmen especially, will only streng- then our hands in that direction, we will see that it is carried,or know the reason why it is not. There is one mat- ter coming up this next year in connection with the gas works. When the gas works were purchased 17 years ago, there was a very serious tungle made in regard to the methodef payment. Thesum of money which was agreed upon be be paid forthis undertaking was £158,350.1 should say, first, that this was not paid down in a lump sum, it was paid for by perpetual 4 per cent. annuities,and one clause of the Gas Act,was to the effect that the Corpor- ation should from time to time buy them up and so re- duce their, debt, the same Act requiring .25 years pur- chase. Well, we have paid off in connection with this undertaking since that period no less a sum than £31,765 and on paper we have reduced the debt on account of the purchase fr0rn.1158,850 to -E128,585. /ler° a very awkward fact comes in. Our Town Council did not ob- tain in the Gas Act, compulsory power to repurchase at 25 years. Since then,the taterest bearing power of money has been materially red•dced,and anything which is bring- ing in 4 per t mt. per annum is worth not 25 years purchase but ''29 or 29,i years. Instead of being £31,765 better off by the money we have levied towards the gas works, we are only £12,000 better off. The in- crease of value of the interest as between 25 and 29 years purchase has added an additional burden of £19,000

upon the ratepayers of this town. (" Shame.") Weave going to Parliament next year to obtain compulsory powers to repurchase. Why should the ratepayers have to pay nearly £20,000 more than the price originally agreed upon, through the bungling of somebody. It is

„ none too soon to go to Parliament, as the interest bear- ing the power of money is reducing,and we rnustget com- pulsory power to repurchase for a sum between 25 years and 29 years. (Hear, hear.) If you think that this is a point upon which my friend Mr. Smith is better qualified than myself, and better able to represent your views in the Council Chamber, send him there and let me have a rest. <Laughter.) lam coming to another matter which is of great satisfaction to me, that is the question of the museum and library and the ' TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION DEPARTMENT of the Corporation works. We have in Warrington a splendid library—(applause)—and for many years that library was practically a close corporation. Ualess a cer- tain subscription was paid no bock could be taken out. We had neveranv right to Make it a close corporation, but when we look back upon the names of the gentlemen who had the management years ago, beginning with the very properly respected, but at the same time very an- tiquated gentleman, Mr. Beamont, I am not surprised that it was kept a close corporation. If You remember on this platform I helped the agitation for the freeing of that library, and the results of freeing that institution have been simply marvellous. From the library the last year before the charge was made,we issued 26,000b00k5, this year we have is..ued 47,760. (Applause.) Instead of having 1,044 on the borrower's roll we have 3,118. Instead of having an average of 823 books cut at the one time we have an average of 1,513. (Applause.) When you remember that every rate!) ryer in the town, every ratepayer's wife, and every ratepayer's child can have a book without any cost whatever, I think that you will agree with me, we did very will. We had a newsroom

but there were no newspaliers in it except a few weeklies and magazines. Mr. Flood and myself put our heads together, thinking that if there was a newsroom, there ought to be daily issues as well as weekly issues, and so in May '1892, we got a resolution passed by the Committee, the chairman being Mr. Monks, of whom I may tell you this, he carried a tremendous amount of energy and light into that institution, and I think he should have credit for it. (Applause.) I hope before very long we shall see him where we should like to see him, as a long resident and native of Warrington, and as a man who is respected all over the town, he ought to be made the first citizen of this town. (Applause.) There was a period not many years ago when the vote of one man decided whether Mr. Monks should be Mayor of this borough or not, and that man was the then Alderman Burgess. A number of us met in the Mayor's parlour, and the vote was unani- mous with that exception. In that case, Alderman Bur- gess had an excellent opportunity of healing a difference ot years. I went to Mr. Burgess and implored him to vote for Mr. Monks telling him that in the words of scripture it would be like putting coals of fire upon his enemy's head. The answer he gave us "If I could put a coal pit on his head I weuld do it." (Laughter.) We have a museum in connection with the library—a library

which for its size, stands second to none fn Euglant. to-day—and to the museum, and I have given a large number of valuable specimens. I don't know I ought to say too much about that, but they are a valuable contri- bution to the contents of that museum as they are the eggs and nests of British birds. I don't expect my opponent will now collect bird's eggs and I think in that direction you must give me a " chalk ': in regard to that
ith which

(Laughter.) There-is another Committee w: have been connected, the RIVERS COMMITTEE. In regard to that, I have occupied for two years, the deputy chairmanship. It has been our duty to watch the interests of Warrington in connection with the action of other Corporations as Manchester and Salford, and the Manchester Ship Canal. Unfortunately cur interests and that of the two great Corpsrations I have mentioned are n,,t always identical. The present is a critical time in the history of Warrington. We shall have to watch very closely our interests in the Ship Canal, or these interest 4 may be lost for ever to Warrington. Gentlemen, having an interest in the town, and representing to some extent the industries of the town, having occupied on ths'

this committee the position of deputy criairman it is worth while to pause before making any change in your representation. (Applause.) We have a department for ThCIINICAL INSTRUCTION in Warrington with regard to which our chairman and other members of the committee feel a very great amount of pride. We Are proud of that institution.—First of all because of the important work it is doing in conni ction with the young men and young women of the town. The object of the institute has been to enable the workman to be better qualified in regard to his trade. When I tell you we have in connection with this institution, eleven classes in the preparatory schools, 17 classes in the School of Art, 25 in the School of Science, 17 conruer- cial classes and one in music, you will see that we h (ye a capital training school. From that fact of the enorm- ous work being done in the town in theinstitute,wesh all have soon to find betteraccommodation. One of the most pleasing items in connection with this institution is the fact that this work has been carried out in its entirety withoutcosting a copper to the town, except one occasion which I will explain further on. We have students in the institute numbering 385, and in the continuation schools 146, making 691 students in the schools in con- nection with the institute. The results have been these. At last examination we had 51 per cent, of our candi- dates passed for the science examination, 52 per cent at the art examination and 68 per cent in commercial sub- jects. This is a higher percentage considerably than the average. On the result of the above examinations, the committee have awarded 57 scholarships and 16 en- trance scholarships have been given to boys and kids from elementary and continuation schools making 73 who obtain assistance this year. The Science and Art Department prizes granted to students are one bronze medal, two book prizes valued 203. each, five book prizes valued 103. each, four free studentships valued £3 each, and two free admissions to short courses at South Kensington. The money grant to the institute from the department is estimated at £325, an increase of £25 on the previous year. The Lancashire County Coun- cil, as a result of a competition open to the whole of the county granted one free scholarship of £6O a year fer three years, and five of £lO for one year, which have been won by Warrington students. The expenditure on this institute for the first year was £l,lOO, and for this year £1,700. I told you we have carried on two years without costing the ratepayers of the town a single far- thing, I was slightly incorrect. The as-ociaiion at South Kensington had power to make grants to local institu- tions for purchasing the necessary appliances for carrying on the classes. They only make these grants provided the local authority provides a like sum. The association granted £7O and the Corporation of Warrington gave another £7O. That is the total amount of trinnev on that institution that has come out of the rates of the borough. ' In conclusi in, I have tried as briefly as I could to put before you the great questions at issue in this contest. Do not be misled by anybody,and think it does not mat- ter whom coa seed to the Council Chamber. It is a huge mistake. The Council touches your every day life. (Hear, hear.) Your comfort and your convenience are influenced hy the Town Council. A newspaper very frequently . . . • • id(

_ ravours me with its attentions. (Laughter.) I allude the " Observer." lam quite used to having some- thing said in regard to myself. If lam not mention•d on Saturday I am not asillappy on Sunday as 1

AN EXPLANANION.

Sir,—ln your last issue, I am reported as having applied for the use of "The Assembly Room in the Earlestown Public Hall—for religious purposes during the winter. Will you kindly allow a word of explana- tion 13 At a meeting of the United Committee of repre- sentatives from local churches—it was decided to arrange for—A week of United Prayer Meetings to commence on January 7, 1894 ; a special United Evangelistic Ser- vice on Sunday, January 14, at 8 p.m. ; also to invite the Rev. C. Musgrave Brown, M.A., of Liverpool, to conduct a mission on the three days, January 15, 16,and 17. And the Committee further decided that the ser- vice on January 14, and the Mission to be conducted by Mr. Brown' the Public Hall would be the most suitable building. It was, therefore, as Secretary to the above Committee, and on behalf of the Caurchos represented, that the application was made by yours truly, GEO. DRING. Oct. 10, 1893.

div.head: LONGFORD
div.p: LONGFORD

it the general management, and the place to-day is as different to what it was a few years ago,as the difference between light arid darkness. There is at the head, a man who knows what he is doing arid a man who would not go down on his knees or bow his head submissively, and no man ought to do that, and no man should be so sub- serviant to his employer as to forget his self-respect. (Applause.) Mr. DPAS is a man of undoubted intelli- gence and ability in his profession, and the result of the change is just beginming. If we examine the results we firicl those twelve months of Mr. Deas' office to have been of a remarkable character. The results during the next few years will be even more satisfactory than they have been during the past twelve months. To give hut one simple idea as to how things have been going on there, we have to carry the ashes from the different houses. The old management spent £l.OOO in making a tip, up which the carts could go and deposit this material close to the appliances for it to be destroyed. Before we had the present manager many weeks, he saw what a costly thing this was, costing £lOO a year in extra labour involved in the carting of the stuff to the tip. Ile saw the need of an elevator and he fitted up an anplia,nce of that character and now they take the stuff, &c., and, as the Lancashire man would say, " keck it up," and it is deposited almost into the appliances for its destruc- tion. We have been as you know for many years, called over the coals by the Warrington Rural Sanitary Autho- rity. rhe Rural Sanitary Authority says we made an intolerable nuisance at Longford. lam not going to say whether we did or we did not. If there was a nuisance, that nuisance in regard to this department, at any rate, will cease to exist. For a committee connected with the sanitary work of the borough to be even possibly ac- cused of creating a nuisance is the most illogical thing imaei nahle. The committee is trying to make every!), dy else look after :themselves, while they are possibly sinners themselves ! (Lauchter.) We are not going to he sinners any longer. (Ffear, hear.) I will now refer for a few moments to the GAS UNDERTAKING. This has been in the hands of the Corporation for 1? Tears. Whether we acted wisely or not, I may safely venture to say that the quality of the gas manufactured in these illustrious gasworks is net too good. (Flear,hear, and applause.) One more argument held nut to us was

that when we sot that undertaking we should have pro- fit for the rerartnent of the capital and interest, and that we should have A very handsome amount in a few Fears, as is the case with Manchester and other places, towards the reduction of the rates of the borough. Nothing of the sort has taken place except .some little reduction in the price of gas and a gift of £l,OOO to the Borough Rates. With this ex- ception the gas works undertaking has not brought in a single cooper. I have referred to the remarkably suc- cessful results attained in the water works undertaking, I have merely tb say there is a matter for inquiry somewhere. (Bear, hear.) We are right in the midst of a coal field. We ought to be able to get our coal without sweating the miners, (applause), as cheaply as anybody. When we have got it we ought to be able to make the best of it. One thing with ruard to this un- dertaking I wish to mention. In the first place. I don't believe in having to pass in the Council as we iira,ticaqv hive to do, contracts for 10,000 and 20,000 tons of fuel for the gas works without having a single idea as to the price. (Ap- plause ) lam not going to enter into the question of elements which make up the present differences between the colliers and owners. This is not the object of this meeting, but Ido say this, if there is any truth in the statement ef those who are leading the men, namely, that the prices at which the fuel is purchased he the corporations of this country is in a large measure the cause of the alleged loss on the part of the employer, it is time the prices of these contracts were published (Applause.) We.have asked frequently when the con- tracts have come for confirmation, for the price at which , they have been let, but we have been met with a firm refusal by the members of the committee to give us these figures. They will give them to us if we will inquire privately. We are not going to do the" sneak" business. (Laughter.) We have got to pay for it, and every ratepayer in this building as a ratepayer has a right to know. We are told that it would not be fair to the colliery owners if the prices were declared. (" Shame.") Cciperations represent very largely the workpeople, and they ought to be the very last to lend any assistance directly or indirectly to things which we are all suffering from to-day. (Applause.) If you semt lac back azain-r,n ;tr.. firOpf IleVagi,ber, by, a majority, C.4* ,

ought to be. (Laughter.) Sometimes it is a little too kind, and then it has to pay for it. It is important tl..at you should send to the Council Chamber, men whe Paave no personal interests to serve. That paper claims for Mr. Smith that he has no personal interest to serve. Well, he was approached by a certain section of his party to contest the ward, but he gave a distinct refusal. Be was approached again,and now he has consented. We all of us used to think it was only feminine and fragile per- sons that wereallowed to whiffle about matters of this kind. We expected a man to know his own mind. (Bear, hear, and laughter.) When he said yes he meant yes, and when he said no, he meant no. When it was toned that Mr. Smith takes so long to make up his mind in regard to questions of such great importance says " " one week and on the following week says "yes," we are entitled to ask what is the reason for this change. .1 have my own ideas as to what that reason is, but it is not necessary to detail them to you. If Mr. Smith can do the work of this ward and do it as well as I can or better, tie is entitled to the position I hold at the present moment. The destitution in Warrington at the present time is so terrible ; such a condition of things, I never have seen an 3 thing like in my life before, men by the hundred walking about the streets with nothing to do, and children are at the very verge of starvation, as also are the women, that I think very good reason should be shown before the contest is forced upon any ward in the town, which will involve the spending of a considerable sum of money. (Applause.) I have done a good deal of canvassing during the last fortnight. I have met on all hands with kindness and courtesy, I have been more than gratified at the very handsome things that have been said to me. I have given satis- faction to the majority of the ratepayers of this ward. (Applause.) I have no personal interests to serve. Many years ago, longer than I care to mention, I made up my mind to this, whenever I had the opportunity to devote a portion of my time to the public service I would do so. I belong to the town so far as my interest in its commercial prosperity is concerned. I have sprung from the ranks and I know the difficulty of having very little 'beforehand, and I was many years before I could feel anything like safe. I have done my work without fear or 'favour. (Applause.) If I have con- sidered a man taking a wrong course I have never hesitated to oppose him. Unfortunately for me, the ability to do is net always equal to the inclination. but I do my best. That ability such as it is, is at your dis- posal. I want to see the conditions of life of workmen in this town and the country generally, very much better than they are to day. The present destitution will result M a condition of things in many families, as will never be overcome in the lives of the present fathers and mothers, in regard to anything that is effective, anything that will enable the workman to better himself I shall consider it my duty to help. (Applause.) There is only one thing morel will mention to night. As there is to be a contest we ought to have as substantial a majority in the ward as the majority three years ago. If it is less, one or two things will follow, that I shall feel that I have to some extent lost the confidence of the ward, or I shall feel it necessary if possible to do my work better than in the past. (Laughter.) Very important questions are coming forward in which Warrington will Involve in the spending of money. I shall not be a party to any action which would not justify itself to me. I wish to spend and save your money, as I would spend or save my own. I wish to gain the kindly feeling of those amongst whom I have lived, so that they may sai7 of me, that I tried to leave the world and this town better than I found it. (Loud and prolonged applause.) Mr. JAMRS EVANS moved the following resolution : " The electors of Whitecross Ward assembled in this meeting beg to offer to Councillor Henry Roberts their hearty thanks for the faithful and efficient manner in ' which he has served the interests of the ratepayers dur- ing the last three rears, and further pledge themselves to use every legitimate effort to secure his re-election on the first day of November next by an overwhelming majority." He was sure that after the manner in which Mr. Roberts had stated the business of the Coaneil that they would do their best to return him to the Council. He had great pleasure in proposing the resolution. _ .

Mr. Alma' seconded the resolution and said that he could say that Mr. Roberts had given a very satisfactory account of his stewardship during the past three years. The motion was passed unanimously.. _ . . . . . _

, Councillor ROBERTS in reply thanked the meeting for its unanimous vote and said that the majority for the ward ought to be 250. He thought that majority was easily obtainable. There was a large number of resi- dents in the ward who left politics entirely out of the contest. He was not joking w hen he challenged Mr. Smith to discuss in public, and he challenged him again. He proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman. Councillor FLOOD seconded, arid said he thought that the meeting that night was a happy omen of the success of Mr. Roberts at the forthcoming election, especially seeing that Mr. Monks was chairman of the meeting. , Mr. WILLIAM PIERPOINT who spoke in response to calls I said that he came that night to pay is respects to their candidate Mr, Roberts. He could not speak to any length as he had another engagment that night. He , might say that he took a deep interest in this election, He was delighted to see Mr. Monks in the chair. He was a personal friend of his, although their politics differed slightly in one respect. But they never talked politics. (Laughter.) Mr. Monks was one of the ablest of War- rimlton's sons, and a man of whom Warrington ought to be proud. He had great pleasure in being present at the meeting that night, and if another meeting was held he would be willing to speak at greater length. Councillor BEAmAN also speaking in support of the re- solution, said that Mr. Monk's name was a household name in Warrington,and was synonymous in everything that was good. Though there might be political differ. °aces between them in one respect, they could meet on a common platform on the rest. (Applause.) The v,ite was carried unanimously.

Mr. Monxs replying, said that he need not refer to differences on political lines. (Hear, hear.) He did not hesitate to give expression to his own view and act up- on it. He hoped he would always have courage of his own opinion. (Hear, hear.) He had always met with respect and consideration from his opponents. If he had been of any use that night, it was only carrying out the determination he had made to be as useful to his fellow countrymen as he could. (Applause.) He believed that Mr. Roberts had felt the same impulses, and would give his services to the inhabitants of Warrington. He (Mr. Monks) had been for 40 years politically and socially occupied in Warrington. Of course it was not given to any man to add very many more years to that. He,howe ever, hoped he would be able yet to render good service to the town, although he was not politically identified with either the Conservative or the Liberal party. The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE AND THE LODOPM VOTE.
div.p: THE ELECTORAL FRANCHISE AND THE LODOPM VOTE.

Sir,—The Revising Barrister for the Manchester dis- trict has refused to register the claims of lodgers to be placed on register of voters, where the rental or rating of the tenements in which they resided was in his opinion too low to entitle the lodger to a valid claim. This is Barrister made law, and runs counter to Act of Parlia- ment and common sense. Such ruling has been upset by the Irish Court of Appeal in the case of McCrea v. Barnard, the revising barrister deciding that where the rating of the house where the lodger claimed to be entitled to a vote was only £2 155., and where the lodger paid for unfurnished apartments £l2 a year, was not of sufficient market value to give the lodger a valid legal claim to the franchise. The Irish judges in the Court of Appeal decided against the barrister—they deciding that what the lodger paid, viz., £l2 a year was the market value and what the law required. If this is registration law in Ireland it surely should hold good in England,and the decision of a revising barrister to the contrary is illegal. In middle class and wealthy families in villa- dom and mansions, in each family there may be several sons each having his room or rooms for 7:llich some may be paying and some may not. Some of these sons may be earning money, others may be having an " allow- ance "—be it hew it may they make their claim as lodgers to be placed on the register and the claim is admitted. On the other hand, a working class family I may have sons paying a pound a week to their parents for their accommodation—many do—but if they make a claim for registration it is refused on no ground of insufficient market value of the residence. Where is the justice or common sense of the ease ? The way to the ballot box is blocked by circumlocu- tion. It is a case of bricks versus brains, of money , versus men, but wo nre gaining experience slowly and may get wiser in time and have keener perceptions of common sense and justice. The publichouza, the race

Course, the Established Church, the Primrose League °bona kindred instit..dions, with the Tory workinguiaorou. the I;vay to the ballot box and emanicipation. prelant system of registration and elecLoral franshifah rotan, contrary to eommon sense and justice, arid. was"i the irresponsible and obstructive House of bordsr be swept away or radically changed, as at Prr,L, wealth swamps the constituencies,laoour as far 0 Pt;il ble, is pushed aside, and the poor man is denied scA• to the Ballot Box.—Yours, Gymso,

BOROUGH OF,WARRINGTON. MUNICIPAL ELECTION, 1893. TO THE ELECTORS OF ST. JOHN'S WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN. Having been nominated by a large and influential body of the Liberal party—(and at the special request of numerous Conservatives)—as the Candidate for the vacant seat in the Town Council, I have consented to offer myself for election. I have lived as a boy and man amongst you for over 30 v 4 ars, and am a property owner and a large ratepayer in the ward. My business is in your midst, therefore understand- ing the wants of its people. I am more likely to attend to them, than one who has no personal connection with the ward. lain In favour of all Corporation Contracts being given to Local Manufacturers and Tradesmen, and so encouraging our own Industries. It will be my earnest endeavour to get the ratepayers a better gas at a less cost, as I am of opinion that the quality and price are net Rhat we ought to expect. lam in favour of using all appliances and means to bring about a more healthy sanitary condition of our town, 110‘all ti prevent a repetition of the epidemic we had in the early part of the year. I shall endeavour to keep down the expenditure of the Borough so as to lessen the rates and enable landlords to re- duce rents, and if you do me the honour of electing me as your representative. I shall do all I eats for the general Interests of the town. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, WILLIAM FURNESS. Havdock-street and Lytlagoes Lane, Warrington, October 13th, 1893.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GEN- ERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be holden at the COURT HOUSE, NETHER KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on MONDAY. the 16th day of October next, at Half-past Eleven in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all appeals arising within the Hun- dreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, form- ing the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury tor the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the, 16th day uf October, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will be adjourned to the Castle of Chester, I on THURSDAY, the 19th day of October next, at Eleven 'o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton,- Ecidisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-mentioned I Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. I The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Che: ter, at the opening of the Court on THURSDAY. the 19th day of October next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS. Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester Chester, 25th September, 1893.

THE RAILWAY MYSTERY AT ST. HELENS. INQUEST AND VERDICT. At St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, Mr. Brig- house, county coroner, held an inquest on the body of Thomas Bromilow, aged twenty-seven, a colli.,ry drawer, Thatto Heath, who was found injured on the London and North-Western Rail way,near That to Reath Station, on Saturday morning, and who died in the Providence Hospital a few hours later.—Mrs. Bromilow stated that she and the deceas‘d and their - child, three years old, went to bed at eleven o'clock on Friday night. He was in good health. He had made it up with her brother to get up at five o'clock next morning and go to Sutton Heath for surface coal for themselves. She went to sleep/ and heard no- thing more with about ten minutes to six the following morning she was knocked up by Mr. Poole, the station master, who said her husband WRS injured. When she went to bed she locked the backdoor, and to get out she had to take off the lock, as the key was gone. She and her mother went to the Providence Hospital, and saw her husband in an unconscious and rambling state, and dhi not know what he was saying. She afte,vvaros re- ceived word that he was dead. There was nothing t lead her to think he would do anything to himself. lie was a comfortable,quiet man, and had no mates. They had no click or watch,but she could not say that he had mistaken the time.—Sergeant Strong, in reply to the coroner, said the place where the man was found was in a different direction to Sutton Heath.—Mrs. firomilow, continuing, said deceased's brother lived at Prescot, and that was the direction in which he was found.—Sergt. Strong said it was an nougat thing for anyone to take the line to Prescot.—Mrs. Bromilow said they were not without food, and they had all had some tea and bread arid butter that day. Her brother did not come at five o'clock to go to Sutton Heath, but it was usual for them on a wet morning to go for coal, and on fine mornings to go and catch green linnets. She did not know why her brother did not come unless he had gone for birds. Deceased did not bother himself about food or fire. They had enough to eat.—rhomas Henry Williams,fireman of the St. Helens bank engine, said he was coming through the cutting,when he heard a shout as of a drunken man. ' Bromilow was lying in the six foot way with his jacket across his shoulder, and his head towards Present. His shirt was ruffled up, and his back bare. He said he had beep knocked down,but witness thought he hardlylknew what he was saying.—The Coroner said he had a punc- tured wound between the legs, and an abrasion on the foreheat. It was an extraordinary case.—A juryman suggested that medical evidence should be called,but the Coroner pointed out that Dr. Jackson,who was railed to tha man,could not say how the injuries were inflicted.— The jury returned a verdict that death was due to wounds received, but how such wounds were inflicted there was DO evidence to show.
